edge_412.relationship: Kelly questions Renaissance emancipation and received period boundaries
edge_412.evidence_note: The opening and note 1 contest Burckhardt’s equality claim through women’s historically differentiated positions. edge_644.relationship: Hobsbawm critically values Gramsci’s historical and political analysis

Revision 1.147: the reception continues in How to Change the World (2011), where, as Eagleton reports (LRB, 2011, read), Hobsbawm "thinks that Gramsci is the most original thinker produced by the West since 1917". Eagleton reports this judgment within a paragraph of criticisms (of the book's handling of Althusser, feminism and Trotskyism), not as his own view; the book is unread.

edge_901.relationship: Ecological change as a two-way relation of people and nature, traced through property, markets and ideas of nature (1983–1995); and the field's institutions: ASEH president 1989–93, editor of the Weyerhaeuser Environmental Books 1994–2014 ('acquiring, editing, and writing forewords for all titles'), and in 2013 'the first self-described environmental historian ever to serve as president of the AHA'
edge_901.evidence_note: Cronon’s own in-period statements. Changes in the Land (1983), ch. 1 'The View from Walden', read in full in an unpaginated web transcription (page numbers not verified): 'The replacement of Indians by predominantly European populations in New England was as much an ecological as a cultural revolution'; 'An ecological history begins by assuming a dynamic and changing relationship between environment and culture, one as apt to produce contradictions as continuities. Moreover, it assumes that the interactions of the two are dialectical'; 'The choice is not between two landscapes, one with and one without a human influence; it is between two human ways of living, two ways of belonging to an ecosystem'; 'The pig was not merely a pig but a creature bound among other things to the fence, the dandelion, and a very special definition of property'; a 'world capitalist system' draws people 'into trade and market relations which lie well beyond the boundaries of their local ecosystems'. He sets this against species-transfer accounts 'as Alfred Crosby and William H. McNeill have done', which are 'bound to be incomplete', and against functionalist ecological anthropology, which risks 'a static and ahistorical view'. In 1992 he calls Nature’s Metropolis 'a natural sequel' to that book, which 'described a comparable set of environmental changes that occurred in New England as that region became linked to London’s markets' (Annals of Iowa forum, p. 517). 'The Uses of Environmental History' (1993): the lesson 'When people buy and sell things in a market, they link together ecosystems and encourage change' is 'a central concern of my own work' (p. 8, n. 14, citing Changes in the Land, Nature’s Metropolis and 'Kennecott Journey'); 'The chief moral of my own version of environmental history is the one I tried to embed in the title of my book Changes in the Land. To live as human beings on this planet is to change the world around us' (p. 19); 'the material history of environmental change is simultaneously a spiritual history of human consciousness and a political economic history of human society' (p. 19); 'All environmental knowledge is culturally constructed and historically contingent—including our own' (p. 14), held together with the claim that 'the natural world exists quite apart from what we believe about it' (p. 15). 'Kennecott Journey' (1992, p. 33): 'The special task of environmental historians is to tell stories that carry us back and forth across the boundary between people and nature to reveal just how culturally constructed that boundary is—and how dependent upon natural systems it remains.' 'The Trouble with Wilderness' (1995, author’s reflow p. 1): wilderness is 'quite profoundly a human creation'. A contribution, not a founding: he makes the claim for materialist analysis that tries 'to finesse a full-blown determinism' on behalf of the field ('One important contribution of environmental history', 1993, p. 13), and places the field among the 'new' histories of the 1960s (p. 2). Contested in period: Danbom (1992) reads Nature’s Metropolis for its 'environmental moralism' (p. 503) and as 'a book about evil unleavened by good' (p. 506); Cronon answers 'I see no pure heroes or pure villains in the stories I tell' (p. 522). His 1990 JAH response to Worster is unread. The 2003 afterword (pp. 182–185: property analysis learned from anthropology, economics and legal theory; his own criticism of schematic capitalism and source asymmetry) is a later reading. edge_342 (anthropology → environment) and edge_343 (environment → culture) stay: they record anthropology as a resource and environmental history’s contribution to cultural history; this arrow is his own framework. Period-4 wave 1 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md) (edge_901 revision): CV pp. 2, 14–15 read in full; the AHA's open text of 'Storytelling' read in passages.

edge_2357.relationship: Questions the internalist/externalist division associated with Kuhn’s1968 history-of-science essay, treating the boundary itself as a historical problem.

edge_2527.relationship: Foner credits Thompson’s social history with helping him integrate ideas and social conflict,and uses The Making of the English Working Class to link class formation with political exclusion and the struggle for the vote.

edge_2530.relationship: Foner criticizes the exaggerated elitism and distrust of mass politics in Hofstadter’s accounts of Populism and reform,while crediting their analytical innovations and distinguishing his critical consensus history from celebratory versions.

edge_2531.relationship: Foner questions whether White’s Greater Reconstruction framework homogenizes federal action in the South and West,and argues that its emphasis on defeat and violence gives too little attention to Black political leaders.
edge_2531.evidence_note: Own 2018 review P17–18 distinguishes protecting freedpeople’s rights against southern elites from dispossessing western Native peoples. P12–16/19–22 praises White’s synthesis, economic explanations and breadth. This is a particular argument/coverage criticism with positive appraisal, not proof every national comparison is invalid. Foner’s reported index omissions not independently collated; White’s complete book unread. Richard White differs from Ronald C. White and Chernow reviewed alongside.

edge_2536.relationship: Furet disputes Marx’s account of the Terror as a plebeian way of completing the bourgeois revolution, arguing that its essential transformation was already achieved in1789–1791.

epistemology.label: Historical epistemology
epistemology.description: Here the label denotes the French tradition associated with Bachelard and Canguilhem: histories of scientific concepts, norms, and discontinuities. It informs Foucault through a route distinct from structural linguistics. It is not an umbrella for every historical or sociological account of scientific knowledge. Bachelard’s own preliminary discourse distinguishes normative epistemology from a chronological history and calls its period labels approximate. Canguilhem’s norm/average discussion draws on Halbwachs and human geography; his later preface distinguishes newly encountered works from resources actually used in1943.
epistemology.representative_figures_and_works: French history and philosophy of science; this connection prevents treating Foucault as merely a descendant of structural linguistics. Bachelard, La formation de l’esprit scientifique (1938); Canguilhem, the normal/pathological essay (1943; expanded 1966) and La formation du concept de réflexe (1955).

anthropology.label: Anthropology & ethnography
anthropology.description: Ethnographic observation, comparison, historical reconstruction and interpretation generate different accounts of social life. Exchanges with historians involve particular works and methods; colonial knowledge, research authority and the representation of cultures are contested within and beyond the discipline.
anthropology.representative_figures_and_works: Distinct stages include Tylor and Frazer, Boasian historical particularism, and later interpretive anthropology associated with Geertz. These do not form one continuous theory.

anthropology.scope_note: A selective teaching map of sociocultural anthropology and ethnography, not all anthropology. Evolutionary, historical, functional, structural, interpretive, feminist and critical inquiries overlap without forming a single succession. Chinese research, Māori scholarship and collaborative histories have distinct trajectories. These approaches and rosters neither establish exclusive membership nor turn anthropology into one transferable theory.

economic.label: Economic history
economic.date_label: 1800s roots · Economic History Society founded 1926 · multiple paradigms
economic.description: Competing explanations investigate institutions, prices and incomes, class relations, growth, households, slavery and empire. Serial history and cliometrics use different questions and models. North’s incentives differ from Polanyi’s historically specific market society; Gerschenkron questions repeated industrial paths; de Vries connects household labor and demand; Pomeranz combines regional comparison with global resource relations.
economic.representative_figures_and_works: Nineteenth-century roots include classical political economy and the German historical school (e.g. Schmoller); twentieth-century examples include R. H. Tawney, Eileen Power, and Douglass North. Further approaches include Polanyi, The Great Transformation (1944); Gerschenkron, Economic Backwardness in Historical Perspective (1962 collection); de Vries’s industrious-revolution article (1994); Pomeranz, The Great Divergence (2000). E. A. Wrigley: People, Cities and Wealth (1987); Continuity, Chance and Change (1988). Richard White, Railroaded (2011): corporate finance, public subsidies and political markets; selected author interview passages checked. N. F. R. Crafts and C. K. Harley, “Output Growth and the British Industrial Revolution” (1992), restatement checked through its abstract.

strands.title: Historical economics and disciplinary institutions
strands.focus: Historical specificity and institutional research; formation of a field does not establish one doctrine.
strands.works: Schmoller’s methodological review (1883); Cunningham’s textbook (1882); Ashley and disciplinary institutions

strands.title: British economic and social history
strands.focus: Economic life studied through social relations, belief, households, and women’s work.
strands.works: Tawney, Religion and the Rise of Capitalism; Power, Medieval People; Clark and Pinchbeck on women’s labour

strands.title: French serial and conjunctural history
strands.focus: Simiand and Labrousse investigate different economic movements. Later rereadings distinguish construction of evidence, causal conditions and routine series; uneven crises need not fit one automatic sequence.
strands.works: Esquisse du mouvement des prix et des revenus en France au XVIIIe siècle (1933); La crise de l’économie française à la fin de l’Ancien Régime et au début de la Révolution (1944); “Panoramas de la crise” (1956); Grenier/Lepetit (1989); Simonin (1992)

strands.title: Capitalist development and contested production relations
strands.focus: Coercion, markets, wage labour and the state are related explanatory problems. Dobb’s reply acknowledges uncertainty about one accumulation hypothesis; Sweezy and Takahashi pose different challenges.
strands.works: Studies in the Development of Capitalism (1946); reply to Sweezy in “The Transition from Feudalism to Capitalism” (1950), pp. 157–167; Takahashi (1952); Unwin (1904)

strands.title: Cliometrics and historical measurement
strands.focus: Economic models and quantitative evidence; neither all economic history nor all quantitative history.
strands.works: Fogel, “Economic Growth, Population Theory, and Physiology” (1993); North, “Economic Performance through Time” (1993)

strands.title: Institutions and economic change
strands.focus: Rules, incentives, learning, and historical paths; overlaps with cliometrics without being identical to it.
strands.works: North, Economic Performance through Time

strands.title: Slavery, empire, and unequal development
strands.focus: Different arguments about capitalist development and colonial power; Drescher contests the decline explanation for British slave-trade abolition.
strands.works: Capitalism and Slavery (1944); How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972); Econocide (1977)

strands.title: Market society and nonmarket economic relations
strands.focus: Polanyi distinguishes a market-regulated economy from reciprocity and redistribution; his broad historical claims are arguments to examine, not settled descriptions of every society.
strands.works: The Great Transformation (1944), chapter IV

strands.title: Different paths of later industrialization
strands.focus: Compare technology borrowing, industrial scale and the roles of banks and states; later industrializers need not repeat England’s sequence.
strands.works: Economic Backwardness in Historical Perspective (1962 collection)

strands.title: Household labor, demand and industrious change
strands.focus: Changes in household resource allocation can increase market labor and demand together. Household members’ interests differ, and the proposed pattern is not universal.
strands.works: “The Industrial Revolution and the Industrious Revolution” (1994)

strands.title: Regional comparison and global divergence
strands.focus: Pomeranz compares developed regions within Eurasia and connects divergence with coal and overseas resources, avoiding an undifferentiated Europe-versus-Asia contrast.
strands.works: The Great Divergence (2000)

strands.title: Material life, markets and capitalism
strands.focus: Braudel distinguishes overlapping economic activities and geographically centered world-economies. His disagreement with Weber and selective Wallerstein dialogue are attributed arguments, not a settled universal history.
strands.works: Afterthoughts on Material Civilization and Capitalism (1977)

strands.title: Market norms and popular action
strands.focus: Thompson asks how customary expectations authorize or constrain protest and exchange; Mintz supplies a named anthropological resource. This is a situated inquiry into English crowds, not a universal premarket economy.
strands.works: “The Moral Economy of the English Crowd” (1971)

strands.title: Agrarian change and documentary comparability
strands.focus: Tawney distinguishes regional and temporal patterns, tenant and landlord activity, legal forms and economic pressures. His introduction treats incomplete statistics and incompatible records as problems of inference.
strands.works: The Agrarian Problem in the Sixteenth Century (1912), introduction

strands.title: Women’s work, household forms and economic change
strands.focus: Clark and Pinchbeck distinguish home production from wages, while differing over the timing and consequences of economic change. Their acknowledgments make research guidance and shared materials part of this scholarship.
strands.works: Working Life of Women (1919); Women Workers (1930)

strands.title: Domestic service as an economic question
strands.focus: Salmon connects household employment with industrial specialization and challenges its reduction to a private complaint. Her historical model and proposed remedies are arguments to assess, not a universal account of women’s experience.
strands.works: Domestic Service (1897), chapters I–II; Progress in the Household (1906), Apologia

strands.title: Brazilian income flows and structural criticism
strands.focus: Furtado’s coffee-crisis argument connects demand and historical change; Novais asks how wage labour and capitalism’s formation explain the transformation. Their exchange keeps macroeconomic analysis open to historical criticism.
strands.works: Furtado (1959/2005), XXXI–XXXII opening; Novais (1961)

strands.title: Managerial coordination and the scale of activity
strands.focus: Chandler’s selected opening links new energy, transport and communication capacities to the conditions for administrative coordination. Earlier growth and specialization could remain compatible with owner-managed firms and market exchange.
strands.works: The Visible Hand (1977), Part I and chapter1 opening

strands.title: Artisans and uneven industrialization in India
strands.focus: Roy examines five crafts rather than treating textile decline as universal. His introduction distinguishes family work, wage labour, markets and organizational change, while acknowledging that adaptation did not yield development comparable to Europe or Japan.
strands.works: Traditional Industry in the Economy of Colonial India (1999), introduction

strands.title: Firms, inventions and forms of work
strands.focus: Compare Chandler’s American enterprise scale, Mokyr’s British technological change and Roy’s Indian artisanal reorganization. These explanations concern different units and periods; none supplies a universal sequence from household to large factory.
strands.works: Chandler (1977); Mokyr (1999); Roy (1999), selected primary passages

strands.title: Railroads and the meaning of social saving
strands.focus: McClelland contests identifying measured transport savings with the railroad’s entire contribution to growth. His notes question the relation between observed freight prices and marginal costs under altered traffic and competition.
strands.works: Railroads and American Economic Growth (1964); McClelland (1968), opening and notes

strands.title: Slavery productivity and a contested inference
strands.focus: Fogel and Engerman’s opening specifies a total-factor-productivity index. David and Temin argue that national-price aggregation across differing crop mixes need not rank technical efficiency: climate, prices and risk complicate the inference.
strands.works: Fogel/Engerman (1977), opening; David/Temin (1979),213–214

strands.title: Household production and disputed divergence
strands.focus: Pomeranz challenges Huang’s involution thesis and compares household labor with industrious change. Huang’s 2002 review argues that output growth can conceal diminishing returns to work; Pomeranz’s reply opening rejects one necessary path to development.
strands.works: Pomeranz (2000),17; Huang and Pomeranz (2002), selected retrospective passages; Huang’s rejoinder and Pomeranz’s response (2003)

strands.title: Coal, constraints and competing explanations
strands.focus: Pomeranz links accessible energy and colonial resources to relief of land constraints. Huang questions whether coal availability explains divergence or industrial demand explains coal development. The exchange leaves causal weights open to examination.

strands.title: Wealth and the measurement of goods
strands.focus: Weatherill acknowledges Shammas’s challenge: ownership patterns associated with occupation or towns may reflect wealth. Their different data constructions ask different questions.
strands.works: Weatherill (1996), xviii–xix and notes 17, 20

strands.title: Agrarian labour and recorded categories
strands.focus: Kumar’s southern Indian inquiry combines documentary interpretation with quantitative reconstruction. Her stated caste/occupation assumptions must remain visible when discussing estimates.
strands.works: Land and Caste in South India (1965), opening extracts I,IV,X

strands.title: Population and the character of industrial growth
strands.focus: Wrigley investigates population change and the contingent character of industrial growth. This bounded summary follows the Economic History Society account and the publisher excerpts of Continuity, Chance and Change (1988, pp. 1–8) and Energy and the English Industrial Revolution (2010, pp. 1–6, 9–11); People, Cities and Wealth (1987) is unread.

economic.scope_note: Distinguish the relevant historians, evidence, and mechanisms before claiming an influence. A subject shared with Annales or Marxism is not itself an explanation. Institutional approaches are not interchangeable, and consumption does not replace production. Household interests can conflict. Gerschenkron’s European comparison and Pomeranz’s Eurasian argument have distinct scales; neither is a universal development law. Furtado’s demand analysis and Novais’s structural criticism offer a Brazilian exchange, with primary-edition and numerical verification limits retained.

military.label: Military history
military.date_label: Earlier roots · Howard 1961 · Keegan 1976 · multiple paradigms
military.description: Studies campaigns and combat alongside institutions, societies, maritime power, gender and remembrance. Ancient historians such as Thucydides and Polybius already wrote about testing reports of battle, terrain and military experience; they are precursors of the genre, not its founders. From about 1900 the field was practised in archive-based campaign and army histories, university lectureships and chairs (Oxford 1905 and 1909), official histories of the world wars and an American society (1933) and journal (1937; renamed Military Affairs in 1941); much of this work was written by or for officers. Howard’s contextual reconstruction, Keegan’s critical study of battle and debates over military revolutions supply different methods and explanations. Source access, narrative framing and geographic scope shape their claims.
military.representative_figures_and_works: Ancient precursors include Thucydides and Polybius on testing reports, terrain and experience; modern roots include Clausewitz, On War (1832), and Hans Delbrück; from c. 1900, Charles Oman and J. W. Fortescue wrote archive-based campaign and army history, Grundy and Kromayer surveyed ancient battlefields, and general-staff and cabinet historical sections wrote official histories of the world wars (Edmonds from 1922; the US Army’s World War II series, such as Matloff and Snell, 1953); later examples: Michael Howard, John Keegan, and Joanna Bourke.

military.scope_note: A research field with overlapping objects, not one school or a progression that supersedes campaign history. Delbrück, campaign and army historians, official historians and strategic writers supply distinct resources; military historians also reinterpret and criticize them. Keegan’s restricted battle definition leaves much colonial and guerrilla experience outside its frame. European military-revolution debates extend to overseas encounters without representing the whole world’s military historiography. Bourke, Winter and Nell retain distinct questions about bodies, mourning and recognition. Scholarly collaboration, library work, editing and archival limits are part of the field’s production. Ancient writers who narrated and judged wars (Thucydides, Polybius, Arrian) are selected precursors. The selected ancient passages document statements about testimony, terrain and experience. Separately checked modern passages discuss these authors; Kromayer explicitly engages Polybius’ criticism of Ephorus. These examples do not establish continuous transmission. Clausewitz ranked ancient military history the least useful while allowing instructive exceptions. Official and semi-official histories were written from privileged records, read in proof by participants or framed by sponsoring institutions; Liddell Hart criticised them in the period. Karsten (1984), describing the ‘new’ military history, concedes that ‘some scholars explored such questions in the past’. The selection before 1960 concentrates on British, American and German scholarship; other historiographies of war are not surveyed here.

strands.title: Campaign reconstruction and documentary limits
strands.focus: Howard, Tuchman and Wedgwood connect decisions and circumstances through different narrative practices. Source access and explanatory selection remain objects of criticism.
strands.works: The Franco-Prussian War (1961); The Guns of August (1962); The Thirty Years War (1938)

strands.title: Combat experience and critical testimony
strands.focus: Keegan joins questions about bodies and behavior to criticism of memoirs, rhetoric and physical possibility. His selected battle frame does not represent all forms of war.
strands.works: The Face of Battle (1976), available excerpt

strands.title: War studies, research and teaching
strands.focus: Howard became lecturer in military studies at King’s in 1953; a new War Studies programme was approved in 1955. His King’s work combines historical study with wider social, ethical and political inquiry. Earlier work and institutional support included Laughton’s naval history, Maurice’s chair of military studies (1927; the department closed in 1948), and C. K. Webster and Hancock, whose official-history work had drawn them to war as a field. Morgan-Owen and Finch (2022) call the story of Howard rescuing the subject from an academic wilderness one he ‘consciously cultivated’. Library access, publishing and translation collaboration form part of the research setting.
strands.works: The Franco-Prussian War (1961); War in European History (1976)

strands.title: Naval history within wider explanation
strands.focus: Sea power and military/naval coordination widen a land-centered account. Mahan and Corbett state different purposes from a simple naval chronicle.
strands.works: Mahan (1890), preface; Corbett (1911), introduction

strands.title: Military revolutions: causes and chronology
strands.focus: Roberts, Parker, Rogers, Black and Lynn debate timing, mechanisms and evidence. Their accounts do not form one settled technological explanation.
strands.works: The Military Revolution Debate (1995), introduction

strands.title: Finance, bargaining and geographic scope
strands.focus: Fiscal bargaining and overseas comparisons complicate a universal route from weapons to centralized power. The selected debate remains weighted toward European questions.
strands.works: The Military Revolution Debate (1995), introduction

strands.title: Bodies, injury and masculinity
strands.focus: Bourke examines men’s bodies and wartime masculinity. This question differs from strategic success or adding women to a roster.
strands.works: Dismembering the Male (1996)

strands.title: Remembrance, mourning and recognition
strands.focus: Winter examines forms of mourning; Nell recovers Black military service from patriotic exclusion. These different projects broaden whose war is remembered.
strands.works: Sites of Memory, Sites of Mourning (1995); The Colored Patriots (1855)

strands.title: Cultural explanations and their critics
strands.focus: Keegan’s later account and Bassford’s opposition distinguish cultural interpretation from the earlier reconstruction of combat. Political purpose and culture need not be mutually exclusive.
strands.works: A History of Warfare (1993), mediated; Bassford (1994)

strands.title: Recruitment as labor and household strategy
strands.focus: Lucassen and Zürcher compare state recruitment options with recruits’ and households’ responses. Pay and freedom vary independently; different systems coexist. Their explicit use of Tilly connects fiscal capacity to recruitment and resistance.
strands.works: “Conscription as Military Labour” (1998), 405–419

strands.title: Official and semi-official history and its critics
strands.focus: General-staff and cabinet historical sections wrote large histories of the world wars from privileged records. Edmonds’s British volumes (from 1922) were ‘based on the British official records’, written partly for ‘students at military schools’ and read in proof by officers who took part. Morison’s naval history was commissioned with full records access yet declared ‘in no sense an official history’ (1947). In the US Army’s series, Matloff and Snell, formerly instructors in history and English respectively and both wartime servicemen, joined the project in 1946; their volume’s foreword, by the Chief of Military History, asked readers to see its controversies as differences ‘among comrades in arms’ (1953), and its preface credits Helen McShane Bailey’s knowledge of the War Department’s records and Evelyn Cooper’s statistics. Liddell Hart attacked documentary and ‘camouflaged’ history (1930, 1944). During and after the Second World War official commissions drew academic historians to war (Hancock and Gowing from 1941, Webster and Frankland from 1950, Howard from 1959), under closure rules and secrecy. Later studies of the genre are unread here, and the German and French official histories are known only from period mentions.
strands.works: Edmonds, Military Operations, France and Belgium, 1914, vol. I (1922), preface; Liddell Hart, The Real War (1930), preface, and Why Don’t We Learn from History? (1944); Morison, Operations in North African Waters (1947), foreword and introduction; Matloff and Snell, Strategic Planning for Coalition Warfare, 1941–1942 (1953), foreword and preface; Hancock and Gowing, British War Economy (1949); Howard, Grand Strategy, vol. IV (1972)

strands.title: Campaign and army history as scholarship, c. 1898–1950
strands.focus: Oman’s art-of-war volume (1898) and Peninsular War (1902) worked from chronicles, Record Office papers and passages omitted from printed dispatches, treated veterans’ memoirs with caution and walked battlefields. Fortescue, a civilian, wrote the army’s history as political as well as military history (1899) and distrusted regimental histories; his 1914 definition held that ‘below a certain stage of civilisation, there can be no military history’, a boundary that bears on the field’s geographic scope. Parker’s preface (1928) proposes an institutional history of the Roman legions’ organisation, recruitment and service; the abbreviation list shows extensive inscription corpora, and the body is unread. Kromayer and Veith’s preface (1928) adds strategy and tactics to the antiquarian study of ancient armies and excludes the Orient, Carthage, Gauls and Germans. Howard (1961, as reported by Kitchen and Mitchell and by Strachan) later named regimental ‘nursery history’ and the historian’s duty to examine its ‘myth’.
strands.works: Oman, A History of the Art of War: The Middle Ages (1898) and A History of the Peninsular War, vol. I (1902), prefaces; Fortescue, A History of the British Army, vols. I–II (1899), preface, and Military History (1914); Parker, The Roman Legions (1928); Kromayer and Veith, Heerwesen und Kriegführung der Griechen und Römer (1928); Howard, ‘The Use and Abuse of Military History’ (1961 lecture; 1962)

strands.title: Chairs, journals and the soldier-scholar before 1960
strands.focus: In the British institutions examined here, university teaching developed alongside officer education. Oxford made military history a special subject after the South African War, created a lectureship in 1905 and a chair in 1909, whose first holder, Spenser Wilkinson, called military history ‘the effort to understand war’; the chair, vacant from 1939, went to Cyril Falls in 1946 rather than Liddell Hart. Trinity College, Cambridge, appointed Fortescue its first lecturer in military history in 1913. At King’s College London Frederick Maurice held a chair of military studies from 1927; the department closed in 1948. In the United States the American Military History Foundation was incorporated in 1933 after discussions among ‘military and civilian archival personnel’; its journal (1937) became Military Affairs in 1941 and nearly collapsed in 1957. Strachan (2002) calls Liddell Hart and Falls ‘in many ways more a journalist than an academic’ and writes that before Howard’s appointment almost nobody who studied the history of war had not experienced it.
strands.works: Wilkinson, The University and the Study of War (1909); Fortescue, Military History (1914), lecture I; Maurice, ‘On the Uses of the Study of War’ (1927), as quoted by Morgan-Owen and Finch; Society for Military History chronology (1933–69 entries)

strands.title: War, state and society before the ‘new military history’
strands.focus: Wilkinson’s inaugural lecture (1909) held that ‘as the State is, so will its army be’ and that in war ‘the architectonic art is policy or politics, not strategy or generalship’. Maurice (1927, as quoted by Morgan-Owen and Finch) counted statecraft, economics, raw materials, science, industry and civilian morale as of ‘prime importance’ to the study of war. Hancock, editing the civil official histories, treated the armed forces as ‘no more than the cutting edge of the nation at war’ (as quoted by the same authors). Roberts (1955) proposed tactical change with wider institutional effects. Quincy Wright’s foreword (1942) describes a study of war begun at the University of Chicago in 1926 that involved ‘over fifty studies by research assistants and members of the faculty’; only the foreword is read. Karsten (1984) calls such questions the ‘new’ military history while conceding that ‘some scholars explored such questions in the past’. Hintze, Vagts, Ritter and Ropp are not yet read for this entry.
strands.works: Wilkinson (1909); Maurice, inaugural lecture (1927); Wright, A Study of War (1942), foreword; Hancock and Gowing, British War Economy (1949); Roberts, ‘The Military Revolution, 1560–1660’ (1955 lecture); Karsten (1984), opening

strands.title: Ancient historians on testimony, terrain and experience
strands.focus: Thucydides tests eyewitness accounts against one another and says Spartan secrecy and bragging prevent accurate numbers at Mantinea. Polybius requires the study of documents, the survey of places and political experience, holds that no one without experience of war can write well about it, and judges Ephorus’ land battles by the ground; his polemic is also self-promotion. Arrian prefers Ptolemy and Aristobulus because they served on the campaign. Grundy (1911) calls Thucydides’ narrative ‘in the main a military history’ subordinated to political teaching, and Kromayer (1903) adopts and qualifies Polybius’ criticism of Ephorus. Delbrück (1913, p. 16) asks: ‘Ought we to believe what Caesar informs us of concerning the gigantic armies of the Gauls, whose conquest is his glory, since we have now seen that neither Napoleon nor Frederick in this respect is to be trusted?’; Caesar’s text itself was not read. Herodotus and Xenophon appear only through modern critics: Delbrück (1913) notes that Herodotus wrote ‘forty or fifty years after the events’, Grundy (1901) that in military matters he ‘seems to have possessed little, if any, special knowledge’, and Kromayer (1903, p. 93) finds Xenophon’s account of Mantinea one-sided. These writers are precursors of a genre, not a single origin of the field.

continuation.basis: The field is older and broader than these selected works; ancient precursors are not its beginning, and no researched universal interval is proposed.

chronology.interpretation: Use dated works with an explicit selective scope. Thucydides, Polybius and Arrian are context: precursors of the genre, placed only by century, not a lineage or the field’s first years. Oman, Fortescue, Delbrück, Grundy and Kromayer (1898–1903) are a selected cluster of modern scholarly work, not a foundation date; Kromayer’s 1900 expedition is context for his 1903 volume. Official and semi-official histories (Edmonds 1922, Morison 1947, Matloff and Snell 1953) and the American society and journal (1933, 1937) are selected later events, not the beginnings of official or American military history. Howard 1961 and Keegan 1976 are contributions to an older field, not its first and last years. Later memoir dates are evidence dates, not new personal interventions by Howard.
retain: Multiple paradigms, colonial/guerrilla limits of Keegan's frame, and collaboration/editorial labour.
Ancient precursors are not a continuous lineage; the modern selection concentrates on British, American and German scholarship.
unresolved: If phase bars are useful, define their subject and geography; do not construct a universal beginning from the oldest source in this selection.
Composition dates of the ancient works were not checked; they are placed by century only. Caesar, Herodotus and Xenophon are discussed only through modern critics and are not dated here.

political.label: Political history
political.description: Examines institutions, diplomacy and struggles over power through different methods. Namier reconstructs parliamentary connections; Benson studies voters; Tilly investigates collective claims; Hunt joins political symbols and social identities. Hill, Dorothy Thompson and Flexner examine radical and rights politics, while Guha and Cooper investigate insurgency and labor under colonial rule. These approaches overlap without replacing all earlier political history.
political.representative_figures_and_works: Ranke is one major nineteenth-century root. Later examples: Lewis Namier, Charles Tilly, and Lynn Hunt’s Politics, Culture, and Class (1984). Further contexts: Namier (1929), Flexner (1959), William Appleman Williams (1959), Hill (1972), Guha (1983), Tilly (1986) and Cooper (1996).

political.scope_note: Diplomatic, institutional, social, and cultural political histories persist and interact; the field did not disappear with the rise of social history. Distinguish institutional elites, electoral categories, popular organization and colonial subjects. Cultural political history can retain social and quantitative evidence; attention to popular action does not make all movements democratic. Regional examples are selective, not a globally complete political canon.

strands.title: Collective claims and governing work
strands.focus: Tilly connects performances and repertoires with state/economic change; Cooper asks how colonial labor categories govern social relations. Their regional units and explanations differ.
strands.works: The Contentious French (1986); Decolonization and African Society (1996)

strands.title: Political rhetoric, symbols and social identities
strands.focus: Hunt uses Geertz in an analysis of revolutionary authority and joins symbolic practices with the sociology of political actors.
strands.works: Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution (1984)

strands.title: Diplomacy, conflict and expansion
strands.focus: Narrative accounts of political choices differ from Williams’s interpretation of ideology, political economy and American expansion; diplomatic history contains disagreement.
strands.works: The Guns of August (1962); The King’s Peace and The King’s War; The Tragedy of American Diplomacy (1959)

strands.title: Radical milieus, hostile sources and disputed labels
strands.focus: Davis questions inherited Ranter accounts; Thompson defends a historical milieu; Scott stresses anachronism and Smith disputes both sides’ handling of evidence and theology. These are different positions, not an adjudicated consensus.
strands.works: The World Turned Upside Down (1972); “On the Rant” and correspondence (1987)

strands.title: Local government, record production and representation
strands.focus: Cam’s inquiry connects the making of records, local courts and parliamentary representation. Documentary criticism and inferences about ordinary lives remain distinct tasks.
strands.works: Cam, Studies in the Hundred Rolls (1921), Liberties and Communities (1944), “Stubbs Seventy Years after” (1948)

strands.title: Narrative, motives and contemporary uncertainty
strands.focus: Wedgwood reconstructs decisions without giving actors knowledge of their outcome. Woolrych also asks what this approach leaves unexplained about allegiance and regional differences.
strands.works: The King’s Peace (1955); The King’s War (1958), prefaces discussed by Woolrych (1998)

strands.title: Narrative synthesis and specialist collaboration
strands.focus: Tuchman’s account of producing A Distant Mirror identifies research, medieval advice and editing. These contributions support a synthesis whose event selection and explanatory claims remain open to criticism.
strands.works: A Distant Mirror (1978), acknowledgments and foreword

strands.title: Political ideas in different social situations
strands.focus: Wood questions applying Namier’s skepticism about ideas to revolutionary America. His reading of Bailyn connects changing beliefs with social circumstances and unintended outcomes; it does not make all political action a deliberate pursuit of abstract principles.
strands.works: Namier, “Human Nature in Politics” (1955/2000); Wood, “Rhetoric and Reality” (1966/1968), 69–78

strands.title: Press freedom and institutional dependence
strands.focus: Goldman traces how municipal protection, financing and censorship shaped political printing. Public controversy emerged through conflicts among editors and authorities, rather than automatically following a declaration of press freedom.
strands.works: “Libertad de imprenta” (2000), 10–15

strands.title: Public spaces and competing explanations
strands.focus: Goldman uses a plural account of public spaces. Sábato asks whether the collection’s cultural emphasis loses explanatory specificity and overlooks republican currents or differences among cases, while recognizing its comparative value.
strands.works: Los espacios públicos en Iberoamérica (1998); Goldman and Sábato (2000)

strands.title: The new political history of Britain, 1993–2011
strands.focus: After the Social History round on Stedman Jones (1992–93), British political history took the linguistic turn and argued with it. Vernon's Politics and the People (1993) held that between the Reform Acts 'the official political subject was redefined in the image of print' and the public sphere narrowed (p. 107, as quoted by Tilly); his Re-reading the Constitution (1996) gathered Epstein, Wahrman, Joyce, Antony Taylor and Anna Clark under 'new narratives'. Vernon credited Epstein's late-1980s articles, subsequently collected in Radical Expression (1994), as inspirational 'for those like myself who followed into the field' of 'the new cultural history of British politics' (2004). Lawrence and Taylor's Party, State and Society (1997) set out to 'examine critically "electoral sociology"' (as quoted by LoPatin), and Lawrence's Speaking for the People (1998) questioned 'the rise of class politics' and 'the triumph of party' for the politics of place and gender; Vernon found it 'ambitious, but ultimately flawed' (1999) and Lawrence answered, in a response posted in 2010, that 'realist' and 'constructivist' approaches must be combined. Electing Our Masters (2009) followed the hustings and the platform; in 2011 Lawrence argued for a 'conservative' rather than 'liberal' modernity. Positions within one field, not a school; the debate entry languages_of_class holds the exchanges.
strands.works: Vernon, Politics and the People (1993), ed., Re-reading the Constitution (1996); Epstein, Radical Expression (1994); Lawrence and Taylor, eds, Party, State and Society (1997); Lawrence, Speaking for the People (1998), Electing Our Masters (2009), 'Paternalism, Class, and the British Path to Modernity' (2011); Vernon's review and Lawrence's response (Reviews in History, 1999/2010)

biography.label: Biography / life writing
biography.date_label: Ancient roots · Strachey 1918 · Davis 1995 · crosses fields
biography.description: Uses individual and collective lives to ask historical questions about character, social relations, power and experience. Documentary reconstruction, psychoanalytic interpretation, contextual comparison and relational trajectories pose different problems. Authors, subjects, editors and collaborators shape the surviving account.
biography.representative_figures_and_works: Ancient roots; Carlyle’s On Heroes (1841) is one nineteenth-century strand, not its sole foundation. Strachey (1918); Erikson (1958); Davis (1995).

representative_people.context: The opening Heroes lecture gives creative individuals and practical belief a large explanatory role. This is one nineteenth-century strand, not biography’s origin or all Carlyle’s historical writing.
representative_people.works: On Heroes (1841), Lecture I opening (5 May 1840)

representative_people.context: Selects compact portraits using French eloges models and existing biographies. Woolf later praises one royal biography while criticizing another; neither authorial impartiality nor a uniform critical verdict is assumed.
representative_people.works: Eminent Victorians (1918), preface; Queen Victoria and Elizabeth and Essex, evaluated by Woolf (1939)

representative_people.context: His 1970 retrospective connects his Luther interpretation with individual crisis and social transformation. The 1958 book has not been independently read; its original metadata remains separate.
representative_people.works: Young Man Luther (1958); “Autobiographic Notes on the Identity Crisis” (1970), especially p. 750

representative_people.context: Compares Glikl, Marie de l’Incarnation and Merian without making them one universal female trajectory. An explicitly imagined prologue tests her categories; stories, religious difference, colonial power and textual mediation shape interpretation.
representative_people.works: Women on the Margins (1995), prologue, selected Glikl opening, conclusion and acknowledgments

representative_people.context: Revises her assessment of Strafford in light of documents and scholarship; sympathy for subjects remains open to criticism.
representative_people.works: Strafford (1935); William the Silent (1944); Thomas Wentworth, First Earl of Strafford, 1593–1641: A Revaluation (1961)

representative_people.context: Collective lives form an argument against racist historical exclusion.
representative_people.works: The Black Man (1863)

representative_people.context: Uses a female sovereign to examine gender and power in a society restricting women’s political participation; a contemporary reviewer challenges parts of the causal argument.
representative_people.works: Queen Victoria: Gender and Power (1990)

representative_people.context: Questions how convincingly Dorothy Thompson connects a female monarch with changes in women’s rights and republicanism; this is a particular review, not a neutral verdict on the whole book.
representative_people.works: “The Ruling Exception” (1990), review of Queen Victoria: Gender and Power

representative_people.context: Connects Mann’s life with a longer history of labour and radical politics. Collaborative preparation and the unfinished continuation matter; Murphy disputes aspects of her interpretive framing.
representative_people.works: Tom Mann and His Times, vol. 1 (1956); further fragments edited by E. P. Thompson, Our History 26–27 (1962)

representative_people.context: Offers a contemporary criticism of Torr’s framing of Mann, drawing on personal acquaintance and stressing moral/religious development; his alternative remains an attributed interpretation.
representative_people.works: “Tom Mann: ‘Courageous man of vision’” (1956 review)

representative_people.context: Uses reconstructed individual lives to teach social and economic relations, explicitly associating different people with different source genres.
representative_people.works: Medieval People (1924), author’s preface

representative_people.context: Eileen acknowledges her indexing of Medieval People. This particular editorial contribution is distinct from authorship of its historical sketches.
representative_people.works: Index to Medieval People (1924), acknowledged in the author’s preface

representative_people.context: Her memoir of Maitland interprets a historian’s scholarship and methods; this is distinct from her medieval institutional research.
representative_people.works: Memoir prefacing Selected Historical Essays of F. W. Maitland (1957)

representative_people.context: Admires Wedgwood’s mature biography while questioning occasional early eulogy and limits of biographical scale.
representative_people.works: “Cicely Veronica Wedgwood, 1910–1997” (1998), especially pp. 523–525

representative_people.context: Uses Enguerrand de Coucy as a vehicle through fourteenth-century events. The foreword explains the selection; Stone questions how well the shadowy protagonist serves biographical understanding.
representative_people.works: A Distant Mirror (1978), foreword; Stone review (1978)

representative_people.context: Mediates the 1877 commission for Delbrück to complete Pertz’s Gneisenau biography, in his retrospective account.
representative_people.works: Gneisenau biography commission (1877), recalled in Delbrück’s 1900 preface

representative_people.context: His unfinished Gneisenau biography supplies the project Delbrück continues; archival biography becomes a route into wider critical war history.
representative_people.works: Gneisenau biography, completed by Delbrück after the 1877 commission

representative_people.context: Uses minor acts and a portrait analogy to explain a life’s selective treatment of character. One ancient practice, not the origin or entirety of biography.
representative_people.works: Alexander, opening paragraph; archive translation credited to Dryden

representative_people.context: Argues that private particulars can make many lives instructive, while proximity and friendship can both supply and distort information. His moral premise remains situated.
representative_people.works: The Rambler 60 (1750)

representative_people.context: Interweaves letters, recollected conversations and narrative, explicitly adapting Mason’s example. Claims candid portrayal rather than pure praise; actual completeness is not established by that claim.
representative_people.works: Life of Johnson (1791), opening selection in Osgood abridgment (1917)

representative_people.context: Examines verifiable evidence, invention and changing biographical conventions. Differentiates Strachey’s books and asks why failures and humble lives should be excluded; her restricted English canon is not universalized.
representative_people.works: “The Art of Biography” (1939)

representative_people.context: Questions retrospectively unified life stories and examines trajectories across changing social fields. Institutional naming and the interview situation help produce the unity being narrated; this does not rule out every life history.
representative_people.works: “L’illusion biographique” (1986)

representative_people.context: Distinguishes modal, contextual, extreme-case and dialogic uses of lives. Accepts Bourdieu’s warning while emphasizing bounded choices within conflicting norms and questioning assumed group cohesion.
representative_people.works: “Les usages de la biographie” (1989), translated by Olivier Christin

representative_people.context: Levi uses his contextual presentation of the glazier Ménétra to discuss how context makes a life intelligible; Levi also questions treating context as static.
representative_people.works: Editor, Journal de ma vie: Jacques-Louis Ménétra (1982), discussed by Levi

representative_people.context: Levi cites reconstruction of Diderot’s youth to examine contextual comparison where direct documentation is missing. This is mediated methodological reception, not independent verification of the biography.
representative_people.works: Jeunesse de Diderot (1939), p. 16, cited by Levi (1989)

representative_people.context: Publishes Glikl’s Yiddish text, enabling later editions; the editorial history here follows Davis, not a new manuscript collation.
representative_people.works: Yiddish edition of Glikl’s memoirs (1896), discussed by Davis

representative_people.context: Her German translation preserves stories and moral reflection. Davis contrasts it with later abridgment; Pappenheim’s imagined reaction remains conjectural. She appears here as translator, not merely the clinical subject Anna O.
representative_people.works: German translation of Glikl’s memoirs (1910), discussed by Davis

representative_people.context: His translation removes tales and moral commentary and changes divisions, as Davis critically assesses it. The original translation has not been collated.
representative_people.works: German translation of Glikl’s memoirs (1913), discussed by Davis

representative_people.context: Davis identifies their jointly taught 1971 course as the setting in which she first encountered the three subjects. Teaching supplies a concrete research context.
representative_people.works: With Davis, Society and the Sexes in Early Modern Europe and America (1971 course), acknowledged in Women on the Margins

representative_people.context: Davis credits her with suggesting Glikl’s memoirs and dedicates the book to her and Certeau. Source discovery and intellectual companionship have a named role.
representative_people.works: Source suggestion and intellectual contribution acknowledged in Women on the Margins (1995)

representative_people.context: Davis credits Russian translation, research companionship and editorial insistence on clarity. These particular contributions do not imply authorship of the historical interpretations.
representative_people.works: Translation and editorial assistance acknowledged in Women on the Margins (1995)

representative_people.context: Davis explicitly draws on his account of stories and dedicates the book partly to him. This specific resource does not make all comparative biography an application of one theory.
representative_people.works: The Practice of Everyday Life, used in Women on the Margins (1995), Glikl opening

representative_people.context: His Schleiermacher biography and later methodological reflections place an individual in an intellectual and social world. The current claim relies on scholarly discussion, not an independently read biographical chapter.
representative_people.works: Leben Schleiermachers, volume I (1870); later reflections on biography and autobiography through SEP

representative_people.context: Advocates attention to unconscious motives while warning that fragmentary evidence and superficial psychological labels can mislead.
representative_people.works: “Human Nature in Politics” (1955; consulted Spanish translation, 2000), 144

representative_people.context: Uses Elizabeth Marsh’s itinerant life to investigate transcontinental connections and women’s place in global history.
representative_people.works: Britons: Forging the Nation, 1707–1837 (1992); Captives: Britain, Empire and the World, 1600–1850 (2002); The Ordeal of Elizabeth Marsh: A Woman in World History (2007).

representative_people.context: Uses the fragmentary, multilingual traces of Kwee Thiam Tjing to investigate local cosmopolitanism without assuming that cosmopolitan subjects must travel widely.
representative_people.works: A Preliminary Analysis of the October 1, 1965, Coup in Indonesia (with Ruth T. McVey; research assistance Frederick P. Bunnell; circulated 1966, published 1971); Java in a Time of Revolution (1972); Imagined Communities (1983; revised and extended 1991; 2006 edition with afterword); “Old State, New Society” (1983); Language and Power (1990, collected essays); The Spectre of Comparisons (1998, collected essays); Under Three Flags (2005; retitled The Age of Globalization, 2013); ヤシガラ椀の外へ (2009 Japanese memoir, translated by Tsuyoshi Kato); The Fate of Rural Hell (2012); A Life Beyond Boundaries (2016 first English memoir, posthumous).

representative_people.context: Reconstructs Augustine through friendship and communal experiments rather than isolating a celebrated religious figure.
representative_people.works: Augustine of Hippo (1967; new edition with epilogue 2000); The World of Late Antiquity (1971); The Cult of the Saints (1981); The Body and Society (1988; twentieth-anniversary introduction 2008); Journeys of the Mind (2023); “Augustine’s Friendship for Freedom” (interview conducted July 2026, published September 2026).

biography.scope_note: A genre and set of methods with ancient and varied roots, not inherently great-man history, psychohistory or microstoria. The selected roster combines earlier practices, modern historical work and critics. Davis’s comparison preserves religious and colonial differences; her imagined prologue is not historical testimony. Bourdieu questions narrated coherence without banning life histories; Levi emphasizes choices within constraints and investigates group formation. Biography can explain wider relations, but its scale and source gaps remain subjects of criticism. Non-European traditions and original translation witnesses require further research; the current selection is not exhaustive.

strands.title: Labour lives and collective authorship
strands.focus: Torr’s Mann project draws on biographical materials and collaborative preparation. The incomplete continuation, manuscript/publication distinction and Murphy’s criticism make the production of a life history visible.
strands.works: Tom Mann and His Times, vol. 1 (1956); further fragments edited by E. P. Thompson, Our History 26–27 (1962)

strands.title: Individual reconstruction and social explanation
strands.focus: Power pairs lives with estate books, letters, household advice and material remains. Her personal treatment is a teaching method; Postan’s later reconstruction makes editorial mediation visible.
strands.works: Medieval People (1924); Postan preface (1963)

strands.title: Biographical sympathy and revision through evidence
strands.focus: Wedgwood’s two Strafford treatments offer a case of reassessment through new sources and scholarship. Woolrych’s criticism of eulogy remains visible alongside his appreciation.
strands.works: Strafford (1935); Thomas Wentworth ... A Revaluation (1961); Woolrych memoir (1998)

strands.title: A life as narrative vehicle: reach and missing evidence
strands.focus: Tuchman selects Coucy to travel across a turbulent period but acknowledges documentary limits. Stone questions whether that organizing device yields a sufficiently understood person or explains wider institutions.
strands.works: A Distant Mirror (1978), foreword; Stone review (1978)

strands.title: Whose lives and which particulars?
strands.focus: Johnson’s private lives, Brown’s collective recovery and Woolf’s changed criteria show different arguments about biographical significance. They are not a single progression from great men to ordinary people.
strands.works: Rambler 60 (1750); The Black Man (1863); The Art of Biography (1939)

strands.title: Narrated unity and relational trajectories
strands.focus: Bourdieu asks how institutions, interviews and retrospective storytelling produce coherent selves, and proposes trajectories within changing fields. Life history remains possible under relational scrutiny.
strands.works: L’illusion biographique (1986)

strands.title: Scale, norms and bounded agency
strands.focus: Levi distinguishes several uses of lives and locates choices within conflicting norms. Group coherence becomes a question to investigate, not an automatic starting assumption.
strands.works: Les usages de la biographie (1989)

strands.title: Contextual reconstruction and its limits
strands.focus: Roche’s Ménétra and Venturi’s Diderot illustrate different contextual procedures in Levi’s account. Context can illuminate gaps while itself requiring a dynamic explanation.
strands.works: Journal de ma vie (1982); Jeunesse de Diderot (1939), mediated by Levi (1989)

strands.title: Comparative lives, religion and colonial power
strands.focus: Davis holds similarities and differences together, tests her categories through an imagined prologue and rejects a single progressive sequence. Marginality does not prevent participation in colonial domination.
strands.works: Women on the Margins (1995), selected primary passages

strands.title: Publishing, translating and cutting a life record
strands.focus: Davis compares Glikl editions with different treatment of stories and moral commentary. Pappenheim’s role as translator is distinguished from the clinical narrative about her.
strands.works: Glikl editions/translations (1896, 1910, 1913), discussed by Davis (1995)

strands.title: Teaching, source discovery and collaborative work
strands.focus: Davis names course development, source suggestions, translation, archives, libraries and editing as resources. A selective roster does not exhaust the acknowledged labor behind the book.
strands.works: Women on the Margins (1995), acknowledgments

strands.title: Psychoanalytic interpretation and critical limits
strands.focus: Erikson’s 1970 retrospective supplies a primary account of his Luther interpretation, while the original 1958 book remains unread. Levi’s generic psychobiography judgment is not an Erikson-specific rebuttal.
strands.works: Young Man Luther (1958); Levi (1989), methodological discussion; Erikson, Autobiographic Notes (1970), p. 750

strands.title: Individual life and historical surroundings
strands.focus: Dilthey’s biographical work and later reflections join individual initiative to institutions and cultural systems. Biography brings contextual factors into view that recollection alone may not supply.
strands.works: Leben Schleiermachers I (1870), through scholarly discussion

strands.title: Psychological motives and limits of inference
strands.focus: Namier argues that professed reasons may conceal unconscious processes, but insists that psychological origins alone do not refute an argument. His warning about fragmentary evidence limits the use of psychological explanations in historical lives.
strands.works: “Human Nature in Politics” (1955), Spanish translation (2000), 143–146

black.label: Black history
black.description: Challenges racist historical narratives and recovers Black agency, institutions, and political struggle. Abolitionism, community scholarship, and Black institutions provide independent roots, not merely applications of European theory.
black.representative_figures_and_works: William Wells Brown; George Washington Williams (1882–83); Carter G. Woodson; W. E. B. Du Bois, Black Reconstruction (1935). Carter G. Woodson and colleagues founded the Association for the Study of Negro Life and History (now ASALH) in 1915. Postwar and later examples include John Hope Franklin, From Slavery to Freedom (1947), and Darlene Clark Hine, Black Women in White (1989).

representative_people.context: Uses collective biography to contest racist claims of inferiority.
representative_people.works: The Black Man: His Antecedents, His Genius, and His Achievements (1863)

representative_people.context: Earlier Black historical writing.
representative_people.works: History of the Negro Race in America (1882–83)

representative_people.context: Studies educational effort before emancipation alongside independent publishing and institution building.

representative_people.context: Black historical scholarship and reconstruction history.

representative_people.context: Postwar synthesis placing African American history within the interpretation of United States history.
representative_people.works: From Slavery to Freedom (1947)

representative_people.context: Black women’s work, professional institutions, and the intersection of racial and gender power.

representative_people.context: 'Critical fabulation', a 'speculative method … which questions historical archives as the sole source of credible information about the past' (MacArthur, 2019); Scenes of Subjection (1997). Unread.
representative_people.works: Scenes of Subjection (1997); 'Venus in Two Acts' (2008); Wayward Lives, Beautiful Experiments (2019)

representative_people.context: Dispossessed Lives (2016) combines 'fragmentary sources with interdisciplinary methodologies that include black feminist theory' (publisher description). Unread.
representative_people.works: Dispossessed Lives (2016)

representative_people.context: 'An unavoidable reference for anyone navigating the streams of Black and Caribbean studies' (Craipain, 2024); 'The Odd and the Ordinary' (1990) against Haitian exceptionalism (as read by Bulamah, Goyatá and Pereira).
representative_people.works: 'The Odd and the Ordinary' (1990); Silencing the Past (1995)

representative_people.context: Interprets Reconstruction through Black political action, contested freedom and the struggle to build democracy. Own interview answers stress change after slavery and oppose treating later injustice as proof that emancipation changed nothing.
representative_people.works: Free Soil, Free Labor, Free Men (1970); Reconstruction: America’s Unfinished Revolution (1988); The Story of American Freedom (1998).

representative_people.context: Berlin’s slavery history emphasizes variation across time and region and agency exercised within coercive relations. Own1999 opening points2–4; negotiation does not imply equality between enslaved people and owners.

representative_people.context: Kelley’s movement histories center visions of freedom that exceed campaign victories or seizure of state power. Own2022 retrospective explicitly says Freedom Dreams was neither roadmap nor prediction; particular movements rather than a universal programme.

representative_people.context: Investigates Black political organization and aspirations across slavery and emancipation.
representative_people.works: A Nation Under Our Feet (2003); The Political Worlds of Slavery and Freedom (2009)

black.scope_note: Independent scholarship, community education, publishing and collecting precede later academic recognition. Biography, national synthesis and Black women’s history pursue different questions. This selection remains weighted toward African American scholarship; diaspora links do not make all Black histories one national tradition.

women.label: Women’s history
women.date_label: Nineteenth-century and interwar work; renewed expansion from the 1960s
women.description: Studies women as historical actors and examines work, family, politics, and structures of power. Earlier scholarship, activism, teaching, and documentary collecting precede the field’s expansion alongside later feminist movements. Recovery, institutional growth, rediscovery, and methodological disagreement overlap; this is not a field created from nothing in the 1960s or one account of a shared female experience.

women.scope_note: Earlier documentary, economic and institutional projects overlap with later feminist reconstruction and theory. Periodization, class, race, caste and regional contexts create disagreements within women’s history. Gender history develops some of these questions without superseding the field; this roster remains selective and uneven geographically.

social.label: New social history
social.description: An overlapping field of work, class formation, households, community and collective action. Thompson, Davis and Gutman already integrate culture and agency; demographic and mobility studies use distinct evidence. Davidoff and Hall connect gender and middle-class life; Chakrabarty and Cooper investigate colonial labor and the limits of inherited categories. Scott’s critique makes experience itself a historical question, not something to discard.
social.representative_figures_and_works: E. P. Thompson and Eric Hobsbawm; Herbert Gutman, Work, Culture, and Society in Industrializing America (1976); Natalie Zemon Davis, Society and Culture in Early Modern France (1975); Charles Tilly; E. A. Wrigley and historical demography. Earlier social inquiry provides comparisons, not membership in a later school. Further readings: Davidoff and Hall, Family Fortunes (1987); Chakrabarty, Rethinking Working-Class History (1989); Scott, “The Evidence of Experience” (1991); Cooper, Decolonization and African Society (1996). Geoff Eley and Keith Nield: “Why does social history ignore politics?” (1980).

social.scope_note: Class formation, demographic reconstruction, communities, and everyday life have different methods; Marxist history is one substantial component. The 1950s–1970s label marks expansion, not termination: later mapped works extend and dispute these programmes. Earlier women’s social inquiry remains visible as comparison. Neither one European class trajectory nor transparent experience supplies a universal model; critical interventions do not erase productive inheritances.

strands.title: Separate spheres: categories, chronology and regional evidence

strands.works: Family Fortunes (1987), prologue opening; Vickery (1993), 393–401

strands.title: Experience, agency and changing discourse
strands.focus: Canning accepts the need to historicize experience but questions treating identity recovery and analysis of difference as alternatives. She asks how subjects reinterpret or transform discourse; this is a sympathetic criticism of Scott, not a return to self-evident experience.
strands.works: Scott, “The Evidence of Experience” (1991); Canning (1994), 374–378

strands.title: Politics within social-history debate
strands.focus: Eley and Nield asked in 1980 why social history ignored politics (article unread; they recalled in 2007 that it 'drew disappointingly little response in print' and that they had been 'trying to create a space for political analysis in the expanded sense given to "politics" by the politics of knowledge of 1968', 2000, p. 14). Joyce's 'The End of Social History?' (1995; unread) drew their 'Starting Over' (1995; unread), which Joyce said equated his questioning of social history 'with contemporary neo-liberalism' (1996). In 'Farewell to the Working Class?' (2000, read in full) they held that 'class discursively understood … is a better starting point' while wanting 'to break this logic of disavowal' (p. 16); Scott's reply (read in full) called this 'Assent to Discourse' and objected that insisting on class forecloses other political categories (p. 69); Cooper answered that 'they did not think to ask Karl Marx' (p. 61). The debate entry languages_of_class holds the exchanges.
strands.works: “Why does social history ignore politics?” (1980), coauthored; “Starting Over” (1995); “Farewell to the Working Class?” and reply (ILWCH 57, 2000); The Future of Class in History (2007)

quant.label: Quantitative history
quant.description: Uses serial evidence, linked records, statistics and explicit models to ask different historical questions. Labrousse’s prices, Henry’s reconstructed families, Benson’s voting groups, Thernstrom’s mobility and Curtin’s slave-trade estimates extend beyond cliometrics. Fogel’s counterfactuals and North’s institutions represent distinct economic programmes; Gutman’s criticism shows that evidence and interpretation remain contested within quantitative debate.

representative_people.works: Comment on Fogel and Engerman (1979),213–214

representative_people.context: Tests how observation dates, migration and occupational coding shape measured mobility.
representative_people.works: “The Entry Into the U.S. Labor Market” (1996 manuscript; published 1997)

representative_people.works: Data contribution credited in Ferrie (1996 manuscript), note 10 and Table 1

representative_people.context: Makes assumptions and category changes explicit in estimates of nineteenth-century agricultural labour in southern India.
representative_people.works: Land and Caste in South India (1965), opening extracts I,IV,X

representative_people.works: With Louis Henry, “Pour connaître la population de la France depuis Louis XIV” (1958),663–665

representative_people.context: Lee and Wang explicitly credit his collaborative publications and intellectual and editorial contributions.

representative_people.works: Review of Darroch and Soltow, Property and Inequality in Victorian Ontario (1996); The Politics of Population (2001)

strands.title: Serial evidence and collective patterns
strands.focus: Prices and incomes support conjunctural and social questions without requiring neoclassical theory.
strands.works: Esquisse du mouvement des prix et des revenus en France au XVIIIe siècle (1933)

strands.title: Population reconstruction
strands.focus: Family linkage and aggregate reconstruction differ in units and assumptions; missing mobile families are a methodological problem Henry explicitly identifies.
strands.works: Anciennes familles genevoises (1956); The Population History of England (1981)

strands.title: Cliometrics
strands.focus: Fogel’s counterfactual railroad comparison and North’s institutional development are different uses of economic reasoning; neither stands for all quantitative history.
strands.works: Railroads and American Economic Growth (1964); “Economic Performance through Time” (1993)

strands.title: Electoral groups and competing explanations
strands.focus: Compare economic interests with ethnic and religious affiliations in New York voting; Benson’s categories overlap and his argument is not a universal law of elections.
strands.works: The Concept of Jacksonian Democracy (1961)

strands.title: Occupations, property and social mobility
strands.focus: Separate occupational change from property accumulation through linked local records; Thernstrom’s use of Weber broadens class beyond a single occupational ranking.
strands.works: Poverty and Progress (1964)

strands.title: Slavery: estimates, coercion and interpretation
strands.focus: Read the cliometric study alongside Gutman’s criticism of its labor/cooperation interpretation; neither efficiency estimates nor a book’s polemical reception alone describe enslaved people’s lives.
strands.works: Time on the Cross (1974); Slavery and the Numbers Game (1975)

strands.title: Estimating the Atlantic slave trade
strands.focus: Reconstruct the scale of forced migration from uneven evidence. Curtin’s influential estimates were later revised; totals do not substitute for histories of violence and agency.
strands.works: The Atlantic Slave Trade: A Census (1969)

strands.title: Household surveys and the limits of response
strands.focus: Salmon combines employer and worker returns, bureau tabulation and wage comparisons. Distribution through college and association networks, reluctance to reply and uneven knowledge qualify her representativeness claims.
strands.works: Domestic Service (1897), preface vii–xiv

strands.title: Counterfactual assumptions and sensitivity
strands.focus: McClelland’s criticism makes alternative transport capacity, pricing and cost assumptions explicit questions. Critiquing a model’s inference is itself quantitative historical work.
strands.works: McClelland (1968), opening and notes

strands.title: Revenue and technical efficiency
strands.focus: David and Temin distinguish revenue from producing the same outputs with fewer inputs. Their specific objection should be read with the authors’ reply; the reply is located here, but its body remains unchecked.
strands.works: David/Temin (1979),213–214; Fogel/Engerman Reply (1980), metadata only

strands.title: Who remains visible in mobility records?
strands.focus: Ferrie questions findings based on local stayers and late observation after arrival. Linking migrants expands observation, but selective linkage and occupational coding still constrain inference.
strands.works: Ferrie (1996 manuscript),1–8,22,28

strands.title: Caste, occupation and colonial counts
strands.focus: Kumar states the assumptions needed to estimate earlier agricultural labour from later caste counts. Changing census categories and officials’ conflation of caste with occupation limit comparison.
strands.works: Land and Caste in South India (1965), opening extracts IV,X

strands.title: Sampling parishes and their surviving records
strands.focus: The Fleury–Henry programme requires more than a collection of convenient local studies. Its later implementation changes sampling to meet practical constraints and treats earlier, poorer records separately.

strands.title: Fertility measures and their denominators
strands.focus: Lee and Wang distinguish synthetic total fertility from fertility within marriage and state adjustments to several underlying estimates. Interpreting those measures requires more than comparing the resulting totals.
strands.works: One Quarter of Humanity (1999), Table 6.1 notes and 86–90

quant.scope_note: Serial history, demographic reconstruction, and cliometrics use numbers differently. A quantitative method does not establish a common theory. Counting, source linkage and formal modeling require different assumptions. Recorded categories, missing people and units of comparison shape conclusions; neither criticism nor narrative history ended quantitative research.

chronology.interpretation: Do not treat ‘1950s–70s expansion’ as either a field lifespan or a precise common phase for serial history, historical demography and cliometrics. Plot sourced milestones across those strands; a common expansion interval remains unestablished.
