strands.focus: Pomeranz names Wong’s reciprocal comparison and Tilly’s encompassing comparison as resources. Regions, states and wider systems answer different questions; the method does not require treating Europe and China as internally uniform.
strands.works: The Great Divergence (2000),7–10

strands.title: Proto-industry and the limits of trade
strands.focus: Pomeranz extends Mokyr’s labor model across regions while questioning unlimited manufacture exports and resource imports at unchanged relative prices. Comparing regions also requires examining their trading partners.
strands.works: The Great Divergence (2000),21–23

strands.title: Legal ordering across empires
strands.focus: Benton uses jurisdictional conflicts to ask how local cultural practices formed repeated institutional patterns across empires. This strategy places legal ordering alongside other ways of relating local encounters to global structures. Her 2002 introduction is read; the 2013 volume with Richard J. Ross and Stern’s separate 2011 corporate-sovereignty book are bibliographic resources, not evidence of a single school or transmission.
strands.works: Benton, Law and Colonial Cultures (2002 imprint); Benton and Ross, eds., Legal Pluralism and Empires (2013, body unread). Further comparative resource: Philip J. Stern, The Company-State (2011, publisher metadata only).

strands.title: Capitalism as connected regional diversity
strands.focus: In his 2020 methodological answer Beckert relates regional differences and connections: merchants, plantations, manufacturing and state power belong in the same global inquiry. His account resists treating Europe’s industrialisation as the whole history of capitalism. This strand records his stated strategy; the empirical adequacy of its global applications and criticism of the cotton argument remain open.
strands.works: Growth Policy interview with Devjani Roy (2020), answer 2; Empire of Cotton (2014, existing limited excerpt)

indigenous.label: Indigenous-authored history & critique
indigenous.date_label: Earlier witnesses 1615–1938 · critiques of the academy 1969–99 · refusal, resurgence and peoplehood 2007–17
indigenous.description: Historical writing, criticism and theory by Indigenous authors, from early manuscript and print witnesses to academic history and political theory. It is plural: Andean, Haudenosaunee, Ojibwe, Cree, Métis, Wendat, Dakota, Māori, Hawaiian and Aboriginal traditions have their own roots and are not branches of one academic field. From 1969 Deloria, Adams, LaRocque, Sioui, Trask and Smith turned criticism on the institutions and disciplines that studied them; LaRocque judged that 'Canadian historiography is not that benign' (1999). After 2000 the criticism became theory: Audra Simpson's 'ethnographic refusal' (2007, 2014); Coulthard's case against 'the politics of recognition' (2009, 2014); Leanne Betasamosake Simpson's resurgence, which turns from efforts to 'Indigenize the academy' toward 'a resurgence of Indigenous intellectual systems' (2014); Andersen's Métis 'peoplehood' against 'mixedness' (2014). Older university scholarship about Indigenous peoples and community-engaged research have their own entries; settler colonial studies is a comparative field.
indigenous.representative_figures_and_works: Earlier witnesses: Guaman Poma (c. 1615/1616), Cusick (checked 1828 edition), Apess (1836), Te Rangikāheke (manuscripts before 1854), Warren (1885), Thunderchild and Ahenakew (1923; 1929), Pei Te Hurinui Jones (1929), Mathews (1932, 1961), Te Rangi Hīroa (1938, 1949), McNickle (1949; Native American Tribalism, 1973). Critiques 1969–99: Deloria, Custer Died for Your Sins (1969); Adams, Prison of Grass (1975); LaRocque, Defeathering the Indian (1975) and her dissertation (1999); Dickason (1984, 1992); Sioui (1989); Walker (1990); Trask, 'Natives and Anthropologists' (1991) and From a Native Daughter (1993); Kameʻeleihiwa (1992); Wilson (1996); O'Brien (1997); Rigney (1999); Smith, Decolonizing Methodologies (1999). After 2000: Audra Simpson, 'On Ethnographic Refusal' (2007) and Mohawk Interruptus (2014); Coulthard, Red Skin, White Masks (2014); Leanne Betasamosake Simpson, Dancing on Our Turtle's Back (2011), 'Land as pedagogy' (2014), As We Have Always Done (2017); Andersen, 'Métis' (2014); Moreton-Robinson, The White Possessive (2015). See the strands for works, collaborators and evidence limits.

representative_people.context: Collected histories from relatives and tribal leaders and addressed a nineteenth-century white readership. The publisher’s account retains his goals and limitations; recording oral knowledge is not equivalent to the later decolonizing programme.

representative_people.context: Recorded Chief Thunderchild’s narratives in Cree in 1923 and wrote through Old Keyam’s literary voice. The 1973 book passed through Ruth M. Buck’s editing; composition, narration and publication are distinct. His 1929 folklore article supplies an interwar publication milestone.

representative_people.context: Recorded Tainui genealogies and historical traditions in Māori and English. Te Ara distinguishes his 1929 publication, English manuscript by about 1936, contested reuse by Kelly and the 1995 posthumous history.
representative_people.works: Māhinārangi (1929); English historical manuscript by c. 1936; Ngā iwi o Tainui (1995, posthumous)

representative_people.context: Her historical scholarship examines European representations and places First Peoples within a broad Canadian historical synthesis. MNO recognizes her Métis contribution. She is one major historian within a wider field, not its sole origin.
representative_people.works: The Myth of the Savage (1984); Canada’s First Nations (1992)

representative_people.context: Métis scholar’s critique of Canadian colonialism joins historical interpretation and Marxist politics. The institutional biography dates his doctorate and university appointment to 1966; detailed book arguments remain outside this description-level inclusion.

representative_people.context: Her 1999 dissertation relates her 1974 research on stereotypes in Alberta history and social-studies texts to Defeathering the Indian and names its targets in Canadian historiography: Walker's survey ('not that benign'), Trigger's foreword to Sioui ('a language of containment') and the cross-cultural approach of Brown and Van Kirk. Distinct from Adams, on whom she draws.
representative_people.works: Defeathering the Indian (1975); Native Writers Resisting Colonizing Practices… (1999), selected passage; When the Other Is Me (2011)

representative_people.context: In his 1991 interview, explains autohistory as bringing Indigenous self-interpretation and transmitted traditions into historical discourse. His moral and philosophical proposal is situated; its account of Amerindian values does not define every nation.

representative_people.context: Enrolled member at Flathead (Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes), per Iverson 1993. Historical synthesis and institution-building: They Came Here First (1949) and Native American Tribalism (1973), whose preface challenged 'the certainty that native America had vanished'; a founder of the NCAI (1944), organiser of the Workshops on American Indian Affairs from 1960, and a creator of the Newberry centre (1972), which he directed in its first fellowship year (1973–74). Not a universal field foundation.

indigenous.scope_note: Part 2 of the Indigenous histories family (split in revision 1.201): history, criticism and theory by Indigenous authors. Membership rests on Indigenous authorship or co-authorship sourced person by person, in the author's own words or an institutional or publisher profile (see the people records), never inferred from a name or a topic. Collaborative and community-directed research has its own entry; settler scholarship about Indigenous peoples is in Ethnohistory and Indigenous–newcomer relations; settler colonial studies is a comparative field. Reviewed through 2017. Read in full: Audra Simpson 2007; Trask 1991 with Keesing's reply; Nicoll's 2015 review of Simpson and Moreton-Robinson. Read in part: Coulthard's 2009 dissertation; Leanne Betasamosake Simpson 2014; Andersen 2009 and the introduction of 2014; LaRocque 1999; Iverson's 1993 introduction to McNickle. Known through named readers or publishers only: Mohawk Interruptus, Red Skin, White Masks, The White Possessive, Dancing on Our Turtle's Back, As We Have Always Done, Native Land and Foreign Desires. Works of 2018–24 are not yet surveyed. In Canadian History PhDs Smith is cited by 47, Audra Simpson by 34, Coulthard by 27 and Leanne Betasamosake Simpson by 26, the last three from almost none before 2010 (History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23).

strands.works: Ka Whawhai Tonu Mātou (1990)

strands.focus: Natick land loss, kinship and the making of an extinction narrative.
strands.works: Dispossession by Degrees (1997)

strands.title: Authority over research
strands.focus: Self-determination affects questions, methods and knowledge ownership; researcher positions differ within as well as across communities.
strands.works: Decolonizing Methodologies (1999)

strands.title: Māori scholarship and material culture
strands.focus: An earlier historical/anthropological trajectory, not a precursor stage superseded by one later method.
strands.works: Vikings of the Sunrise (1938); The Coming of the Maori (1949)

strands.title: Criticism of institutions and researchers
strands.focus: Deloria’s manifesto supplies a distinct Native American intervention; specific chapters remain to be read. As a guest speaker in 1965 he criticised the McNickle-organised workshops (Beck 1995, mediated); Audra Simpson cites Custer with Asad and Said for anthropology's place in empire (2007, n. 2).
strands.works: Custer Died for Your Sins (1969)

strands.title: Tribal and family historians
strands.focus: Wilson connects historical interpretation to sustained relationships and authority to share particular knowledge.
strands.works: “American Indian History or Non-Indian Perceptions…” (1996)

strands.title: Australian Indigenist methodology
strands.focus: Rigney’s 1999 article broadens the methodological bibliography; detailed arguments await primary reading.
strands.works: “Internationalization…” (1999)

strands.title: Early Andean manuscript history
strands.focus: An early colonial-period historical manuscript, situated in a Christian and royal political framework. It demonstrates earlier Indigenous-authored historical writing without making a modern field or THOA descend directly from it.
strands.works: El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno (manuscript c. 1615/1616)

strands.title: Haudenosaunee histories in print
strands.focus: Cusick’s preface presents gathering materials and translation as historical work. The 1828 second edition is a verified witness; printed publication is not the origin of the traditions it recounts.
strands.works: Sketches of Ancient History of the Six Nations (checked second edition, 1828)

strands.title: Historical argument and colonial commemoration
strands.focus: Apess challenges colonial historical judgments and Pilgrim celebration. His Christian moral argument is an earlier intervention; no borrowing by later theorists is asserted.
strands.works: Eulogy on King Philip (1836), selected paragraphs

strands.title: Ojibwe oral knowledge and written history
strands.focus: Warren’s history draws on relatives and tribal leaders while addressing white readers. The publisher’s discussion retains the author’s nineteenth-century assumptions and limitations.
strands.works: History of the Ojibway People (first publication, 1885)

strands.title: Māori manuscript authorship and colonial publication
strands.focus: Te Rangikāheke’s genealogy and historical narration survive within manuscripts and Grey’s altered publications. Attribution reveals an Indigenous author behind texts circulated under a governor’s name.
strands.works: Historical and genealogical manuscripts before 1854; material reused in Grey’s publications, 1853–55

strands.title: Cree narration and interwar writing
strands.focus: Thunderchild’s narration, Ahenakew’s 1923 recording and literary writing, his 1929 publication, and the 1973 edited book carry different dates and authorial roles. Cuthand’s 1995 criticism makes editorial selection visible.
strands.works: 1923 narration/recording; Cree Trickster Tales (1929); Voices of the Plains Cree (1973; 1995 introduction)

strands.title: Tainui genealogies and historical writing
strands.focus: Jones’s Māori-language historical work and the history of its publication distinguish interwar research from the 1995 posthumous volume. The institutional biography describes disputed reuse of an earlier English manuscript.
strands.works: Māhinārangi (1929); English historical manuscript by c. 1936; Ngā iwi o Tainui (1995, posthumous)

strands.title: Canadian historical synthesis and regional inquiry
strands.focus: Dickason’s studies of representations and historical synthesis sit alongside Stonechild and Waiser’s Saskatchewan study. These are different scales and collaborations, not one doctrinal programme.
strands.works: The Myth of the Savage (1984); Canada’s First Nations (1992); Stonechild and Waiser, Loyal Till Death (1997)

strands.title: Métis scholarship and criticism of representation
strands.focus: Adams’s colonial and class interpretation and LaRocque’s criticism of representation broaden the 1970s bibliography. Her 1999 dissertation p. 34 explicitly connects the earlier book to curriculum research and resistance. These are distinct intellectual positions. The dissertation names its targets: James Walker's survey of Canadian historical writing ('Canadian historiography is not that benign'), Trigger's foreword to Sioui as 'a language of containment', and the 'neo cross-cultural approach' of Bailey, Jaenen, Trigger, Brown and Van Kirk; Adams is her 'Metis historian and social critic' (PDF pp. 47, 119, 135–136, 249). When the Other Is Me (2011) is the revised book.
strands.works: Prison of Grass (1975); Defeathering the Indian (1975)

strands.title: Wendat autohistory and historical interpretation
strands.focus: Sioui’s author interview supplies an explicit historiographical proposal about self-interpretation and oral transmission. His moral account remains attributed and situated; French and English publication dates are distinct.
strands.works: Pour une autohistoire amérindienne (1989); author interview (1991); English translation by Sheila Fischman (1992)

strands.title: Historical synthesis and Native history institutions
strands.focus: McNickle’s 1949 work and role in creating the Newberry centre in 1972 establish an earlier bibliography and institutional contribution. Neither the centre nor a university is treated as the origin of Indigenous historical knowledge. His 1973 preface challenged administrators' 'certainty that native America had vanished before the march of progress'; Iverson (1993) noted that 'few Native historians have tried to provide an overview of the national Indian experience'. He helped found the NCAI (1944), organised the Workshops on American Indian Affairs from 1960, and directed the Newberry centre in its first fellowship year (1973–74).
strands.works: They Came Here First: The Epic of the American Indian (1949); Newberry history centre (1972)

strands.title: Osage historical writing across the century
strands.focus: Mathews’s 1932 work and 1961 history supply earlier and mid-century examples. The publisher describes oral and documentary historical resources; detailed methodological claims await the works.
strands.works: Wah’Kon-Tah (1932); The Osages: Children of the Middle Waters (1961)

strands.title: Hawaiian land history and sovereignty
strands.focus: Kameʻeleihiwa’s land history and Trask’s political essays provide distinct Hawaiian contributions. Hawaiian-language historiography has earlier authors; neither regional programme is a subset of the Māori examples. In 1991 Trask answered Keesing's charge that Pacific nationalists 'invent' their pasts: genealogy is 'solid evidence from Native forms of history', and Hawaiians do not want 'to be "liberated" from our past'. Keesing replied that her 'insider' versus 'outsider' dichotomy was 'a great leap backward'; Linnekin, that 'Traditions are neither genuine nor spurious'.
strands.works: Native Land and Foreign Desires (1992); From a Native Daughter (1993; revised 1999)

strands.title: Aboriginal interviews and life writing
strands.focus: Gilbert’s interviews and Ginibi’s autobiography broaden the historical bibliography beyond university monographs. Their forms and authorial positions differ from each other and from community-transmitted oral histories.
strands.works: Living Black (1977); Don’t Take Your Love to Town (1988)

strands.title: Refusal, resurgence and the critique of recognition
strands.focus: Three linked but distinct arguments, each with its own target. Audra Simpson proposed 'a sharp move away from the ethno-historical/salvage paradigm that evacuates theory' in Iroquois studies and made refusal a method: ethnography as a calculus 'of what you need to know and what I refuse to write in' (2007); Mohawk Interruptus (2014) carries the argument into Kahnawà:ke's history and Morgan and Parker's ethnology. Coulthard challenged 'the now commonplace assumption' that colonial relations in Canada 'can be reconciled via such a politics of recognition', using Fanon against Taylor and reworking Marx: 'dispossession, not proletarianization' shaped Indigenous–state relations (2009; book 2014). Leanne Betasamosake Simpson defined resurgence as 'the rebuilding of Indigenous nations according to our own political, intellectual and cultural traditions' and met the academy's 'colonial refusal' with 'Indigenous refusal' (2014), citing Coulthard on recognition and Simpson on refusal. Alfred's Wasáse (2005) is a shared reference. In the pages read none of them criticises Wolfe.
strands.works: Audra Simpson, 'On Ethnographic Refusal' (2007), Mohawk Interruptus (2014); Glen Sean Coulthard, Subjects of Empire? (PhD, 2009), Red Skin, White Masks (2014); Leanne Betasamosake Simpson, Dancing on Our Turtle's Back (2011), 'Land as pedagogy' (2014), As We Have Always Done (2017)

strands.title: Peoplehood against mixedness
strands.focus: Andersen argues that Métis are misrecognised 'as a hybrid off-shoot of two races … rather than as an Indigenous people'. To the question 'Have not fur trade historians … already extensively documented numerous instances of Métis mixedness?' he answers that 'the racialization of the Métis has never begun nor ended with us'. Peoplehood rests on 'a "national core" historically located in Red River', and 'History is thus a crucial resource in Indigenous claims to peoplehood' (2014). His 2009 essay asks Indigenous studies to start from 'density' rather than 'difference', using disciplines including history. He draws on the historian Brenda Macdougall.
strands.works: Chris Andersen, 'Critical Indigenous Studies: From Difference to Density' (2009); 'Métis': Race, Recognition, and the Struggle for Indigenous Peoplehood (2014)

freud.label: Freudian psychoanalysis
freud.description: A clinical practice and family of theories concerning unconscious conflict, development, sexuality, interpretation and relationships. Freud’s changing methods, later child-analysis disputes, psychosocial history, linguistic rereading and feminist adaptations require distinct accounts.
freud.representative_figures_and_works: Sigmund Freud; later adaptations include Erik Erikson’s historical psychobiography and Jacques Lacan’s rereading through language. Historical interpretation must address evidence and context rather than assume access to an unrecorded inner life.

representative_people.context: Develops an account of repression, association, dreams, sexuality and transference, then investigates group bonds. These are historically situated theoretical arguments; his clinical claims are not a substitute for evidence about people in the past.
representative_people.works: The Origin and Development of Psychoanalysis (1910; lectures 1909); Group Psychology and the Analysis of the Ego (1921; English 1922)

representative_people.context: Connects individual development with historical social orders, and asks that the identity-crisis concept itself face historical scrutiny. His later Luther formulation remains his interpretation.
representative_people.works: Young Man Luther (1958), existing metadata; “Autobiographic Notes on the Identity Crisis” (1970), selected primary passages

representative_people.context: Rereads Freud through identification, signifying relations and symbolic exchange; his return is a contested intervention in psychoanalysis.
representative_people.works: “Le stade du miroir” (1949); “Fonction et champ” (report 1953; publication 1956); “L’instance de la lettre” (1957); collected Écrits (1966)

representative_people.context: Freud credits an earlier cathartic practice while distinguishing it from his later account of repression. Breuer treated the patient later known as Anna O.; Freud did not.
representative_people.works: Studies on Hysteria (1895), with Freud, as discussed in the Clark lectures

representative_people.context: Freud recalls his Paris training as a resource while distinguishing later psychological explanations. This is Freud’s account, not a complete review of Charcot.
representative_people.works: Clinical work recalled in Freud’s Clark Lecture II (1910)

representative_people.context: Hypnotic recall supplies an experimental prompt in Freud’s account; he later questions treating suggestion as a final explanation.
representative_people.works: Nancy observations recalled in Clark Lecture II (1910); Group Psychology IV (1921)

representative_people.context: Freud explicitly credits association experiments and the Zurich complex vocabulary in 1909. This dated collaboration does not imply agreement throughout their later careers.
representative_people.works: Diagnostische Assoziationsstudien (1906), cited in Clark Lecture III

representative_people.context: Freud uses his catalytic analogy for the analyst’s role in transference. The cited article remains mediated through the lecture.
representative_people.works: “Introjektion und Übertragung” (1909), cited in Clark Lecture V

representative_people.context: Her defense concepts are a named resource for Gay’s proposed historical research; her work also belongs to contested developments in child analysis. Lacan’s 1949 mirror-stage paper explicitly invokes her defense concepts; this is another specific reception, without implying agreement across child-analysis schools.
representative_people.works: Defense concepts discussed by Gay (1997); child-analysis practice discussed by Amos (2015)

representative_people.context: Uses children’s play to interpret an inner world and develops accounts of anxiety and defense. The institutional overview describes disagreements; original clinical writings remain unread.
representative_people.works: The Psycho-Analysis of Children (1932); “Notes on Some Schizoid Mechanisms” (1946)

representative_people.context: The publisher presents her feminist use of psychoanalysis as an explanation of patriarchy rather than its endorsement; this is one contested feminist position.
representative_people.works: Psychoanalysis and Feminism (1974; reissue 2000)

representative_people.context: Challenges Freud’s Leonardo interpretation through translation, source context and alternative explanations. Faulty application is distinguished from disproof of all psychoanalysis.
representative_people.works: “Leonardo and Freud: An Art-Historical Study” (1956), selected passages

representative_people.context: Linguistic resource explicitly credited by Lacan for his discussion of metonymy; this is a psychoanalytic appropriation, not a clinical affiliation.
representative_people.works: Fundamentals of Language, with Morris Halle, cited in Lacan’s “L’instance de la lettre” (1957), notes 3 and 10

representative_people.context: Defends Lacan’s return to Freud while later qualifying culturalist overtones of his own reading. A philosophical intervention in Communist debates, not a clinical case study.
representative_people.works: “Freud and Lacan” (written 1964; NLR 1969), public opening and editorial qualification

representative_people.context: Reworks Freud’s destruction drive and recording models in a philosophical account of archives; raises questions about technical supplements to memory without independently validating psychoanalytic mechanisms.
representative_people.works: Archive Fever (1994/1996), pp. 7–15; references there to Civilization and Its Discontents and the Mystic Pad

freud.scope_note: This is a tradition entry, not an individual Freud node. Clinical claims and normative sexual classifications are historically situated. Breuer treated Anna O.; Freud’s account is not an independent outcome audit. Klein, Anna Freud, Erikson, Lacan and feminist interpreters pursue divergent questions. Historical motive inference requires documentary criticism; neither clinical access nor a uniform Freudian school can be assumed. Primary readings here cover the Clark lectures and selected Group Psychology chapters, not Freud’s entire career.

strands.title: Catharsis, repression and changing methods
strands.focus: Freud distinguishes Breuer’s earlier practice, hypnotic experiments and his developing use of association. His retrospective narrative does not establish clinical outcomes.
strands.works: Clark Lectures I–III (1910)

strands.title: Association, dreams and indirect expression
strands.focus: Manifest and latent dream material, condensation, displacement and everyday errors form different routes in Freud’s interpretation. Psychic determination remains a theoretical premise to examine.
strands.works: Clark Lecture III (1910)

strands.title: Development, transference and sublimation
strands.focus: Freud’s sexuality extends beyond reproduction; transference and sublimation connect his developmental and clinical account. Its normative sexual classifications are historical judgments.
strands.works: Clark Lectures IV–V (1910)

strands.title: Individual relations and group bonds
strands.focus: Group Psychology starts with relations already present in individual life and questions suggestion as a sufficient explanation, proposing libidinal attachments.
strands.works: Group Psychology, I and IV (1921/1922)

strands.title: Child analysis and divergent developments
strands.focus: Klein’s play interpretation differs from other early child-analysis practices. Anna Freud and Klein are not interchangeable extensions of Freud; support here is a retrospective institutional profile.
strands.works: The Psycho-Analysis of Children (1932); Amos (2015)

strands.title: Psychosocial and historical adaptations
strands.focus: Erikson examines identity in historical orders; Gay argues for a place within contextual history. Neither position represents all psychoanalytic traditions.
strands.works: Erikson (1970); Gay (1997)

strands.title: Feminist questions and subjectivity
strands.focus: Mitchell’s published program and Alexander’s historical work show productive feminist uses with different source support. These do not imply feminist consensus.
strands.works: Psychoanalysis and Feminism (1974); Becoming a Woman (1994/1995)

strands.title: Translation, context and historical inference
strands.focus: Schapiro’s Leonardo criticism tests an application against historical knowledge while retaining the possibility of psychological inquiry. Unrecorded motives are not directly accessible clinical facts.
strands.works: Leonardo and Freud (1956), selected passages

strands.title: Identification and the signifier
strands.focus: The mirror-stage argument concerns identification and misrecognition; the later linguistic essay reformulates dream-work through metaphor and metonymy. This is a changing program, not the whole history of psychoanalysis.
strands.works: Mirror-stage paper (1949); “L’instance de la lettre” (1957)

strands.title: Archives and technical models of memory
strands.focus: Derrida reworks Freud’s destruction drive and Mystic Pad while asking whether changing recording technologies alter a model or its object. These are philosophical questions, not clinical findings.
strands.works: Archive Fever (1994/1996), pp. 7–15

science.label: History of science
science.date_label: Earlier roots · History of Science Society founded 1924 · later approaches
science.description: Studies scientific knowledge, practices, instruments, institutions, and their historical settings. Histories of ideas, social and cultural histories, and material approaches coexist. The field predates Kuhn and STS, which transform parts of its questions without founding or exhausting it.
science.representative_figures_and_works: George Sarton; Alexandre Koyré, Études galiléennes (1939); Robert K. Merton; Thomas Kuhn, The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962); Steven Shapin and Simon Schaffer, Leviathan and the Air-Pump (1985). Yates and Foucault provide additional, distinct contributions; they do not substitute for these historians and programmes. Further approaches include Metzger’s history of chemistry (1923), Maier’s medieval natural philosophy (1949), Fleck’s scientific fact (1935), Needham’s collaborative Chinese science project (from 1954), Rossiter’s Women Scientists in America (1982), and Merchant’s The Death of Nature (1980).

strands.focus: Distinguish disciplinary organization from accounts of conceptual transformation.

strands.focus: Normal science, paradigms, and revolutions offer a major reorientation within an existing field.

strands.title: Scientific institutions and social contexts
strands.focus: The social explanation of scientific activity has roots preceding later laboratory studies.

strands.title: Bacon’s metaphors and experimental power
strands.focus: Pesic’s 1999 abstract reads Proteus as mutual struggle and testing. strands.title: Moral economies of science
strands.focus: Certain forms of empiricism, quantification and objectivity rest on collectively held, affect-laden values, “a web of affect-saturated values”; Daston distinguishes this sense of “moral economy” from Thompson’s and draws on Elias for the self-discipline of observers.
strands.works: Daston, “The Moral Economy of Science” (1995), 3–5, 21–24

science.scope_note: Kuhn is a central reorientation, not the field’s sole founder. Sarton, Koyré, Merton, and historians of experimental practice distinguish important approaches; Yates and Foucault are additional contributions. Chinese science and women’s scientific work expand this selection; it still needs fuller coverage of other regions and material practices. Named Chinese-series contributors and Daston/Galison’s image and instrument studies deepen the selection. Publication credits do not replace primary argument checks; wider regional coverage remains selective. Arabic mathematics, colonial Indian science, African healing and a Beninese knowledge programme are separate selected projects, not regional proxies or exhaustive coverage.

psychohistory.label: Psychohistory / psychoanalytic history
psychohistory.description: A contested range of historical uses of psychological interpretation: psychosocial life studies, psychoanalytically informed contextual history and theories of childrearing and collective fantasy. Disagreements concern sources, explanatory scale, historical variability and retrospective inference.
psychohistory.representative_figures_and_works: Erik H. Erikson, Young Man Luther: A Study in Psychoanalysis and History (1958); Peter Gay, Freud for Historians (1985). These projects should not be treated as straightforward applications of Lacan.

psychohistory.scope_note: Erikson, Gay and deMause have different explanatory ambitions; they are not interchangeable applications of Lacan. Schapiro’s art-historical criticism supplies a methodological interlocutor, not blanket rejection of psychoanalysis. Pollock’s thesis and deMause’s later response address distinct texts and disputed evidential procedures. Original case books and wider political, religious and regional applications remain selective research limits; theoretical or clinical assertions are not established diagnoses of past people.

philhistory.label: Explanation & objectivity debates
philhistory.date_label: Earlier roots · Becker address 1931 · Hempel 1942 · Carr 1961 · Elton 1967
philhistory.description: Disputes concern general laws, understanding actions, historical facts, and the possibility of objectivity. Analytic philosophy’s covering-law debate overlaps with historians’ arguments about evidence and interpretation without being identical to them. Narrative theory enters a discussion already under way.
philhistory.representative_figures_and_works: Becker’s 1931 address (published 1932); Hempel, “The Function of General Laws in History” (1942); Dray, Laws and Explanation in History (1957); Carr, What Is History? (1961); Elton, The Practice of History (1967).

representative_people.works: Everyman His Own Historian (address 1931; publication 1932)

representative_people.context: Proposes testable laws and initial conditions, allowing probability and incomplete explanation sketches.

representative_people.context: Challenges reducing all historical explanations to a covering-law model; rational action and pragmatic questions are distinct concerns.
representative_people.works: Laws and Explanation in History (1957)

representative_people.context: Treats selection, interpretation and research as reciprocal while rejecting equal validity for every account.

strands.title: Genealogy, values and historical explanation

strands.title: Rhetoric, reference and historical achievement

strands.title: The historian, surviving sources and the historical picture

strands.title: Evidence, understanding and the historical question
strands.focus: Droysen, Dilthey, Croce and Collingwood offer different accounts of what inquiry does with traces, thought, context and practical concerns. These are explicit conceptual resources, not a common doctrine or a proved genealogy of later debate.

strands.title: Language use and following rules

strands.title: Knowing how, action and accomplishment

strands.title: Selection, relevance and revisable interpretation

frankfurt.description: Critical theorists draw differently on Marx, Weber, and Freud to examine domination, culture, and rationality. Benjamin’s reflections on historical time and Habermas’s public sphere offer distinct resources for historians. Benjamin’s association with the Institute and Habermas’s later work should not imply a single institutional position or doctrine.

Georg Lukács: History and Class Consciousness (1923), as precursor; Siegfried Kracauer.

practice.label: Practice theory
practice.description: Examines how embodied dispositions and situated activities reproduce or alter social relations. Bourdieu’s habitus and strategies, de Certeau’s tactics, and Sewell’s account of structure offer different ways to connect agency, constraint, and meaning. These are several resources for reassessing cultural history, not a single replacement paradigm.

culturalstudies.label: British cultural studies
culturalstudies.description: Examines culture as lived and contested, including popular forms, class, media, race, and gender. Debates among culturalist, structuralist, feminist, and antiracist projects reshape the field. It exchanges ideas with historical scholarship while retaining distinct institutional and disciplinary histories.

Contributors listed as theoretical resources are not thereby CCCS members. Exchanges with history do not make the fields identical.

newleft.label: New Left & radical history (US)
newleft.description: Challenges consensus interpretations through studies of class, race, capitalism, and empire. Radical diplomatic, labour, and slavery histories overlap with new social history but differ in politics and method. Their engagements with Black history do not supply that field’s independent origins. Gutman’s cultural labor history also criticizes some New Left institutional accounts. Alice and Staughton Lynd make organizer testimony and participant review part of research practice; Zinn’s selective Marxian commitments differ from Genovese’s paternalism interpretation.

demography.label: Historical demography & history of the family
demography.description: Combines related inquiries into population, households, childhood and intimate relations. Henry’s family reconstitution and Cambridge’s aggregate and household studies differ from Ariès’s historical concepts and Stone’s family interpretation. Pollock’s criticism questions evidence and sweeping changes in parental care. Lee and Wang’s Chinese population study challenges received Malthusian comparisons without making the field’s regional patterns uniform.

representative_people.works: “Reflections on the European Marriage Pattern” (1991)

representative_people.context: Connects the postwar baby boom to marriage timing, employment constraints and policy as well as prosperity. Own PBS answer gives multiple mechanisms; does not reduce family history to fertility statistics.
representative_people.works: Great Expectations (1980); Homeward Bound (1988); America and the Pill (2010).

demography.scope_note: Family reconstitution and aggregate reconstruction differ from histories of childhood or family meanings; Henry, Annales, and Cambridge are not interchangeable. Household composition, marriage behavior, concepts of childhood and parental conduct are different objects of study. England and France are prominent in this selection; Chinese comparative research broadens the questions without representing all non-European family histories. Later institutional webpages are retrospective sources, not an extension beyond 2000.

strands.title: Reconstituting families from historical records
strands.focus: Link records of family events while examining who disappears from observation; Henry flags mobility and social differences, and Cambridge’s 1997 study is explicitly collaborative.
strands.works: Anciennes familles genevoises (1956); English Population History from Family Reconstitution (1997)

strands.title: Reconstructing aggregate population
strands.focus: Use historical demographic observations to estimate population and vital rates; a national reconstruction is distinct from following the observed life of one family.
strands.works: The Population History of England 1541–1871: A Reconstruction (1981)

strands.title: Households and comparative marriage patterns
strands.focus: Compare household composition and marriage patterns without inferring feelings from household size or treating one region as universal.
strands.works: Household and Family in Past Time (1972); “European Marriage Patterns in Perspective” (1965)

strands.title: Childhood concepts, conduct and evidence
strands.focus: Ariès examines childhood as a historical concept; Pollock questions broad change narratives through personal documents. Affection and recognition of a separate life stage are not identical claims.
strands.works: Centuries of Childhood (1962); The Forgotten Children (1981); Forgotten Children (1983)

strands.title: Marriage, intimacy and disputed change
strands.focus: Stone’s affective-individualism interpretation meets criticism of its explanation and evidential selection. Neither prescriptive literature nor diary writers transparently represent everyone.
strands.works: The Family, Sex and Marriage in England (1977); Pollock’s thesis, pp. 96–98 and 143–144 (1981)

strands.title: Chinese population and Malthusian comparisons
strands.focus: Lee and Wang argue for forms of population regulation missed by received China/West contrasts. Their fertility and marriage claims remain arguments to test against evidence and regional variation.
strands.works: One Quarter of Humanity (1999)

strands.title: Patterns, exceptions and explanation
strands.focus: Hajnal distinguishes late marriage from remaining unmarried, acknowledges regional variation and separates identifying a pattern from explaining it. Goody questions its uniqueness and the scale of comparison.

strands.title: Local monographs and collective sampling
strands.focus: Fleury and Henry credit Goubert and other researchers, but argue that chosen parish monographs cannot simply be added into a national sample. Biraben joins their subsequent register inventory.
strands.works: Fleury/Henry (1958),665; Biraben/Fleury/Henry (1960), metadata

strands.title: Population totals and family subsets
strands.focus: Henry’s survey account distinguishes aggregate reconstruction from the smaller rural sample used for family reconstitution. Changes in sampling and uneven record quality constrain what each can establish.
strands.works: INED survey account (1978),230–232

strands.title: Observed fertility and deliberate control
strands.focus: Lee and Wang interpret delayed first births, longer intervals and earlier stopping as marital restraint. Harrell’s later review questions source completeness, regional reach and whether these patterns establish intentional control.
strands.works: One Quarter of Humanity (1999),86–90; Harrell review (2003),543

strands.title: Local evidence and collaborative reconstruction
strands.focus: Harrell’s collection brings local demographic studies together; Lee and Wang acknowledge Campbell’s contributions. A broad comparative argument still requires attention to differences among local sources.
strands.works: Chinese Historical Microdemography (1995); One Quarter of Humanity (1999), opening acknowledgment

strands.title: Family change, social differences and source selection
strands.focus: Stone qualifies affective individualism with reversals and overlapping patterns across social groups, while making a debatable assumption about surviving documents. Pollock separates childhood concepts, affection and discipline and questions how family histories generalize from their sources.
strands.works: Stone, abridged edition (1979), 21–29; Pollock, Forgotten Children (1983), 1–10

strands.title: Italian residence and marriage patterns
strands.focus: Kertzer and Hogan report patrilocal residence without the expected combination of early female marriage, large spousal age differences and low nonmarriage. Similar marriage ages among wage workers and sharecroppers complicate a simple account of proletarianization.
strands.works: “Reflections on the European Marriage Pattern” (1991), Casalecchio, 1861–1921

historicalsociology.label: Comparative historical sociology
historicalsociology.description: Compares how states, rights, class relations and collective struggles change. Moore studies agrarian routes; Skocpol combines state breakdown with class and international relations; Tilly follows contention; Mann maps intersecting power networks. Bendix, Goldstone, Somers and Block supply different questions about authority, demography, citizenship and economic institutions. Sewell’s exchange with Skocpol makes ideology an explicit debate.
historicalsociology.representative_figures_and_works: Barrington Moore, Social Origins of Dictatorship and Democracy (1966); Theda Skocpol, States and Social Revolutions (1979); Charles Tilly; Michael Mann, The Sources of Social Power I (1986); Perry Anderson (1974).

representative_people.context: Compares agrarian elites, peasants and political routes; violence accompanies even paths to democracy.
representative_people.works: Social Origins of Dictatorship and Democracy (1966)

representative_people.context: Explains revolutionary breakdown and reconstruction through class relations, state organization and international pressures; later acknowledges shortcomings in her treatment of ideology.
representative_people.works: States and Social Revolutions (1979); “Cultural Idioms and Political Ideologies” (1985)

representative_people.context: Historical sociologist connecting political/economic transformations, collective struggles and repertoires; treats movements as historically specific.
representative_people.works: The Contentious French (1986); “Social Movements as Historically Specific Clusters of Political Performances” (1993–1994)

representative_people.context: Distinguishes ideological, economic, military and political resources and their overlapping spatial networks.
representative_people.works: The Sources of Social Power I (1986)

representative_people.context: Marxist comparisons of transitions from ancient slavery to feudalism and of divergent absolutist states, centered on Europe.
representative_people.works: Passages from Antiquity to Feudalism; Lineages of the Absolutist State (1974)

representative_people.context: Compares authority and citizenship while questioning a uniform route to modernity.
representative_people.works: Nation-Building and Citizenship (1964; enlarged editions 1977, 1996)

representative_people.context: Investigates population pressures interacting with institutions and elites in European and Asian state crises.
representative_people.works: Revolution and Rebellion in the Early Modern World (1991)

representative_people.context: Studies citizenship through law, political culture and regional associations; with Block, reconsiders Polanyi’s resources for historical sociology.
representative_people.works: “Citizenship and the Place of the Public Sphere” (1993); with Fred Block, “Beyond the Economistic Fallacy” (1984)

representative_people.context: Collaborates with Somers in interpreting Polanyi for historical sociology; not sole author of their intervention.
representative_people.works: With Margaret R. Somers, “Beyond the Economistic Fallacy” (1984)

representative_people.works: The Great Transformation (1944); reconsidered by Block and Somers (1984)

representative_people.context: Critic of Skocpol’s treatment of ideology who also values her comparative structural analysis.
representative_people.works: “Ideologies and Social Revolutions: Reflections on the French Case” (1985)

representative_people.context: Compares multiple, continually reconstructed modern programs and their institutional settings, rejecting simple Western convergence and uncomplicated optimism. His earlier empire comparison examines political leadership, resource mobilization and conflicts; later reflection retains qualifications about its structural-functional assumptions.
representative_people.works: Multiple Modernities (2000), pp. 1–4, 24–26; The Political Systems of Empires (1963), selected prefaces in 1993/2017 reissue; Stein Rokkan Lecture (1985)

representative_people.context: Compares Chinese and European economic/state trajectories, using and testing historical categories.
representative_people.works: China Transformed (1997), selected chapter openings

representative_people.works: Review of Revolution and Rebellion in the Early Modern World (1992), 827

representative_people.works: “Dimensions of State Formation and Nation-Building” (1975), discussed by Eisenstadt in the Stein Rokkan Lecture (1985)

representative_people.context: A regional historian’s challenge to treating states and ideological categories as self-contained comparative units.
representative_people.works: “Connected Histories” (1997), especially 758–759

representative_people.context: Comparative analysis of agrarian property relations; Callinicos (1994) places the work 'within the canon of what has come to be known as historical sociology'.
representative_people.works: Past and Present (1976; 1982)

representative_people.context: Argues that Guha’s Dominance without Hegemony and Chakrabarty’s work misread European history, holding that the bourgeois revolutions did not create the inclusive political order Guha’s contrast assumes (2013–14); Sewell and Steinmetz accept his critique of Guha’s Europe while questioning parts of his own history.
representative_people.works: Postcolonial Theory and the Specter of Capital (2013); “Confronting Postcolonial Theory: A Response to Critics” (2014)

representative_people.context: Comparative teaching context for group solidarity and political change; no direct influence on the modern field or its named practitioners is established.
representative_people.works: Muqaddimah; retrospective comparison through the Stanford entry and Hannoum

representative_people.context: His account of state legibility joins names, cadastral surveys and standardization to the capacity to intervene. The read 2008 interview also follows practical counter-planning and applies standardization to capitalist firms.
representative_people.works: Seeing Like a State (1998); “Seeing Like a Society,” author interview with Erik Gerritsen (2008)

representative_people.context: Historicizes familiar family institutions and social attitudes, opening comparative questions between modernity and earlier arrangements.
representative_people.works: Histoire des populations françaises et de leurs attitudes devant la vie depuis le XVIIIe siècle (1948); L’Enfant et la vie familiale sous l’Ancien Régime (1960); Centuries of Childhood, translated by Robert Baldick (1962); L’Homme devant la mort (1977).

representative_people.context: Noiriel’s socio-history connects archival reconstruction to relationships of power and social interdependence. Own 2012 opening describes a collective project influenced by sociology, not a claim of sole foundation or institutional membership.
representative_people.works: Les Ouvriers dans la société française (1986); Le Creuset français (1988); Introduction à la socio-histoire (2006).

representative_people.context: Treats historical social science as a challenge to fixed disciplinary boundaries and ahistorical universal laws. Williams’s framing (p. 203) and Wallerstein’s replies (pp. 206–207), read: historical systems, knowledge structures and disciplinary restructuring. The framing is attributed to Williams. A methodological contribution, without a founding claim or treating future-system predictions as established fact.
representative_people.works: Unthinking Social Science (1991); Open the Social Sciences (collective Gulbenkian Commission report, 1996)

historicalsociology.scope_note: A field of competing comparisons, not one state-centered theory. Cases range beyond Europe, but this selection is uneven and does not exhaust regional traditions. Cultural and institutional explanations can be combined; political outcomes are not inevitable stages.

strands.title: Agrarian relations and political routes
strands.focus: Class alliances and rural power produce divergent, often violent paths rather than a smooth democratic sequence.
strands.works: Moore, Social Origins (1966)

strands.title: States and revolutionary transformations
strands.focus: State organizations, agrarian classes and international competition enter a combined explanation.
strands.works: Skocpol, States and Social Revolutions (1979)

strands.title: Contention and repertoires
strands.focus: Historically specific performances link local claims to wider transformations.
strands.works: Tilly, The Contentious French (1986); political-performances essay (1993–1994)

strands.title: Overlapping networks of power
strands.focus: Forms and reach of power are differentiated rather than enclosed in one homogeneous society.
strands.works: Mann, The Sources of Social Power I (1986)

strands.title: Comparative Marxian transitions
strands.focus: European transitions and divergent state forms frame a contested comparative synthesis.
strands.works: Anderson, Passages and Lineages (1974)

strands.title: Authority, law and citizenship
strands.focus: Bendix compares authority; Somers examines how local relations and national law shape rights. Their methods are distinct.
strands.works: Bendix (1964); Somers (1993)

strands.title: Reconsidering Polanyi
strands.focus: A specific collaborative engagement with economic institutions broadens the field’s conceptual resources.
strands.works: Block and Somers (1984) on Polanyi (1944)

strands.title: Population, institutions and state crises
strands.focus: Demographic pressures acquire political effects through institutions and elite relations, not population alone.
strands.works: Goldstone, Revolution and Rebellion (1991)

strands.title: Ideology within structural explanation
strands.focus: Sewell criticizes a restricted account of ideology; Skocpol acknowledges a problem and responds. Her reply’s opening also questions Sewell’s anonymous conception of culture; the exchange contains disagreement in both directions.
strands.works: Sewell–Skocpol exchange (1985; reprinted 1994)

strands.title: Interdependence and group power
strands.focus: Court settings and community exclusion are distinct research scales.
strands.works: The Court Society (1969); The Established and the Outsiders (1965)

strands.title: Sport and regulated excitement
strands.focus: Sport opens a further historical problem of affect and interdependence.
strands.works: Quest for Excitement (1986)

strands.title: Comparing crises and their different outcomes
strands.focus: Goldstone compares England and the Fronde, then distinguishes Castile from the Spanish monarchy’s rebellious peripheries. Similar pressures need not produce identical outcomes. Perry values the comparison but questions how far its claims travel across different societies and periods.
strands.works: Goldstone (1991), 156–169; Perry review (1992), 827

strands.title: Empire formation and conflicting political aims
strands.focus: Eisenstadt’s prefaces distinguish social conditions from the emergence of leaders able to organize an imperial polity. Rulers seek resources less bound to traditional groups while trying to control those resources themselves. This comparison retains structural-functional and evolutionary assumptions that his retrospective introduction discusses rather than simply disowns.
strands.works: The Political Systems of Empires (1963), selected prefaces

strands.title: Questioning the units of comparison
strands.focus: Eisenstadt takes up Rokkan’s attention to cultural and territorial settings and questions exporting European state categories. Subrahmanyam separately uses Eurasian circulation to challenge autonomous-state and ideological partitions. These are distinct arguments, not a demonstrated intellectual lineage between the authors.
strands.works: Eisenstadt, Stein Rokkan Lecture (1985); Subrahmanyam, Connected Histories (1997)

strands.title: State legibility and the limits of imposed plans
strands.focus: Scott asks how names, addresses, surveys and standards make societies open to administrative intervention, and how planning is altered by the social practices it encounters. His 2008 account also applies standardization to capitalist firms. These are comparative questions with attributed examples, not a single theory of every state.
strands.works: Seeing Like a State (1998); “Seeing Like a Society,” author interview (2008)

nationalismstudies.label: Nationalism studies
nationalismstudies.description: Makes the formation of nations and traditions an object of historical explanation. Anderson, Gellner, and Hobsbawm offer different modernist accounts; ethno-symbolist and postcolonial critics question their premises. Treating national identity as historical does not require assuming that every tradition is a recent invention.
nationalismstudies.representative_figures_and_works: Benedict Anderson, Imagined Communities (1983); Ernest Gellner, Nations and Nationalism (1983); Hobsbawm and Ranger, The Invention of Tradition (1983); Anthony D. Smith; Partha Chatterjee, Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World (1986).

representative_people.context: Connects national imagining to print markets and language; imagined communities are not thereby unreal.
representative_people.works: Imagined Communities (1983)

representative_people.context: Relates nationalism to modern mobility and mastery of a shared literate culture; his reply to Smith allows varied cultural continuities.
representative_people.works: Nations and Nationalism (1983); Warwick reply (1995/1996)

representative_people.context: Combines constructed traditions with uneven and changing national identifications.
representative_people.works: With Ranger, The Invention of Tradition (1983); Nations and Nationalism since 1780 (1990; second edition 1992)

representative_people.works: The Ethnic Origins of Nations (1986); Warwick opening statement (1995/1996)

representative_people.context: Criticizes accounts that leave anticolonial nationalists only derivative models; develops a distinct argument from colonial Bengal.
representative_people.works: Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World (1986); The Nation and Its Fragments (1993)

representative_people.works: Social Preconditions of National Revival in Europe (English 1985); “From National Movement to the Fully-formed Nation” (1993)

representative_people.works: Rescuing History from the Nation (1995)

representative_people.works: The Chinese Nation Is One (1939; through named readers)

representative_people.context: Interprets French national belonging as historically produced through uneven rural integration. Agulhon’s substantive review843reports the thesis and questions its political periodization; not automatic adoption of the modernization label.
representative_people.works: Peasants into Frenchmen (1976); France: Fin de Siècle (1986); The Hollow Years (1994).

representative_people.context: Challenges claims of unbroken ancient national identity by tracing changing medieval identifications and the modern political uses of their history.
representative_people.works: Furta Sacra (1978); “Sacred Commodities” (1986); Living with the Dead (1994); Phantoms of Remembrance (1994).

representative_people.context: Studies national belonging as a historical product of imperial power, difference and negotiated identities.
representative_people.works: The Sense of the People (1995); The Island Race (2003); A New Imperial History (edited, 2004); Strolling Players of Empire (2021).

nationalismstudies.scope_note: Anderson, Gellner, Hobsbawm, Smith, and Chatterjee supply competing accounts, not a common modernist theory. Hroch’s comparative phases, Billig’s everyday reminders and Yuval-Davis’s gender analysis address different questions. Nations, states and nationalist movements are not interchangeable; European typologies require testing beyond their original cases.

strands.title: Print markets and national imagining
strands.focus: Language and circulating print help make unfamiliar people imaginable as a community.
strands.works: Imagined Communities (1983)

strands.title: Modern mobility and literate culture
strands.focus: The changing social role of culture supplies Gellner’s explanation; it is not merely a story of ancient identities awakening.
strands.works: Nations and Nationalism; Warwick reply

strands.title: Historically produced traditions
strands.focus: Rituals and claims of continuity have specific histories in national and imperial settings.
strands.works: The Invention of Tradition (1983)

strands.title: Ethnic ties, myths and memories
strands.focus: Earlier cultural inheritances help explain particular nationalisms without making all nations timeless.
strands.works: The Ethnic Origins of Nations; Warwick opening

strands.title: Comparing national movements
strands.focus: Scholarship, agitation and mass participation are distinguished in a model attentive to social conditions and interrupted development.
strands.works: Social Preconditions (1985); Hroch (1993)

strands.title: Anticolonial imagination and difference
strands.focus: The material/spiritual distinction identifies a claimed cultural domain of autonomy before political sovereignty.
strands.works: The Nation and Its Fragments (1993), pp. 4–7

strands.title: Routine reproduction of nationhood
strands.focus: Everyday language and symbols sustain belonging outside conspicuous nationalist movements.
strands.works: Banal Nationalism (1995)

strands.title: Gender, citizenship and national projects
strands.focus: Gender relations organize national reproduction and membership across, within and beyond state boundaries.
strands.works: Gender and Nation (1997)

atlantic.label: Atlantic & diaspora histories
atlantic.description: Studies movements and connections across the Atlantic, including slavery, empire, commerce, and the African diaspora. Oceanic history and diaspora studies overlap without being identical. Gilroy’s critique of national and racial absolutism differs from demographic reconstruction and from histories centered on imperial institutions.
atlantic.representative_figures_and_works: Philip Curtin, The Atlantic Slave Trade: A Census (1969); John Thornton, Africa and Africans in the Making of the Atlantic World (1992); Paul Gilroy, The Black Atlantic (1993); Bernard Bailyn’s Atlantic history initiatives. Earlier resources include James and Williams. Paul E. Lovejoy: “The African Diaspora” (1997).

consumption.label: Consumption & material culture
consumption.description: Examines commercial promotion, household demand, goods’ changing value, taste, gender and provisioning. McKendrick, Brewer and Plumb distinguish commercial and social changes; de Vries connects consumption with household labor; Mintz links diets to colonial production. Anthropological and feminist approaches ask how objects acquire meanings and how consumer roles depend on unequal social relations.
consumption.representative_figures_and_works: McKendrick, Brewer, and Plumb, The Birth of a Consumer Society (1982); Appadurai, ed., The Social Life of Things (1986); Brewer and Porter, eds., Consumption and the World of Goods (1993); Mintz, Sweetness and Power (1985). Additional readings: Douglas and Isherwood, The World of Goods (1979); Kopytoff on cultural biography (1986); de Vries on industrious change (1994); de Grazia and Furlough, The Sex of Things (1996). Maxine Berg and Helen Clifford, eds.: Consumers and Luxury (1999).

consumption.scope_note: Demand, taste, provisioning, commodities, and material objects are not one theory; gender and empire connect consumption to production. Commodity circulation, cultural biography and goods as communication are distinct questions. De Vries acknowledges conflicting household interests; feminist research does not reduce women to consumers. Much of this selection concerns Europe and the United States; Mintz’s colonial production connects regions but does not make the coverage global in every respect.

strands.focus: Fashion and pottery promotion, politics, leisure and childhood are different parts of the 1982 collaboration. Its consumer-revolution framing and gender assumptions invite criticism.

strands.title: Households, labor and demand

strands.works: “The Industrial Revolution and the Industrious Revolution” (1994)

strands.works: The Social Life of Things (1986), introduction

strands.focus: A thing’s commodity status can change over time or differ between people; material production alone does not settle its social classification.
strands.works: “The Cultural Biography of Things” (1986)

strands.title: Goods as social communication
strands.focus: Douglas and Isherwood examine goods as an information system through which people conduct social relations.
strands.works: The World of Goods (1979)

strands.title: Taste and social position
strands.focus: Read tastes and cultural practices in relation to social position, alongside approaches centered on circulation or household provisioning.
strands.works: Distinction (1979; English 1984)

strands.title: Gendered consumption, work and identity
strands.focus: Investigate the division of family labor, male and female consumer identities, class differences and state definitions; avoid one universal consumer.
strands.works: The Sex of Things (1996)

strands.title: Inventory evidence and its boundaries
strands.focus: Weatherill records selected goods across probate inventories. Missing laborers, debts, real estate and reliable clothing values constrain what household ownership can establish about society.

strands.title: Purchasing as household work
strands.focus: Vickery’s selected households distribute purchasing tasks and authority unevenly. Expenditure diaries show practical expertise, but incomplete income records limit reconstruction of financial power.

strands.title: Material meanings and unequal possibilities
strands.focus: Vickery finds social ambition alongside attachment and remembrance. Age, resources and inheritance matter; her chapter does not establish one feminine attitude to possessions.
strands.works: The Gentleman’s Daughter (1998), “Elegance” closing discussion

strands.title: Competing chronologies and questions
strands.focus: Compare McKendrick’s eighteenth-century acceleration, Weatherill’s earlier middling ownership and de Vries’s household labor argument. Vickery questions universal motives. Different evidence and outcomes do not yield one automatic date for a consumer society.
strands.works: McKendrick (1982), introduction; Weatherill (1996), preface; de Vries (1994); Vickery (1998)

strands.title: Ming consumers and social distinctions
strands.focus: Clunas reads Wen Zhenheng’s judgments about appropriate objects as elite distinctions, then compares them with Yan Song’s confiscation inventory. These are different sources, not interchangeable records of actual purchasing.
strands.works: Superfluous Things (1991), 40–53

strands.title: Whose consumption becomes visible?
strands.focus: Clunas’s selected texts privilege elite men. Rules assigning objects to women do not directly recover women’s own meanings; subsistence consumers also remain poorly represented. Pagani highlights this limit while praising the method.
strands.works: Clunas (1991), 53–56; Pagani (1993), paragraphs 14–16

strands.title: Relics and changing value
strands.focus: Geary follows transfers and renewed authentication of relics. Their careers may change how communities value them; price equivalences and the relative frequency of different transfers remain uncertain.

strands.title: Specific historical uses of theory

truthdebate.label: Historians’ responses to postmodernism
truthdebate.description: Brings together disputes about evidence, narrative, realism, and social explanation. Defences of historical knowledge, postmodern arguments, and revisions of cultural history are competing positions rather than a consensus or final resolution. Hunt participates in several of these reassessments, making them useful companions to her later global-era argument.

urbanhistory.label: Urban history
urbanhistory.date_label: Earlier city histories · postwar expansion · Urban History Yearbook 1974
urbanhistory.description: Studies cities and urbanization through institutions, populations, built environments and connections beyond city boundaries. Local reconstruction, quantitative mobility research, colonial spatial analysis and histories of segregation or public landscapes form different approaches.

David Harvey: Social Justice and the City (1973); Walter Benjamin: Das Passagen-Werk (1982); Michel de Certeau: “Walking in the City” (1980). Sven Beckert, The Monied Metropolis (2001), selected introduction on urban bourgeois class formation.

urbanhistory.scope_note: British institution-building and US quantitative urban studies do not define one school or exhaust the field. Cities are not self-contained units. Journal milestones mark consolidation, not the first historical study of cities.

intellectualhistory.label: Intellectual history
intellectualhistory.date_label: Earlier histories of thought · Lovejoy 1936 · Skinner 1969 · plural programmes through the 1990s
intellectualhistory.description: Studies thought, concepts, arguments and their production, circulation and interpretation in historical settings. History of ideas, contextual political thought, conceptual history, textual criticism and the material history of publishing supply overlapping but disputed methods. Intellectual history extends beyond the Cambridge School and beyond a canon of European philosophers.

Pocock: “The history of political thought” (1962); The Machiavellian Moment (1975); Annabel S. Brett: Liberty, Right and Nature (1997); Reinhart Koselleck: Futures Past (German 1979; English 1985); Dominick LaCapra: Rethinking Intellectual History (1983); John E. Toews: “Intellectual History after the Linguistic Turn” (1987); Robert Darnton: The Business of Enlightenment (1979); Masao Maruyama: Studies in the Intellectual History of Tokugawa Japan (essays 1940–1944; English 1974); Mikiso Hane: English translation of Maruyama’s Studies (1974).

intersectionality.label: Intersectional analysis
intersectionality.date_label: Earlier Black feminist roots · Crenshaw 1989 · Cohen 1997
intersectionality.description: Examines how relations of race, gender, class and sexuality interact in specific structures of power. Crenshaw challenges single-axis frameworks that obscure Black women; Cohen brings an explicit intersectional critique to queer politics. The approach connects distinct fields without merging their objects or methods.
intersectionality.scope_note: An analytical approach with Black feminist and other intellectual and political roots, not a single school founded from nothing in 1989. Crenshaw’s legal critique and Cohen’s political intervention are distinct. Connections to gender, racial formation and queer history do not establish that every practitioner adopts this approach, or a direct Crenshaw–Omi/Winant borrowing.

cdn_religion_reform.label: Religion, social reform & secularization in Canada
cdn_religion_reform.date_label: Allen, The Social Passion 1971 · Cook, The Regenerators 1985 · secularization debate: Gauvreau 1991, Marshall 1992 and 1993–94, Christie and Gauvreau 1996 · selected later readings
cdn_religion_reform.description: Historical writing on Christianity as a force in Canadian reform, culture and everyday life, and on whether and when Canada secularized. Its central argument came in 1985–96. Ramsay Cook’s The Regenerators (1985) read late Victorian social criticism as the sacred becoming secular, and David Marshall’s Secularizing the Faith (1992) followed Protestant clergy through a crisis of belief to the 1920s as “an era of drift”. Their critics attacked this as the secularization thesis. Michael Gauvreau’s The Evangelical Century (1991) argued that the evangelical creed adapted to Darwinism and higher criticism; Marshall replied in 1993–94 that attempts to dismiss secularization were premature. In A Full-Orbed Christianity (1996) Nancy Christie and Gauvreau argued that the Protestant churches reached their greatest cultural influence before 1940 and placed secularization after the Second World War. Behind the debate stands Richard Allen’s The Social Passion (1971), which made the social gospel central to the history of reform, though recent doctoral work cites it far less. Social histories of Protestant culture, Methodism, gender and leisure (Westfall, Semple, Marks) moved the question from doctrine to lay practice. Catholic history developed alongside: Hamelin and Gagnon’s synthesis of Quebec Catholicism, Perin on Rome, McGowan on Irish Toronto. Gauvreau later carried the revision into Quebec, tracing the Quiet Revolution to Catholic Action (2005). Later work studies irreligion in settler British Columbia (Marks 2017), distinguishes political from social secularization (Van Die) and treats religion as a vehicle of the liberal order (Christie). Moral reform as regulation belongs to a neighbouring field.
cdn_religion_reform.representative_figures_and_works: Allen, The Social Passion (1971); Cook, The Regenerators (1985); Van Die, An Evangelical Mind (1989); Westfall, Two Worlds (1989); Gauvreau, The Evangelical Century (1991); Marshall, Secularizing the Faith (1992) and “Canadian Historians, Secularization and the Problem of the Nineteenth Century” (1993–94); Christie and Gauvreau, A Full-Orbed Christianity (1996); Marks, Revivals and Roller Rinks (1996); Semple, The Lord’s Dominion (1996); Hamelin and Gagnon, Histoire du catholicisme québécois: Le XXe siècle (1984); Perin, Rome in Canada (1990); McGowan, The Waning of the Green (1999); Ferretti (1999); Hubert (2000); Gauvreau, The Catholic Origins of Quebec’s Quiet Revolution (2005; strand in Quebec historiography); Christie and Gauvreau, Christian Churches and Their Peoples (2010); Marks, Infidels and the Damn Churches (2017). Comparison: Brown, The Death of Christian Britain (2001).
cdn_religion_reform.scope_note: A research field containing a debate. “Secularization thesis” is the name its critics gave to Cook’s and Marshall’s accounts (Laverdure’s 1998 review of Christie and Gauvreau); Marshall defended the concept in 1993–94. Both sides appear as historians. Catholic and Protestant histories have different genealogies; Irish Catholic history (McGowan, Perin) stays here. The Catholic Action revision of the Quiet Revolution (Meunier and Warren, Bienvenue, Gauvreau 2005) has its main home in Quebec historiography. Moral reform as regulation (Valverde) is placed in Moral regulation.

cdn_women_gender.label: Canadian women's & gender history
cdn_women_gender.date_label: Earlier women writers of history (recovered by Boutilier and Prentice 1997) and Cleverdon’s suffrage history 1950 · collections and studies 1976–79 · Collectif Clio 1982 · Prentice et al. 1988 · Parr 1990 · Left History exchange 1995–96 · selected publication milestones, not boundaries
cdn_women_gender.description: Canadian women's history studies women as historical actors in Canada and, increasingly from the 1990s, gender as a relation shaping work, family, politics, law and the state. Earlier women wrote national, local and regional history, recovered by Boutilier and Prentice (1997); Cleverdon studied the suffrage movement (1950); collections and studies of reform and women's organizations followed in the later 1970s (Cook and Mitchinson; Strong-Boag; Kealey). Two syntheses had different starting points. The Collectif Clio's L'histoire des femmes au Québec depuis quatre siècles (1982) rejected a male-centred history presented as everyone's history; Prentice and colleagues' Canadian Women: A History (1988) offered a collaborative survey. Studies of women and war (Pierson), women on the left (Sangster), working families in Montreal (Bradbury) and housewives in the Depression (Baillargeon) joined the field to labour and family history. Parr's comparison of two Ontario towns (1990) challenged assumptions about the separateness of gender and class roles. In the 1990s historians argued over whether gender history extended or displaced women's history: Pierson weighed the turn to deconstruction and Scott's theory of gender against experience and voice (1991), and Sangster's 'Beyond Dichotomies' (1995), by her later account, protested a hierarchy that set gender history above a 'limited' women's history; replies in Left History defended gender history (1996). Later work examined masculinity and gendered political languages (Morgan), sexuality and the law, and postwar domesticity and consumption (Parr, Korinek, Fahrni). Lévesque asked how far Quebec historiography had integrated women (1997); Quebec women's history is treated mainly under Quebec historiography.

cdn_women_gender.scope_note: A Canadian research field joining women's history and gender history; the entry does not decide the 1990s argument between them. Quebec women's history (Collectif Clio, Lévesque, Baillargeon) has its primary treatment in Quebec historiography; this entry keeps those authors' work on family, work and sexuality and a critique edge to Quebec historiography. Fur-trade women (Van Kirk) and gender and empire (Perry) are treated mainly in Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history and Settler colonialism and appear here as comparison rows; sexuality, law and regulation overlap with Moral regulation; childhood and family with Childhood, youth & family in Canada. Palmer's Descent into Discourse is treated in Canadian working-class history, as a critique of the linguistic turn, not of women's history.

strands.title: Earlier women writers of history
strands.focus: Women wrote Canadian history long before women’s history was a field: popular, local and regional historians (Machar, Skinner, Esther Clark Wright), the independent scholar Isabel Skelton, and a few university historians, among them Hilda Neatby and Margaret Ormsby, the CHA’s first and second women presidents (1962–63; 1965–66). In French Canada, Marie-Claire Daveluy wrote on New France. Most wrote national, local, fur-trade or political history; only Skelton (who “sought to write women back into Canadian history”, per Coulter’s reading of Crowley) and Daveluy (Bienvenue 2018) are documented as writing women in. They are earlier women writers of history, not founders of women’s history. Boutilier and Prentice’s Creating Historical Memory (1997) recovered this work and asked how professionalization masculinized history; the editors note that their subjects come mainly from “the white, Anglo-Celtic segment of society”. Cleverdon’s suffrage history (1950) is the earlier study of women that PhDs still cite. Bienvenue and Dorais (2023) extend the recovery to French Canada (after 2000).
strands.works: Boutilier and Prentice, eds., Creating Historical Memory (1997); Prentice, “Laying Siege to the History Professoriate” (1997); Cleverdon (1950); Bienvenue on Daveluy (2018)

strands.title: Gender history and women's history: the dichotomies exchange
strands.focus: Whether gender history extends or displaces women’s history. Pierson’s 1991 essay opens on the turn to deconstruction and Scott. She later found the exchange “not very satisfying, with discussants sometimes talking at cross-purposes”. The four Left History papers (1995–96) were read for revision 1.136 (Joy Parr's person entry): Iacovetta and Kealey call Parr 'a major figure in the field', and Sangster answers both replies.

strands.focus: Van Kirk’s women in fur-trade society (1980) and Perry’s gender and race in colonial British Columbia (1995, 2001) are treated mainly in Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history and Settler colonialism. McPherson (2000) credits Van Kirk’s research ‘and the critical debates it has aroused’ with ‘bringing cultural difference and conflict into Canadian women’s history’.
