cdn_childhood_youth.label: Childhood, youth & family in Canada
cdn_childhood_youth.date_label: Sutherland 1976 · Parr, ed., 1982 · Rooke and Schnell 1983 · 1990s expansion (Comacchio 1993 to Gleason 1999; Marshall 1998) · selected publication milestones, not boundaries
cdn_childhood_youth.description: Studies children, adolescents and families in Canadian history, and the reformers, experts, courts, schools and welfare programmes that sought to shape them. Neil Sutherland's Children in English-Canadian Society (1976) traced the reformers who pursued social improvement through children. Parr's study of British child immigrants (1980) and her collection Childhood and Family in Canadian History (1982), Rooke and Schnell's history of child rescue and the welfare state (1983) and Bradbury's family economies of industrial Montreal (1993) tied the field to family and labour history. The 1990s brought studies of maternal and infant welfare (Comacchio 1993), the baby boom (Owram 1996), youth and the making of heterosexuality (Adams 1997) and psychology and the 'normal' family (Gleason 1999). Francophone work examined family allowances and compulsory schooling (Marshall 1998), juvenile reform schools (Ménard 2003) and the medicalization of motherhood (Baillargeon 2004). Comacchio treats adolescence as a sociohistorical construction (2006); Myers studies girls, the courts and the policing of children in Montreal and beyond (2006, 2019). John Bullen's review essay on recent approaches to child-welfare history (1985) is the one early critique found. Historians also ask how young people's own experience can be recovered: Sutherland on adult memories of childhood (1992), and Gleason's critique of 'agency traps' (2016). The field overlaps with women's and gender history and with moral regulation; residential schooling of Indigenous children is treated primarily in the Native–newcomer entry.

Later readings: Sangster, Girl Trouble (2002); Ménard, Des enfants sous surveillance (2003); Baillargeon, Un Québec en mal d'enfants (2004); Comacchio, The Dominion of Youth (2006); Myers, Caught (2006) and Youth Squad (2019); Gleason et al., eds., Lost Kids (2010); Gleason, Small Matters (2013) and "Avoiding the Agency Trap" (2016).

It combines histories of children, youth and family with histories of child welfare, health, schooling and juvenile justice. Rosters overlap heavily with Canadian women's & gender history and Moral regulation; roster inclusion is not an exclusive placement. native_newcomer.label: Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history
native_newcomer.date_label: Earlier resources: Innis 1930, Stanley 1936 · Ray 1974 · Van Kirk and Brown 1980 · Trigger 1985 · Miller 1989 · Milloy 1999 · Ray, Miller and Tough 2000 · Podruchny 2006 · Carlson 2010 · Andersen's critique 2014 · CHA statement 2021
native_newcomer.description: A Canadian historiography of relations between Indigenous peoples and newcomers, centred first on the fur trade and then on policy, treaties, schools, missions, health and labour. Innis (1930) made the fur trade 'an introduction to Canadian economic history'; from the 1970s Ray, Van Kirk, Brown and Trigger recast it with Indigenous people as actors, and Trigger's Natives and Newcomers (1985) gave the field its older name. Later work studied reserves (Carter 1990), residential schools (Miller 1996; Milloy 1999), treaties (Ray, Miller and Tough 2000), health (Kelm 1998), labour (Lutz), voyageurs (Podruchny 2006), authenticity (Raibmon 2005) and Stó:lō historical consciousness (Carlson 2010). Critics questioned the frame: Brownlie and Kelm on agency as alibi (1994), Wheeler (1998) and LaRocque (1999) on its reliance on one side's records, Andersen on reading Métis through 'mixedness' rather than peoplehood (2014). In 2010 Peers and Podruchny wrote that the field had moved 'far beyond older narratives'; in 2021 the CHA Council said historians had 'contributed in lasting and tangible ways' to Canada's refusal to face this history.
native_newcomer.representative_figures_and_works: Innis, The Fur Trade in Canada (1930); Stanley, The Birth of Western Canada (1936); Ray, Indians in the Fur Trade (1974); Fisher, Contact and Conflict (1977); Van Kirk, “Many Tender Ties” (1980); Brown, Strangers in Blood (1980); Trigger, The Children of Aataentsic (1976), Natives and Newcomers (1985), “The Historians’ Indian” (1986); Delâge, Le pays renversé (1985); Dickason, The Myth of the Savage (1984), Canada’s First Nations (1992); Smith, Sacred Feathers (1987); Miller, Skyscrapers Hide the Heavens (1989), Shingwauk’s Vision (1996); Carter, Lost Harvests (1990); Coates, Best Left as Indians (1991); Lutz, “After the Fur Trade” (1992); Brownlie and Kelm, “Desperately Seeking Absolution” (1994); Kelm, Colonizing Bodies (1998); Milloy, “A National Crime” (1999). Later: Rutherdale (2002), Brownlie (2003), Raibmon (2005), Podruchny (2006), Lutz, Makúk (2008). Critics and alternatives: Sioui (1989), Paul, We Were Not the Savages (1993; 2000 edition), Stevenson [Wheeler], “The Othering of Indigenous History” (1998), LaRocque (1999); in the US, Fixico (2009) and S. A. Miller (2009). Later: Ray, Miller and Tough, Bounty and Benevolence (2000); Miller, Compact, Contract, Covenant (2009); Peers and Podruchny, eds., Gathering Places (2010); Carlson, The Power of Place, the Problem of Time (2010); Daschuk, Clearing the Plains (2013); Brown, An Ethnohistorian in Rupert's Land (2017); Milloy, 'A National Crime' (2017 reissue, foreword by McCallum). Critics: Andersen, 'Métis' (2014).
native_newcomer.scope_note: Part 1 of the Indigenous histories family (revision 1.201): mostly academic, mostly non-Indigenous Canadian scholarship about Indigenous–newcomer relations, built on company, church and state archives together with archaeology, anthropology and, increasingly, oral history. Indigenous-authored history and critique (Indigenous history) and community-engaged research are separate entries; Indigenous critics of the 'relations' framing (Sioui, Wheeler, LaRocque, Andersen; Fixico and S. Miller in the US) appear here as critics, not members, and the roster records no identity classification. The settler-scholar approaches formerly housed in Indigenous history (Miller's syntheses, Lutz's labour history, Harris's colonial geography, settler work on conservation and dispossession) now sit here. It is not Settler colonialism, which reads dispossession as a continuing structure; after 2000 settler-colonial analysis read this history as continuing dispossession, and Greer replied that commercial penetration was a different form of invasion. Francophone work is thin (Delâge, Sioui) and was not surveyed after 2000. The label keeps the field's word 'newcomer' but uses 'Indigenous'; 'native–newcomer', Trigger's 1985 term, is the field's historical name. Extended to 2024: Peers and Podruchny 2010 and Andersen 2014 introductions read; Podruchny 2006, Raibmon 2005, Carlson 2010 and Brownlie and Kelm 1994 unread in the body. History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23, Canadian theses citing: Carter 154, Perry 143, Harris 117, Ray 99, Trigger 97, Kelm 84, Brown 74, Milloy 74, Raibmon 72, Lutz 65, Podruchny 63, Carlson 49 (J. R. Miller's citation keys are not merged and he is not counted).

strands.title: The fur trade in national history
strands.focus: Innis makes the fur trade an introduction to Canadian economic history (1930); Stanley’s history of the West and the Riel resistances (1936) is reprinted and cited for decades. Both are resources the field later reworks, not its founders.
strands.works: Innis, The Fur Trade in Canada (1930); Stanley, The Birth of Western Canada (1936)

strands.title: Indigenous people as actors in the trade
strands.focus: Ray reconstructs Indigenous people’s roles as trappers, hunters and middlemen (1974); Fisher writes British Columbia contact as Indian–European relations (1977).
strands.works: Ray, Indians in the Fur Trade (1974); Fisher, Contact and Conflict (1977)

strands.title: Fur-trade families, Métis peoples and voyageurs
strands.focus: Women and kinship (Van Kirk) and company families (Brown) recast fur-trade society in 1980; Peterson and Brown’s collection treats Métis peoples in their own right (1985). Podruchny (2006) and Macdougall (2010) carry the strand past 2000. Andersen (2014) criticised 'the simplistic tropes of mixedness and hybridity that seem to fascinate so many scholars who write of Métis histories' and located Métis peoplehood in a Red River historical core. Brown had written that 'there is no single Metis core identity but rather a range along a spectrum' (as translated by Peers and Podruchny, 2010) and in 2017 named The New Peoples and Andersen's book as the older and newer poles of the field.
strands.works: Van Kirk (1980); Brown (1980); Peterson and Brown, eds. (1985); Podruchny (2006); Macdougall (2010)

strands.title: Contact, the Wendat and European representations
strands.focus: Trigger joins archaeology and documents to Wendat/Huron history before and after contact (1976) and reconsiders the ‘heroic age’ of New France (1985). Delâge writes the same encounter in French (1985); Dickason studies European representations (1984). Shared with the Ethnohistory entry.
strands.works: Trigger, The Children of Aataentsic (1976), Natives and Newcomers (1985); Delâge, Le pays renversé (1985); Dickason, The Myth of the Savage (1984)

strands.title: How historians wrote about Indigenous peoples
strands.focus: Walker (1971) and Trigger (1986) survey Canadian historical writing about Indigenous peoples. Trigger dates such studies from 1971 and describes ethnohistorical work across disciplines moving into national history.
strands.works: Walker, “The Indian in Canadian Historical Writing” (1971); Trigger, “The Historians’ Indian” (1986)

strands.title: Syntheses of relations and policy
strands.focus: Miller’s national synthesis of ‘Indian–white relations’ (1989), Dickason’s history of First Nations (1992), and regional or biographical studies (Smith 1987; Coates 1991). Miller’s and Dickason’s books differ in authorship and standpoint; they are grouped here as syntheses, not as one interpretation.
strands.works: Smith, Sacred Feathers (1987); Miller, Skyscrapers Hide the Heavens (1989); Coates, Best Left as Indians (1991); Dickason, Canada’s First Nations (1992)

strands.title: Reserves, residential schools and Indian agents
strands.focus: Reserve agriculture and policy (Carter 1990), residential schools (Miller 1996; Milloy 1999) and Indian agents (Brownlie 2003). Most predate the settler-colonial framework; whether any adopts it was not checked.
strands.works: Carter, Lost Harvests (1990); Miller, Shingwauk’s Vision (1996); Milloy, “A National Crime” (1999); Brownlie, A Fatherly Eye (2003)

strands.title: Health, missions and authenticity
strands.focus: Kelm reads health and healing through the body and colonial power (1998); Rutherdale studies gender and race in the mission field (2002); Raibmon treats authenticity as made by unequal collaborators (2005).
strands.works: Kelm, Colonizing Bodies (1998); Rutherdale, Women and the White Man’s God (2002); Raibmon, Authentic Indians (2005)

strands.title: Indigenous labour after the fur trade
strands.focus: Lutz treats Aboriginal people in British Columbia as a labouring class (1992) and later rewrites Aboriginal–white relations (2008). This is the strand that meets Canadian working-class history.
strands.works: Lutz, “After the Fur Trade” (1992); Makúk (2008)

strands.title: Agency as alibi? An internal critique
strands.focus: Brownlie and Kelm (1994) criticised agency-centred work on Indian policy and the potlatch law (Cole and Chaikin 1990; Miller; Loo 1992): stressing Native agency exaggerated how far it became effective self-defence, trivialising the harm of colonial policy and serving as an ‘alibi’ for it. A critique within policy history, not of the fur-trade literature; targets known from a secondary source, essay unread.
strands.works: Robin Brownlie and Mary-Ellen Kelm, “Desperately Seeking Absolution: Native Agency as Colonialist Alibi?” CHR 75:4 (December 1994): 543–56

strands.title: Indigenous critiques of the relations frame
strands.focus: Sioui (1989), Stevenson/Wheeler (1998) and LaRocque (1999) criticise the relations framing from Indigenous standpoints: its reliance on colonial documents, its disregard of oral history and its ethnological distance. Fixico and S. Miller (2009, US) question ‘Indian–white relations’ as the premise of Indian history. Paul’s We Were Not the Savages (1993; the 2000 Fernwood edition is the one PhDs cite), subtitled ‘a Mi’kmaq perspective’, rejects the ‘savage’ category (title and subtitle only). Adams’s Prison of Grass (1975) is an earlier counter-history of official history, not a critique of this field, and Dickason is a member of the field. Trigger (1986) and Brownlie and Kelm (1994) are non-Indigenous critiques from inside. These are critics and alternatives, not members.
strands.works: Sioui (1989); Paul (1993; 2000 ed.); Stevenson [Wheeler] (Fall 1998); LaRocque (1999); Fixico (2009); S. A. Miller (2009)

strands.title: After 2000: the settler-colonial reading and its critics
strands.focus: Settler-colonial analysis reads reserves, schools and dispossession as a continuing structure. Greer replies that the settler mode dominates some periods and regions and fades in others, and that commercial penetration (the fur trade’s mode) and extractivism are other forms of invasion. Konishi records Indigenous scholars’ critiques of settler colonial studies. Later readings only.
strands.works: Greer, “Settler Colonialism and Beyond” (JCHA 2019); Konishi (2019)

strands.title: Colonial geography and displacement
strands.focus: Harris's historical geography of British Columbia reads colonial land policy and reserves as geographical dispossession (1997, 2002). Val Napoleon's review held that Making Native Space 'recreates, from a settler perspective, BC history' (2004). Moved from Indigenous history in revision 1.201.
strands.works: The Resettlement of British Columbia (1997); Making Native Space (2002)

strands.title: Miller: relations and residential schools (moved)
strands.focus: Miller's national synthesis of 'Indian–white relations' (1989) and his history of residential schools (1996), which the publisher describes as archives plus interviews. Moved from Indigenous history in revision 1.201; it overlaps the strands on syntheses and on reserves and schools.
strands.works: Skyscrapers Hide the Heavens (1989); Shingwauk’s Vision (1996)

strands.title: Indigenous labour and exchange
strands.focus: Lutz's 1992 article on the Aboriginal labouring class of British Columbia. Moved from Indigenous history in revision 1.201 with its id; it overlaps the strand on labour after the fur trade, which also carries Makúk.
strands.works: After the Fur Trade (1992)

strands.title: Parks, game laws and dispossession
strands.focus: Settler historians of conservation: Binnema and Niemi (2006) on the Stoney excluded from Banff for game, sport, tourism and assimilation; Sandlos (2007) on northern game laws and sanctuaries as the state's authority over Dene and Inuit hunting; Spence (1999) on Indian removal and the national parks as the United States comparison. Carried over from Indigenous history's 'Land' strand in revision 1.201; O'Brien's Natick history stays there. The environment entry carries the same scholarship in its own strand.
strands.works: Spence, Dispossessing the Wilderness (1999); Binnema and Niemi (2006); Sandlos, Hunters at the Margin (2007)

strands.title: Treaty histories
strands.focus: Ray, Miller and Tough's history of the Saskatchewan treaties draws 'on a wide range of documentary sources' to show how the treaties were shaped by Hudson's Bay Company diplomacy, eastern treaty practice and western change, and why misunderstandings and disputes followed (2000, publisher's description). Miller's general history of treaty-making followed (2009).
strands.works: Ray, Miller and Tough, Bounty and Benevolence (2000); Miller, Compact, Contract, Covenant (2009)

strands.title: The field's accounts of itself after 2000
strands.focus: In 2010 Peers and Podruchny called Aboriginal history 'one of the most significant changes in Canadian historiography since the 1970s', said it had 'moved far beyond older narratives', and criticised archive-only work for 'shallow ethnocentric interpretations'; Brown's collected essays (2017) revisit her own terms. In 2021 the Canadian Historical Association's Council stated that historians 'have often been reticent to acknowledge this history as genocide' and had 'contributed in lasting and tangible ways' to Canada's refusal to come to grips with it. In 2022 Fraser and Stevenson evaluated 'the foundations of professional historical writing in Canada' in the light of the TRC (abstract).
strands.works: Peers and Podruchny, eds., Gathering Places (2010); Brown, An Ethnohistorian in Rupert's Land (2017); CHA Council statement (2021); Fraser and Stevenson, CHR (2022)

coverage.basis: Reviewed through 2000 in the original 1920–2000 experiment; extended to 2024 in revision 1.201 (reading of 2026-10-27): Canadian books after 2000 by description, review or sample chapter (Peers and Podruchny 2010 and Andersen 2014 introductions read); Podruchny 2006, Raibmon 2005, Carlson 2010 and Brownlie and Kelm 1994 unread in the body. Francophone work after 2000 not surveyed.

quebec_historiography.label: Quebec historiography
quebec_historiography.date_label: Earlier national history (Groulx) · Institut d’histoire de l’Amérique française founded 1946, its Revue from 1947 · Montreal and Laval schools 1950s–60s · Histoire du Québec contemporain 1979 · Rudin’s critique 1992 · selected later readings (Catholic Action revision 2002–05)
quebec_historiography.description: Historical writing on Quebec and French Canada, mostly in French, long organized around the nation, the Conquest of 1760 and the meaning of modernity. Lionel Groulx’s national history of French Canada closes what a francophone anthology calls the time of the ‘ancients’; Groulx founded the Institut d’histoire de l’Amérique française (1946) and its Revue (1947). In the 1950s historians at Montréal (Séguin, Frégault, Brunet) made the Conquest and its consequences their central problem. At Laval, Trudel wrote the history of New France, and Hamelin and Ouellet economic and social history, Ouellet in a conjunctural idiom indebted to Labrousse. Their agricultural-crisis thesis (1962) was contested by Paquet and Wallot (1972–73); Dechêne, trained in the Annales milieu in France, wrote the social history of seventeenth-century Montreal (1974). After 1970 a modernist generation turned to contemporary, urban and industrial Quebec and to its whole population (Linteau, Durocher and Robert, 1979). Women’s history followed, from the Collectif Clio (1982) to Baillargeon (1991); Lévesque (1997) asked how far colleagues had integrated it. Behiels (1985) found the Quiet Revolution’s prelude in 1945–60; Rouillard (1997) recorded a shift from reading it as rupture to turn. Ronald Rudin (1992, 1997) argued that the modernists’ search for a ‘normal’ society muted religion, rurality and ethnicity; Linteau and Fecteau replied (1995). Bouchard and Lamonde (2000) close the period; after 2000, Meunier and Warren, Bienvenue and Gauvreau traced the Quiet Revolution to Catholic Action.
quebec_historiography.representative_figures_and_works: Groulx, Histoire du Canada français depuis la découverte (1950); IHAF (1946) and RHAF (1947); Séguin, La “nation canadienne” et l’agriculture (thesis 1947; 1970); Frégault, La guerre de la Conquête (1955); Brunet, La présence anglaise et les Canadiens (1958); Trudel, L’esclavage au Canada français (1960) and Histoire de la Nouvelle-France (1963–); Hamelin, Économie et société en Nouvelle-France (1960); Ouellet and Hamelin, “La crise agricole dans le Bas-Canada” (1962); Ouellet, Histoire économique et sociale du Québec, 1760–1850 (1966); Paquet and Wallot (1972–73); Wallot, Un Québec qui bougeait (1973); Dechêne, Habitants et marchands (1974); Savard (1974); Gagnon, Le Québec et ses historiens (1978); Linteau, Durocher and Robert, Histoire du Québec contemporain (1979; 1986); Collectif Clio (1982); Linteau, “La nouvelle histoire du Québec vue de l’intérieur” (1983); Behiels, Prelude to Quebec’s Quiet Revolution (1985); Lévesque, La norme et les déviantes (1989) and “Réflexions sur l’histoire des femmes dans l’histoire du Québec” (1997); Baillargeon, Ménagères au temps de la Crise (1991); Rudin, “Revisionism and the Search for a Normal Society” (1992; French 1995) and Making History in Twentieth-Century Quebec (1997); Linteau and Fecteau (1995); Dumont, Genèse de la société québécoise (1993); Dickinson and Young, A Short History of Quebec (1993 ed.); Bouchard (1996, 2000); Martel (1997); Rouillard, “La Révolution tranquille: rupture ou tournant?” (1997); Lamonde (2000). Later: Meunier and Warren, Sortir de la « grande noirceur » (2002); Bienvenue, Quand la jeunesse entre en scène (2003); Gauvreau, The Catholic Origins of Quebec’s Quiet Revolution (2005); Bédard and Goyette, eds., Parole d’historiens (2006); Baillargeon, Brève histoire des femmes au Québec (2012).
quebec_historiography.scope_note: A research field defined by its object (Quebec and French Canada) and largely by its language. The Montreal school, Laval, the modernists and their critics are distinct and overlapping positions, not one school; Savard warns against treating ‘École de Québec’ as a unit. The post-1970 generation is called ‘modernist’ after Bédard and Goyette’s part title; Linteau calls it a ‘nouvelle histoire’; Rudin’s polemical name for it is used only in the normal-society debate strand. Annales influence is indirect and contested: Ouellet’s Labroussian economic history, Mandrou’s preface and Dechêne’s training in the Annales milieu are documented, while Linteau says his generation owed more to sociology and American historians. Groulx’s nationalism and clerical politics are historical subjects here, not the atlas’s categories. Quebec women’s history (Clio, Lévesque, Baillargeon) and the Catholic Action revision of the Quiet Revolution have their primary homes here. English-language historians of Quebec (Behiels, Dickinson, Young, Rudin, Greer) belong to the field. Acadian and francophone-minority historiography outside Quebec is only touched by Martel. New France encounter history with Indigenous peoples is in Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history.

strands.title: Groulx and French-Canadian national history
strands.focus: Groulx’s national history and his conception of history. Groulx founded the Institut d’histoire de l’Amérique française in 1946 and its Revue in 1947, and wrote in its first issue. The anthology places him at the end of ‘le temps des Anciens’.
strands.works: Histoire du Canada français depuis la découverte (1950); IHAF (1946); RHAF 1:1 (1947)

strands.title: The Montreal school and the Conquest
strands.focus: Séguin, Frégault and Brunet make the Conquest and its economic and national consequences their central problem; Savard groups them by shared ideological outlook. Ouellet (1985) calls Séguin the ‘théoricien de l’École néo-nationaliste’, for whom the Conquest decapitated the national bourgeoisie, a thesis Brunet took up in the 1950s; Tousignant (1980) calls Séguin the school’s ‘maître à penser’ and describes the gulf between it and Ouellet.
strands.works: Séguin (thesis 1947; 1970); Frégault, La guerre de la Conquête (1955); Brunet, La présence anglaise et les Canadiens (1958)

strands.title: Laval: economic and social history
strands.focus: Trudel’s history of New France and of slavery in French Canada; Hamelin and Ouellet’s economic and social history of New France and Lower Canada. Savard notes Ouellet’s debt to Labrousse and Chaunu, and Mandrou prefaces his 1966 book. Savard treats Trudel and Ouellet as distinct despite the label ‘École de Québec’.
strands.works: Trudel, L’esclavage au Canada français (1960), Histoire de la Nouvelle-France (1963–); Hamelin, Économie et société en Nouvelle-France (1960); Ouellet, Histoire économique et sociale du Québec (1966)

strands.title: The Lower Canadian agricultural crisis debate
strands.focus: Ouellet and Hamelin’s 1962 thesis that a fall in wheat production from 1802, with population pressure and peasant routine, lay behind French-Canadian nationalism and, ‘en grande partie’, the rebellion of 1837–38; Paquet and Wallot’s 1972 rejection of it as ‘irrecevable’ and their market-rational habitant, with Wallot’s Quebec ‘qui bougeait’; Ouellet’s reply (1976), defending the production-based explanation and disputing his critics’ reading of his argument; Le Goff’s review of the controversy (1974, unread); Tousignant’s critique of Le Bas-Canada (1980); and Greer’s rejection of the ‘atavistic mentality’ explanation (1981). Ouellet (1985) names later entrants (Isbester, McCallum, McInnis, Courville). The 1962, 1972, 1976 and 1980 texts and Greer (1981) were read for the Ouellet person entry. The exchange is not presented as resolving the crisis’s chronology, causes or explanatory reach; Paquet and Wallot themselves doubted the debate was settled.
strands.works: Ouellet and Hamelin (1962); Ouellet (1966, 1976); Paquet and Wallot (1972, 1973); Wallot (1973); Le Goff (1974); Tousignant (1980); Greer (1981)

strands.title: New France as social history
strands.focus: Dechêne’s habitants and merchants of seventeenth-century Montreal, from a Paris doctorate (1973) after training in the Annales milieu of Mandrou and Goubert; Hamelin’s economy and society of New France.
strands.works: Dechêne (1974); Hamelin (1960)

strands.title: The modernist synthesis
strands.focus: Linteau describes his generation’s turn to c. 1850–present, to urban and industrial Quebec, and to the history of Quebec’s whole population rather than French Canadians alone; social history and serial sources, with Annales influence filtered through sociology and American history. Histoire du Québec contemporain and Dickinson and Young’s Short History are its syntheses.
strands.works: Linteau, Durocher and Robert (1979; 1986); Linteau (1983); Dickinson and Young (1993 ed.)

strands.title: Quebec women’s history
strands.focus: Collectif Clio’s four-century history (1982), Lévesque’s norms and “deviant” women (1989), Baillargeon’s Depression housewives (1991) and her short synthesis (2012). Lévesque (1997) judged that women’s history had redefined traditional Quebec history while some colleagues were slow to integrate women. The anthology places Clio and Micheline Dumont in its modernist part. Primary here: 31 of 34 PhDs citing this literature engage Quebec historiography; Canadian women's & gender history keeps its critique edge (edge_841). The Collectif Clio (1982) was Micheline Dumont, Michèle Jean, Marie Lavigne and Jennifer Stoddart; shared methods or positions are not inferred.
strands.works: Collectif Clio (1982); Lévesque (1989, 1997); Baillargeon (1991, 2012)

strands.title: Origins of the Quiet Revolution: rupture or turn?
strands.focus: Behiels finds the Quiet Revolution’s prelude in 1945–60 liberal and neo-nationalist debate (1985); Rouillard records historians’ shift from ‘rupture’ to ‘tournant’ (1997). The Catholic Action strand extends the argument after 2000.
strands.works: Behiels (1985); Rouillard, “La Révolution tranquille: rupture ou tournant?” (1997)

strands.title: Catholic Action and the Quiet Revolution
strands.focus: Against the Quiet Revolution’s own story of a clerical “grande noirceur”, Catholic Action, personalism and lay movements from the 1930s are read as preparing the 1960s. Two versions (Baum): social democracy (Meunier and Warren) and the family and gender (Gauvreau). Gauvreau judged that Quebec religious history had repeated the Quiet Revolution’s own ideology until these studies. After 2000; moved from Religion, social reform & secularization in Canada: 75 of 85 PhDs citing this literature engage Quebec historiography (lift 5.6), 36 of them at francophone universities.
strands.works: Meunier and Warren (2002); Bienvenue (2003); Gauvreau (2005)

strands.title: The ‘normal society’ debate
strands.focus: Rudin argues that the revisionists’ normal, Western Quebec muted religion, rurality and ethnicity (1992; 1995; 1997). Linteau and Fecteau reply in the Bulletin d’histoire politique (1995), and Fecteau reviews Rudin’s book on nationhood and the “revisionist school” (CHR 1999). A named controversy with dated published contributions.
strands.works: Rudin (CHR 1992; BHP 1995; 1997); Linteau (BHP 1995); Fecteau (BHP 1995); Fecteau (CHR 1999)

strands.title: Quebec historians on their historiography
strands.focus: Savard’s quarter-century survey (1974), Serge Gagnon on Quebec historians from Garneau to Groulx (1978), Rudin (1997), and Bédard and Goyette’s anthology (2006), whose four parts give a francophone periodization.
strands.works: Savard (1974); Gagnon (1978); Rudin (1997); Bédard and Goyette, eds. (2006)

strands.title: Society, ideas and comparison at the turn of the century
strands.focus: Dumont’s genesis of Quebec society (1993), Bouchard’s Saguenay and comparative New World nations (1996, 2000), Lamonde’s social history of ideas (2000) and Martel on the end of a pan-Canadian French Canada (1997).
strands.works: Dumont (1993); Bouchard (1996, 2000); Martel (1997); Lamonde (2000)

strands.title: Interpreting the rebellions of 1837–38
strands.focus: Ouellet’s reading of the rebellion as, in large part, ‘une réponse détournée’ to agricultural crisis and demographic pressure (1962), with a peasantry led by the liberal professions; the national and social readings Ouellet himself describes as polarised (1985: Bernard, Bernier, Bourque, Dubuc, Ouellet, Ryerson); Bernard’s collection on the Patriotes in memory and historiography (1983, unread); and Greer’s rural history of 1837 (1993, unread; through reviews), which reviewers say breaks with Ouellet’s manipulated peasantry.
strands.works: Ouellet and Hamelin (1962); Ouellet, 'Le mythe de « l'habitant sensible au marché »' (1976); Bernard, ed. (1983); Greer (1993)

settler_colonialism.label: Settler colonialism
settler_colonialism.date_label: Earlier settler-society studies 1983–95 · Wolfe 1999, 2006 · journal 2011 · Tuck and Yang 2012 · critiques 2013–14 · TRC 2015 · Wolfe d. 2016 · Englert 2020 · reviewed through 2024
settler_colonialism.description: Historical inquiry into colonial formations in which newcomers came to stay, took land and claimed sovereignty over Indigenous territories. Patrick Wolfe gave the field its programme: settler colonialism 'destroys to replace'; it is 'inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal'; 'invasion is a structure not an event' (1999, 2006). Lorenzo Veracini founded Settler Colonial Studies (2011) and distinguished colonialism ('you, work for me') from settler colonialism ('you, go away'), adding that the structure 'persistently pursues a specific end point': it 'extinguishes itself'. Two questions organise this selection: how elimination persists while pursuing its own completion, and how settler-colonial analysis relates to Indigenous sovereignty, refusal and resurgence. Veracini develops Wolfe's formula: self-supersession means the settler project's attempted elimination of the settler–Indigenous relation, not a successful decolonisation. The Indigenous reading adopts Wolfe's formula while insisting that 'Settler Colonial Studies does not, should not, and cannot replace Indigenous Studies' (Kauanui), that 'decolonization is not a metaphor' (Tuck and Yang) and that refusal, not recognition, answers the settler state (Simpson, Coulthard). Settler scholars warn against 'colonial fatalism' (Macoun and Strakosch); Marxists ask whether elimination or exploitation defines the form (Englert). In Canada the frame met an older historiography of reserves, treaties, gender and the state, and the TRC's finding of 'cultural genocide' (2015).
settler_colonialism.representative_figures_and_works: Earlier: Sayegh (1965), Rodinson (1973), Denoon, Settler Capitalism (1983); Stasiulis and Yuval-Davis, eds., Unsettling Settler Societies (1995). Wolfe, Settler Colonialism and the Transformation of Anthropology (1999), “Settler Colonialism and the Elimination of the Native” (2006), “Structure and Event” (2008), Traces of History (2016); Veracini, Settler Colonialism: A Theoretical Overview (2010), “Introducing settler colonial studies” (2011), “Career of a Concept” (2013), The Settler Colonial Present (2015); Elkins and Pedersen, eds. (2005); Cavanagh and Veracini, eds. (2016). Indigenous critique and theory: Byrd (2011), L. B. Simpson (2011, 2017), Tuck and Yang (2012), Coulthard (2014), A. Simpson (2014, 2017), Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel (2014), Moreton-Robinson (2015), Kauanui (2016), Goeman (2016). settler_colonialism.scope_note: A research field whose consolidation came after 2000; reviewed through 2024 in the period-4 wave (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md). Read in full: Wolfe 2006 (in an Internet Archive capture of the journal's free-to-read page), Veracini 2011 and his 2016 obituary of Wolfe, Kauanui 2016, Englert 2020, Goeman 2016; in most pages, Tuck and Yang 2012 and Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel 2014; Macoun and Strakosch 2013 in the authors' version; Veracini 2013 in its author manuscript (abstract, opening, conclusion); the TRC summary pp. 1–3. Unread, known through publisher pages or named readers: Wolfe 1999 beyond pp. 1–2, 2001, 2008, 2016; Veracini 2010, 2015; Coulthard; A. Simpson (book; 2017 abstract read); Byrd; Moreton-Robinson; L. B. Simpson; Rowse; Konishi; Sexton; Garba and Sorentino; King; Daschuk; Miller 2009; Perry 2015; Carter 2016; McCallum; Mawani; Stanger-Ross; Lowman and Barker; Regan. Settler-colonial theory, Indigenous political thought, Canadian histories of dispossession and comparative imperial history have different genealogies; Veracini (2013) and Kauanui (2016) both record uses of the term before Wolfe (Sayegh 1965, Rodinson 1973, Denoon 1983, Stasiulis and Yuval-Davis 1995). Roster inclusion is not adoption of the paradigm: Carter, Perry, Harris, Miller, Daschuk and McCallum wrote earlier or beside it, and their publisher descriptions do not use the phrase. Critics appear as critics; Kauanui and Goeman defend Wolfe's theory against shallow citation while asking the field to attend to Indigenous studies. History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23: two or more of the field's authors are cited by 3.2% of Canada + US theses in 2000–09 and 11.0% in 2020–25 (Canada 15.2%, US 6.8%); Wolfe and Veracini are co-cited by 3.0% of theses in 2020–25 and Wolfe with Tuck and Yang, Simpson or Coulthard by 2.3% (the release's category 'Wolfe and his Indigenous critics' names a co-citation pairing, not every author's declared position: Tuck and Yang build on Wolfe, and Kauanui criticises his reception), the only rising two-sided citing after 2000; the Canadian neighbourhood of the founders is the largest and youngest of any field (51 works, median year 2006), its 2020–25 entrants Coulthard, Simpson, Carter, Miller, Daschuk, Kauanui and Greer. The earlier pilot of 2026-10-12 (Canadian strict History PhDs, 2009–26) found 54 citing a work of Wolfe's and 17 the 1999 book (first in 2012), and Daschuk the work most co-cited with Wolfe and Veracini (19 of 58); these figures say more about Canadian history than about him. Bibliographies record consultation, not influence. Francophone uptake in the corpus remains near zero.

date_span.basis: Selected publication milestones only. 1983 and 1995 are earlier settler-society witnesses, not the field's origin; Wolfe 1999 is the only selected milestone inside 1920–2000. The term itself has decolonization-era usage (Veracini 2013); the field's theoretical consolidation falls after 2000; neither endpoint bounds the field. Drawn to the atlas coverage limit (2000); later works are cited readings, not registered extension coverage (revision 1.128). Open from revision 1.133: the former 2000 end was the atlas boundary, not an ending.

strands.title: Structure, not event: the logic of elimination
strands.focus: Wolfe's programme, now read in his own pages. Settler colonialism 'destroys to replace'; it 'is inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal'; 'the primary motive for elimination is not race … but access to territory. Territoriality is settler colonialism's specific, irreducible element'; 'settler colonizers come to stay: invasion is a structure not an event'; elimination has a 'positive' aspect (allotment, citizenship, child abduction, assimilation) that persists after the frontier, so that the form is 'relatively impervious to regime change'; 'structural genocide' names its convergence with genocide without 'hierarchy among victims' (2006). The formula goes back to the 1999 book (p. 2) and the 1994 essay (p. 96, per his note 7). Kauanui: the phrase 'often seems to stand-in for a serious engagement of his theory'.
strands.works: Patrick Wolfe, Settler Colonialism and the Transformation of Anthropology: The Politics and Poetics of an Ethnographic Event (London and New York: Cassell, 1999). Writing Past Colonialism series.; Patrick Wolfe, "Land, Labor, and Difference: Elementary Structures of Race," American Historical Review 106, no. 3 (2001): 866–905.; Patrick Wolfe, "Settler Colonialism and the Elimination of the Native," Journal of Genocide Research 8, no. 4 (2006): 387–409.; J. Kēhaulani Kauanui, "'A Structure, Not an Event': Settler Colonialism and Enduring Indigeneity," Lateral 5, no. 1 (2016).

strands.title: Veracini: the field, the journal and the self-superseding structure
strands.focus: Veracini founded Settler Colonial Studies (2011; open access, volunteer-run, on an ARC grant; to Taylor & Francis in 2013) 'to contribute to the consolidation of a new scholarly field'. Colonialism says 'you, work for me'; settler colonialism says 'you, go away'; the two 'should be understood in their dialectical relation'. Developing Wolfe's formula rather than disputing it, he adds that the structure 'persistently pursues a specific end point': 'settler colonialism, by contrast, extinguishes itself' and is 'least visible in the settler cities'. This self-supersession is the settler project's attempted extinction of the settler–Indigenous relation by the disappearance of Indigenous peoples, not a successful decolonisation, which would instead end 'with an indigenous ultimate permanence'; 'decolonisation is not settler decolonisation', and the politics of recognition 'cannot be considered a genuinely decolonising move' (2011). His history of the concept (2013) finds three earlier careers of the term and a consolidation 'from approximately the mid 1990s', with 'both the Canadian and US historiographies … late in adopting' it. Englert calls him Wolfe's 'self-styled intellectual successor'; Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel find in his history 'Indigenous studies and Indigenous resistance … pretty much erased'.
strands.works: Lorenzo Veracini, "Settler Collective, Founding Violence and Disavowal: The Settler Colonial Situation," Journal of Intercultural Studies 29, no. 4 (2008): 363–379.; Lorenzo Veracini, Settler Colonialism: A Theoretical Overview (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2010).; Lorenzo Veracini, "Introducing: Settler Colonial Studies," Settler Colonial Studies 1, no. 1 (2011): 1–12.; Lorenzo Veracini, "'Settler Colonialism': Career of a Concept," Journal of Imperial and Commonwealth History 41, no. 2 (2013): 313–333.; Edward Cavanagh and Lorenzo Veracini, eds., The Routledge Handbook of the History of Settler Colonialism (London: Routledge, 2017).

strands.title: The Indigenous reading: land, refusal, incommensurability
strands.focus: Indigenous political theory read alongside Wolfe in Canadian and US theses, each work with its own target: Tuck and Yang take up Wolfe's formula directly; Coulthard's target is the politics of recognition, Audra Simpson's salvage anthropology and statist recognition, Leanne Betasamosake Simpson's the academy and state education. Tuck and Yang: settler colonialism's violence 'is not temporally contained in the arrival of the settler but is reasserted each day of occupation. This is why Patrick Wolfe (1999) emphasizes that settler colonialism is a structure and not an event'; 'decolonization brings about the repatriation of Indigenous land and life; it is not a metaphor'; the settler–native–slave triad; 'settler moves to innocence'; 'an ethic of incommensurability' against reconciliation, which 'is about rescuing settler normalcy' (2012). Audra Simpson: 'a sharp move away from the ethno-historical/salvage paradigm' and refusal as method (2007, read in full); 'refusal' as 'an alternative to recognition politics in settler colonial society', consent 'as a technique of recognition and simultaneous dispossession' (2017, abstract; the 2014 book is known through Nicoll's review). Coulthard: settler colonialism 'territorially acquisitive in perpetuity'; in Canada the means of elimination changed but 'the ends have always remained the same: to shore up continued access to Indigenous peoples' territories' (2014, p. 125, as quoted by Englert); a 'place-based' reworking of primitive accumulation (publisher); his 2009 dissertation's named target is 'the politics of recognition' that Taylor defended, and Wolfe is not cited in the pages read. Byrd is unread and known only through catalogue metadata and other authors' citations; L. B. Simpson's 'Land as pedagogy' (2014, read) meets the academy's 'colonial refusal' with 'Indigenous refusal', citing Coulthard on recognition and Audra Simpson on refusal; Moreton-Robinson is known through her publisher's checked description ('a white possession', 'the disavowal of Indigenous sovereignty'). These works have their own genealogies; in Canadian and US theses they are read with Wolfe (History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23), and the user ruled (2026-10-12) that they may sit in more than one field.

strands.title: Health, starvation and state policy
strands.focus: Daschuk's Plains history is the work most co-cited with Wolfe and Veracini by Canadian History PhDs: 19 of 58 citing theses in the 2026-10-12 pilot (Canadian strict History PhDs, 2009–26), and a 2020–25 entrant to the Canadian settler-colonial neighbourhood (support 12, lift 6.1) in the History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23. Its publisher describes 'a policy of starvation' that 'sparked widespread debate about genocide in Canada' and does not use 'settler colonialism'; the 2019 edition adds responses by Kelm, Mosby, Neylan and Woolford. His own framing remains unchecked; the TRC summary's 'cultural genocide' (2015) is the public text beside which the book is read. A comparison strand.
strands.works: James Daschuk, Clearing the Plains: Disease, Politics of Starvation, and the Loss of Aboriginal Life (Regina: University of Regina Press, 2013).

strands.title: Labour and the settler order
strands.focus: Integrates settler workers' ongoing appropriation of Indigenous land into Canadian working-class history.
strands.works: Fred Burrill, "The Settler Order Framework: Rethinking Canadian Working-Class History," Labour/Le Travail 83 (2019): 173–197.

strands.title: Critiques: fatalism, region, period, exploitation
strands.focus: From inside the theory, Macoun and Strakosch: SCT 'posits a structural inevitability', 'can depict colonization as structurally inevitable', risks 'colonial fatalism' and 'does not account for Indigenous lives'; yet 'the fact that settler colonialism struggles to narrate its own ending does not mean that it cannot end' (2013). Rowse: a 'teleology of elimination' (2014, abstract). Greer: one mode among several, dominant in some periods and regions (2019). Shoemaker: universal theory or English heritage? (2019). Englert: 'the elimination of the native … does not accurately define the overall logic of settler colonialism'; settler colonies in Africa and South America 'were built on the exploitation of indigenous peoples'; accumulation by dispossession 'carried out by all classes of settlers, including by workers' (2020, with Kelley and Speed 2017).
strands.works: Alissa Macoun and Elizabeth Strakosch, "The Ethical Demands of Settler Colonial Theory," Settler Colonial Studies 3, nos. 3–4 (2013): 426–443.; Tim Rowse, "Indigenous Heterogeneity," Australian Historical Studies 45, no. 3 (2014): 297–310.; Allan Greer, "Settler Colonialism and Beyond," Journal of the Canadian Historical Association / Revue de la Société historique du Canada 30, no. 1 (2019): 61–86.; Allan Greer, "Settler Colonialism and Empire in Early America," William and Mary Quarterly 76, no. 3 (2019): 383–390.; Nancy Shoemaker, "Settler Colonialism: Universal Theory or English Heritage?" William and Mary Quarterly 76, no. 3 (2019): 369–374.; Jeffrey Ostler and Nancy Shoemaker, "Settler Colonialism in Early American History: Introduction," William and Mary Quarterly 76, no. 3 (2019): 361–368.

strands.title: Indigenous studies and the field: who made it, whom it displaces
strands.focus: Kauanui: Wolfe 'insisted … that he did not create the field of settler colonial studies—that Native scholars did', yet 'he tends to be most frequently cited as if he had'; 'Settler Colonial Studies does not, should not, and cannot replace Indigenous Studies'; indigeneity is 'a category of analysis that is distinct from race, ethnicity, and nationality'; Warrior counted ASA panels and feared the field had become 'an answer to the chronic need for more attention to … Native and Indigenous studies' (2016). Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel: the field 'can displace, overshadow, or even mask over Indigenous studies'; 'when settlers take up these questions, it's suddenly considered a legitimate field of study' (2014). Goeman answers from the same field: Wolfe 'critically engaged our field in a respectful and nuanced manner' and his work 'became a place to engage Indigenous studies concerns in relation to settler colonial studies' (2016). Konishi surveys Indigenous scholars who advocate, interrogate and challenge the field (2019, abstract).
strands.works: Shino Konishi, "First Nations Scholars, Settler Colonial Studies, and Indigenous History," Australian Historical Studies 50, no. 3 (2019): 285–304.; J. Kēhaulani Kauanui, "'A Structure, Not an Event': Settler Colonialism and Enduring Indigeneity," Lateral 5, no. 1 (2016).; Corey Snelgrove, Rita Kaur Dhamoon and Jeff Corntassel, "Unsettling Settler Colonialism: The Discourse and Politics of Settlers, and Solidarity with Indigenous Nations," Decolonization: Indigeneity, Education & Society 3, no. 2 (2014): 1–32.

strands.title: Slavery and Black studies critiques
strands.focus: How settler-colonial and decolonial frameworks place slavery and Black people. Wolfe 2006 (read) sets out the opposed racialisations of Black and Indigenous people in the United States; Tuck and Yang's settler–native–slave triad (read) is what Garba and Sorentino answer. Both authors' words are now read; the critics' remain at abstract level.
strands.works: Tapji Garba and Sara-Maria Sorentino, "Slavery Is a Metaphor: A Critical Commentary on Eve Tuck and K. Wayne Yang's 'Decolonization Is Not a Metaphor'," Antipode 52, no. 3 (2020): 764–782.; Jared Sexton, "The Vel of Slavery: Tracking the Figure of the Unsovereign," Critical Sociology 42, nos. 4–5 (2016): 583–597.; Tiffany Lethabo King, The Black Shoals: Offshore Formations of Black and Native Studies (Durham: Duke University Press, 2019).

strands.title: Structure and its end: Wolfe and Veracini read together
strands.focus: Two emphases within one formula, not a documented exchange between opponents. Wolfe's structure is 'a continuity through time' that 'does not stop' with frontier homicide and 'has not been subject to election results' (2006). Veracini accepts the 'frequently quoted passage' and adds that 'the structure persistently pursues a specific end point' and 'extinguishes itself', so that settler colonialism 'covers its tracks' (2011): the end point is the settler project's attempted elimination of the settler–Indigenous relation, which Veracini distinguishes from decolonisation. The History PhD citation graph (release 2026-10-23) records the two authors co-cited by 3.0% of Canada + US theses in 2020–25, a readership pairing that does not itself establish a dispute. Englert reads both as drawing 'a sharp analytical separation' between eliminatory settler and exploitative franchise colonies and finds the separation does not fit Africa or South America (2020); Macoun and Strakosch find in the structure a 'colonial fatalism' and recall the label 'very much a structuralist stuck in a poststructuralist world' (2013): these readings establish different emphases placed on the same structure. Veracini's obituary records Wolfe as 'still a Marxist' of 'the young Marx' for whom 'things are not things in themselves but relationships' (2016).
strands.works: Wolfe, "Settler Colonialism and the Elimination of the Native" (2006); Veracini, "Introducing settler colonial studies" (2011) and "Patrick Wolfe (1949–2016)" (2016); Macoun and Strakosch, "The Ethical Demands of Settler Colonial Theory" (2013); Englert, "Settlers, Workers, and the Logic of Accumulation by Dispossession" (2020).

strands.title: Canadian history beside and under the frame, 2009–2020
strands.focus: Works that Canadian PhDs read with Wolfe and Veracini, few of which adopt his vocabulary. Treaty history (Miller 2009, a distinctive riser among Canadian PhDs inside the Indigenous family in the 2026-10-23 release), racialisation and law in British Columbia's 'contact zone' (Mawani 2009), settler self-examination after residential schools (Regan 2010; Battell Lowman and Barker 2015: 'Canada and Settler Colonialism', 'It's Always All About the Land'), starvation policy (Daschuk 2013), Indigenous women's work 'in modern Native ways' (McCallum 2014), the TRC's finding that Canada's policy aimed 'to eliminate Aboriginal governments … and … cause Aboriginal peoples to cease to exist as distinct … entities' and 'can best be described as "cultural genocide"' (2015), imperial family and archive (Perry 2015), women homesteaders in 'the spadework of British colonialism' who 'took part in dispossessing Indigenous people' (Carter 2016), the settler-colonial city (Hugill 2017), the settler order in working-class history (Burrill 2019), Japanese Canadian dispossession (Stanger-Ross 2020), and Harris's reflections (2020). Veracini's own history says the Canadian historiography was 'late in adopting settler colonialism as a category of analysis' (2013). Publisher descriptions, not the books, are read; none of Miller, Daschuk, McCallum, Perry 2015, Carter 2016 or Stanger-Ross uses the phrase on its page.
strands.works: Miller, Compact, Contract, Covenant (2009); Mawani, Colonial Proximities (2009); Regan, Unsettling the Settler Within (2010); Daschuk, Clearing the Plains (2013); McCallum, Indigenous Women, Work, and History (2014); Battell Lowman and Barker, Settler (2015); TRC, Honouring the Truth, Reconciling for the Future (2015); Perry, Colonial Relations (2015); Carter, Imperial Plots (2016); Hugill, "What Is a Settler-Colonial City?" (2017); Burrill, "The Settler Order Framework" (2019); Stanger-Ross, ed., Landscapes of Injustice (2020); Harris, A Bounded Land (2020).

strands.title: A field's institutions: journal, associations, memorials
strands.focus: NAISA founded 2008 after an ASA panel of 2002 asked whether American Studies could be 'an intellectual home' for Native studies (Kauanui). Settler Colonial Studies founded 2011 'in an open access format (entirely run on volunteer labour)' and moved to Taylor & Francis 'within two years' (Snelgrove et al.; Edmonds and Carey 2013). Wolfe edited paired issues of the journal and of AICRJ (2013) and answered the binary charge with The Settler Complex (2016). ASA 2015: Goldstein's reappraisal and Warrior's count of panels. Wolfe's death (18 February 2016) brought obituaries from the journal (Veracini), AICRJ (Goeman), Aboriginal History (Birch) and an American Quarterly forum (2017); a Festschrift followed (Race, Place, Trace, 2022).
strands.works: Kauanui (2016); Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel (2014); Edmonds and Carey, "A New Beginning for Settler Colonial Studies" (2013); Wolfe, ed., "Recuperating Binarism" (2013) and The Settler Complex (2016); Veracini (2016); Goeman (2016); Birch (2016); American Quarterly 69:2 (2017); Slyomovics and Veracini, eds., Race, Place, Trace (2022).

capitalismdebates.label: Capitalism, divergence and industrialisation
capitalismdebates.date_label: Capitalism and Slavery 1944 · Dobb–Sweezy 1950 · Brenner debate 1976–85 · Wrigley 1988 · de Vries 1994 · The Great Divergence 2000 · Allen and The Enlightened Economy 2009 · Empire of Cotton 2014 · Hilt 2017 · Burnard and Riello 2020
capitalismdebates.description: A set of linked arguments about why capitalism, industrialisation and Western wealth arose where and when they did. Marxist historians disputed whether trade or class relations ended feudalism: Dobb answered Sweezy that trade worked 'to the extent that it accentuated the internal conflicts' (1950). Brenner's property-relations thesis (1976) opened a second round, in which Bois called his approach 'political Marxism' and Wood made it a programme. Economic historians slowed the British Industrial Revolution while reasserting 'an important discontinuity' (Crafts and Harley, 1992), and Berg and Hudson answered that growth accounting had 'mis-specified' it; explanations multiplied in Wrigley's escape from an 'organic economy', de Vries's 'industrious revolution', Mokyr's 'Industrial Enlightenment' and Allen's high wages and cheap energy. Wong challenged Europe's status as the comparative norm; Pomeranz acknowledged that method while giving greater weight to global conjunctures, ecological constraints, coal and New World resources; critics answered from property relations, knowledge, wages and the state. Williams's Capitalism and Slavery (1944) returned through Inikori, the Legacies of British Slave-ownership project and an American 'history of capitalism' whose economic-historian critics charged 'specious arguments' (Hilt, 2017). Readers join these debates themselves: Burnard and Riello set the new history of capitalism beside the Brenner debate and Pomeranz (2020).

Brenner debate and political Marxism: Brenner (1976; 1977; 1982); Postan and Hatcher, Croot and Parker, Wunder, Le Roy Ladurie, Bois, Cooper (1978); Klíma (1979); Aston and Philpin (eds), The Brenner Debate (1985); Wood (1981; 1991; 1999/2002; 2001); Harman (1989); Callinicos (1990). Industrialisation: Toynbee (1884, context); Mendels (1972); Kriedte, Medick and Schlumbohm (1977); Wrigley (1988); Berg and Hudson (1990/1992); Crafts and Harley (1992); de Vries (1994; 2008); Mokyr (2002; 2009); Allen (2009; 2015); Humphries (2013); Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda (2014; 2023). (2011); Broadberry, Guan and Li (2021). Slavery and capitalism: Williams (1944); Drescher (1977); Solow and Engerman (eds, 1987); Inikori (2002); Hall et al. (2014); Johnson (2013); Baptist (2014); Beckert (2014); Beckert and Rockman (eds, 2016); Olmstead and Rhode (2017; 2018); Hilt (2017); Burnard and Riello (2020). capitalismdebates.scope_note: A Debate entry with five components, each with its own strands: the transition debate; the Brenner debate and political Marxism; explaining industrialisation; the Great Divergence; slavery and capitalism. It gathers exchanges; the related field strands remain in place, while person entries hold the relationships stated below. The field strands, not moved, are: marx/transition, economic/marxist, economic/household_demand, economic/wrigley_growth, economic/regional_divergence, economic/divergence_household_dispute and economic/coal_constraints_dispute (the Huang–Pomeranz exchange), economic/slavery_productivity_exchange, economic/empire, global/comparison, global/reciprocal_comparison_resources, global/protoindustry_trade_limits, consumption/household_labor, technology/invention_adoption, demography/aggregate_population, dependency/worldsystems, atlantic/earlier and quant/slavery_debate. Existing person entries (Dobb, Hilton, Williams, Pomeranz, Huang, Hall) keep their own relations; Brenner and Wood gained person entries in 1.145; Mokyr, Wrigley, de Vries and Wong follow in 1.146. Readings are recorded per source, many through publisher excerpts, abstracts, Cambridge Core chapter openings or reviewers; unread books are given only as named readers report them. Quotations from The Brenner Debate (1985) beyond its Cambridge Core chapter openings were withdrawn before drafting. The 'California School' is a readers' label, attributed by Frank (2001) and Vries (2009) to Goldstone. Toynbee (1884) is a dated precursor, not a start. Mokyr, Wrigley, de Vries and Wong hold their contributions to the debate on their own entries (the arrows drawn for them in 1.145 from demography, consumption and technology now start from those entries); Allen and Beckert remain roster rows here.

strands.title: The transition debate: Dobb, Sweezy and their readers, 1946–1976
strands.focus: Dobb's Studies (1946) defined feudalism by the coercive relation between producer and lord; Sweezy (1950) answered that feudalism was 'a system of production for use' dissolved by 'causes external to the system', above all trade, while granting that 'no theory which fails to take into account the factors which Dobb stresses … can be regarded as correct'. Dobb replied that trade 'exercised its influence to the extent that it accentuated the internal conflicts', and carried the argument to the absolutist state and the English Revolution. Takahashi (1952) developed an analysis of production relations and the social form of labour, and pressed for fuller French and German comparison. Hilton collected the exchange with later essays in 1976. Positions within one Marxist debate, not a school. The field strands marx/transition and economic/marxist keep each author's own contribution.
strands.works: Dobb, Studies in the Development of Capitalism (1946); Sweezy and Dobb, Science & Society 14:2 (1950): 134–167; Takahashi (1952); Merrington, 'Town and Country in the Transition to Capitalism' (NLR, 1975); Hilton (ed.), The Transition from Feudalism to Capitalism (1976); see marx/transition and economic/marxist

strands.title: Against 'neo-Smithian Marxism': Brenner on Sweezy, Frank and Wallerstein, 1977
strands.focus: Brenner traced Wallerstein's world-system and Frank's development of underdevelopment back to Sweezy's side of the 1950 debate and, through it, to 'the model put forward by Adam Smith'. He acknowledged a 'great debt' to Dobb, and credited Frank with breaking 'the suffocating orthodoxies' of stage theory. Callinicos (1990) called the critique 'a valuable corrective'. See dependency/worldsystems for Wallerstein's own account.
strands.works: Brenner, NLR I/104 (1977); Wallerstein, The Modern World-System I (1974); Frank (1966–)

strands.title: The Brenner debate in Past and Present, 1976–1985
strands.focus: Brenner argued that class structure decides how demographic and commercial change affects growth. Postan and Hatcher called his charges against them 'groundless'; Le Roy Ladurie defended a 'neo-Malthusian' model; Croot and Parker, Wunder and Klíma tested his English, French, German and Bohemian comparisons; Bois agreed against 'the Malthusian model' but not with Brenner's method. Brenner's reply (1982) spoke of 'social-property systems'. Hilton introduced the collection (1985) as 'a continuation' of the transition debate. The respondents are read only in their Cambridge Core openings; their later pages are unread, and Bois's specified later passages (pp. 115–116) are known only as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos (1990); see annales/serial for Le Roy Ladurie's Languedoc.
strands.works: Past and Present 70 (1976) to 97 (1982); Aston and Philpin (eds), The Brenner Debate (1985)

strands.title: Political Marxism: from Bois's charge to a school, 1978–2016
strands.focus: Bois called Brenner's approach 'political Marxism', 'a voluntarist vision of history' (1978, as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos, 1990). By the accounts of Callinicos (1990) and Brenner (2016), Wood accepted the label while rejecting the charge of voluntarism. She argued that 'the economic' and 'the political' are differently joined in pre-capitalist and capitalist societies (1981), against G. A. Cohen's technological determinism. Critics answered that it was 'little more than a sociology of domination' (Callinicos) and that Brenner, taking up Dobb, narrowed class struggle to the countryside (Harman).
strands.works: Bois (1978); Wood, 'The Separation of the Economic and the Political in Capitalism' (NLR, 1981), Democracy Against Capitalism (1995); Harman (1989); Callinicos, 'The Limits of "Political Marxism"' (NLR, 1990); Harman and Brenner (2004, printed 2006); Brenner (2016) and Hirschkop (2016) on Wood

strands.title: The origin of capitalism and its critics, 1991–2004
strands.focus: Wood argued that England was 'the world's first capitalist society' (1991), siding with Thompson against the Nairn–Anderson theses. In 'Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism' (2001) she set the transition debate and Brenner's 'market dependence' against the 'commercialization model'; The Origin of Capitalism (1999; 2002), unread here, is known through its jacket and McAuley's quotations. McAuley (2001), drawing on Blaut, criticised 'the Brenner-Wood thesis' for treating colonialism as marginal; Wood replied that slave plantations mattered 'quite a while after the emergence of capitalism in the English countryside'. This exchange joins the strand to the slavery and divergence components.
strands.works: Wood, The Pristine Culture of Capitalism (1991), The Origin of Capitalism (1999; 2002), 'Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism' (2001), replies (2002); McAuley (2001)

strands.title: Revolution or gradual growth? The Industrial Revolution revised, 1884–1994
strands.focus: Toynbee's posthumous lectures (1884) defined the Industrial Revolution as 'the substitution of competition for the medieval regulations'. Crafts and Harley's output estimates slowed its pace while reasserting 'the industrial revolution as an important discontinuity' (1992); Berg and Hudson answered that growth accounting had 'mis-specified' the subject and left out women's and children's labour, regional specialisation and innovation (1990 working paper; 1992). De Vries (1994) read the revisionists as 'cleansing the temple of the "false god of the take off"', not pulling down the pillars.
strands.works: Toynbee, Lectures on the Industrial Revolution in England (1884); Crafts and Harley (1992); Berg and Hudson (1990 working paper; EHR 1992); de Vries (JEH 1994), pp. 249–251; see historicalecon/british_teaching

strands.title: Rural industry and industrious households, 1972–2016
strands.focus: Mendels (1972) treated market-oriented rural industry as 'a first phase which preceded and prepared modern industrialization proper', and later called it 'a plausible and interesting set of hypotheses' (1984); the Göttingen group (Kriedte, Medick, Schlumbohm, 1977) placed rural industry in 'the genesis of capitalism'. Coleman (1983) titled his critique 'a concept too many'. De Vries's 'industrious revolution' (1994; 2008), a term he and van Nederveen Meerkerk trace to Akira Hayami, made household labour and demand precede the Industrial Revolution; reviewers asked whether consumption had become 'a new deus ex machina' (2009). Rosenband (2016), from French and English papermaking, challenged the model: paperworkers 'already labored exhausting hours at the outset of de Vries's period of newfound industriousness', and women and adolescents worked for wages long before it (abstract). See economic/household_demand, consumption/household_labor and global/protoindustry_trade_limits for the field contributions.
strands.works: Mendels (JEH 1972) and NYRB letter (1984); Kriedte, Medick and Schlumbohm (1977; English 1981); Medick (1976); Coleman (1983); de Vries (1994; 2008); van Nederveen Meerkerk (2009); Rosenband (2016)

strands.title: Why Britain? Energy, knowledge and wages, 1988–2023
strands.focus: Wrigley (1988) questioned the Industrial Revolution as 'a cumulative, progressive, unitary phenomenon' and contrasted an 'organic economy' bounded by land with a mineral-based energy regime. Mokyr's 'Industrial Enlightenment' was 'the key to sustained and accelerating invention' (2002 draft); reviewing The Enlightened Economy (2009), Harley questioned whether the Industrial Enlightenment explained economic change or largely redescribed it (2010). Allen (2009) argued that 'Wages were remarkably high, and energy was remarkably cheap', so 'it paid to invent it there'; Humphries charged the high-wage account with a 'patriarchal perspective' (2013), and Allen replied with evidence 'that women and children participated in the high wage economy' (2015, abstract). Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda found that, across English counties, industrialisation occurred where wages began low and mechanical skills high (2023); the result concerns differences within England, not Britain's international wage advantage. The article sets it 'directly counter' to Allen's argument (pp. 60–61), as their 2014 essay had argued from British workers' human capital against his high wages. Clark and Jacks's coal-rent estimates imply a negligible income contribution from England's possession of coal reserves (2007). See economic/wrigley_growth and technology/invention_adoption.
strands.works: Wrigley, Continuity, Chance and Change (1988), The Path to Sustained Growth (2016); Mokyr (2002 paper), The Enlightened Economy (2009); Harley (2010); Allen (2009; 2015); Humphries (2013); Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda (2014; 2023); Clark and Jacks (2007)

strands.title: The Great Divergence and the so-called California School, 1997–2021
strands.focus: Wong (1997) challenged Europe's status as the comparative norm. Pomeranz (2000) followed 'a procedure outlined in Wong's recent China Transformed' while giving 'greater stress than Wong does on global conjunctures', and greater weight to ecological constraints, coal and New World resources; he dated divergence late. Readers attribute the label 'California School' to Goldstone (Frank 2001; Vries 2009), whose 'efflorescences' (2002) put pre-modern growth outside Europe too while locating the modern breakthrough in British engines, science and craft culture. Frank's ReOrient (1998) and a debate with Landes scheduled for December 1998, announced in a notice written from Frank's side, marked the polemical poles. Parthasarathi carried the argument to India (2011). Rosenthal and Wong explained divergence by political fragmentation and war (2011, as Ma's review reports and Wong restated in 2016); Ma found the hypothesis 'supported by fairly meager evidence'. Critics answered from property relations (Brenner and Isett 2002), knowledge (Mokyr 2002, 2012), wages and national accounts (Broadberry and Gupta 2006; Allen et al. 2011; Broadberry, Guan and Li 2021) and the state (Vries 2009, 2013). The Huang–Pomeranz exchange stays in economic/divergence_household_dispute and economic/coal_constraints_dispute.
strands.works: Wong, China Transformed (1997); Frank, ReOrient (1998); Landes, The Wealth and Poverty of Nations (1998); Pomeranz, The Great Divergence (2000); Frank's review (2001); Goldstone (2002); Brenner and Isett (2002); Mokyr (2002; 2012); Broadberry and Gupta (2006); Vries (2009; 2013); Parthasarathi (2011); Rosenthal and Wong (2011); Allen et al. (2011); Broadberry, Guan and Li (2021); see global/comparison and global/reciprocal_comparison_resources

strands.title: Capitalism and Slavery and its critics: the Williams thesis, 1944–2020
strands.focus: Williams (1944) advanced distinct propositions, which readers keep apart: that slave-trade and plantation wealth financed and stimulated British industry; that slave-derived wealth mattered in eighteenth-century Britain; and that the West Indies' economic decline, with changing economic interests, explains abolition. Drescher's Econocide (1977), in its publisher's description, challenged decline-based explanations of the 1807 abolition and stressed public mobilisation; Solow and Engerman's volume (1987) sifted the 'legacy'. Solow judged that slavery 'did not cause the Industrial Revolution but played an active role in its pattern and timing' (as quoted by Burnard and Riello), while Eltis and Engerman (2000), as Hilt and Burnard and Riello report them, judged its growth linkages to British industry small. Inikori (2002), as O'Rourke reports, reasserted the thesis through Atlantic trade and African producers and consumers. Hall (2014) and Burnard and Riello (2020) identify modified Williams arguments in Pomeranz and Inikori. The Legacies of British Slave-ownership team investigates slave-ownership's British legacies; its compensation evidence supports some Williams propositions, on slave-derived wealth, and qualifies the decline thesis, while leaving the industrialisation controversy unresolved ('Our material cannot resolve these controversies'). See economic/empire and atlantic/earlier.
strands.works: Williams, Capitalism and Slavery (1944); Drescher, Econocide (1977) and 'Capitalism and Slavery after Fifty Years' (1997); Solow and Engerman (eds), British Capitalism and Caribbean Slavery (1987); Eltis and Engerman (JEH 2000); Inikori, Africans and the Industrial Revolution in England (2002); Hall et al., Legacies of British Slave-ownership (2014)

strands.title: Slavery's capitalism and its economic-historian critics, 2013–2020
strands.focus: This strand selects the slavery controversy within the broader history of capitalism, a field whose early definition by Beckert, Hilt notes, is so broad that it 'includes most of the fields of labor, political, social, and business history', and whose work, Regele notes, began before the 2007–2009 financial crisis. Mainly Americanist historians, publicised as historians of capitalism in 2013, put slavery at the centre of American and global capitalism: Johnson's River of Dark Dreams (2013; Johnson does not count himself a historian of capitalism, Hilt notes), Baptist's argument, in Hilt's account, that torture drove cotton productivity (2014), Beckert's 'war capitalism' (2014) and Beckert and Rockman's Slavery's Capitalism (2016). Olmstead and Rhode answered that the books 'make fundamental errors in economic reasoning' (2017); Hilt, that 'specious arguments and failures of analytical reasoning sometimes undermine' them as social criticism, while granting that economic research supports some of their arguments and calling for 'dialogue, if not collaboration' (2017); Burnard and Riello, that US cotton came 'too late to cause an Industrial Revolution' (2020). Readers trace the movement to Polanyi, the 2008 crisis and a turn from labour history (Hilt; Regele) and to Williams and Pomeranz (Burnard and Riello). Fogel and Engerman's earlier slavery debate stays in quant/slavery_debate.
strands.works: Johnson, River of Dark Dreams (2013); Baptist, The Half Has Never Been Told (2014); Beckert, Empire of Cotton (2014); Beckert and Rockman (eds), Slavery’s Capitalism (2016); Olmstead and Rhode (AHA 2017; EEH 2018); Hilt (JEH 2017); Burnard and Riello (JGH 2020); Regele (2023)

strands.title: Corporate capitalism, finance and public power
strands.focus: White’s Railroaded asks how debt-financed corporations, public subsidies and political markets could enrich insiders despite repeated corporate failure. This is an inquiry into the institutional operation of American capitalism, distinct from the feudal transition, industrial growth and slavery controversies grouped elsewhere here.
strands.works: Richard White, Railroaded (2011)

coverage.basis: Surveyed through 2000 in the research of 2026-10-18 (data/extension-2026/capitalism-debate-2026-10-18/evidence-industrialisation.md, evidence-great-divergence.md, evidence-slavery-capitalism.md; data/extension-2026/brenner-2026-10-18/evidence-brenner.md, evidence-transition-political-marxism.md). archival_turn.label: The archive as object
archival_turn.date_label: Le goût de l'archive 1989 · Archive Fever 1994/1996 · Silencing the Past 1995 · Dust 2001 · Archival Science 2 'archives, records, and power' 2002 · Archive Stories 2005 · 'Venus in Two Acts' 2008 · Along the Archival Grain 2009 · Dispossessed Lives 2016 · Trouillot Remixed 2021
archival_turn.description: This editorial grouping brings together distinct inquiries into archives as institutions, practices, sources and objects of interpretation. Trouillot's Silencing the Past (1995) located the silences of history in 'the making of sources', 'the making of archives', 'the making of narratives' and 'the making of history in the final instance' (as quoted by Davidson, 2020), and made the Haitian Revolution the case of an event 'unthinkable' as it happened. Stoler asked colonial historians to move 'from archive-as-source to archive-as-subject' (2002) and to read 'along the archival grain' before reading against it, finding in Dutch colonial records a 'repository of good taste and bad faith' (2009, as quoted by Gouda). Farge's Le goût de l'archive (1989), Derrida's Archive Fever (1994) and Steedman's Dust (2001) wrote the archive's allure, fever and dust; Schwartz and Cook, from the archival profession, called archives 'active sites where social power is negotiated' (2002); Burton's Archive Stories (2005) collected historians' encounters with their sources; Hartman's 'critical fabulation' (2008) and Fuentes (2016) confronted the violence of slavery's archive.
archival_turn.representative_figures_and_works: Earlier works: Arlette Farge, Le goût de l'archive (1989; The Allure of the Archives, 2013, foreword Natalie Zemon Davis); Thomas Richards, The Imperial Archive (1993); Jacques Derrida, Mal d'archive / Archive Fever (lecture 1994; Diacritics 1995; Chicago 1996); Michel-Rolph Trouillot, Silencing the Past (1995; 20th-anniversary edition with Hazel V. Carby's foreword, 2015); Saidiya Hartman, Scenes of Subjection (1997). Selected interventions: the History of the Human Sciences issue 'The Archive' (1999); Terry Cook, 'Fashionable Nonsense or Professional Rebirth' (Archivaria 51, 2001); Carolyn Steedman, Dust and 'Something She Called a Fever' (2001); Archival Science 2:1–2, 'archives, records, and power' (2002: Joan M. Schwartz and Terry Cook; Ann Laura Stoler, 'Colonial Archives and the Arts of Governance'); Refiguring the Archive (2002: Achille Mbembe, 'The Power of the Archive and its Limits'; Stoler); From the Margins (2002: Nicholas B. Dirks, 'Annals of the Archive'); Diana Taylor, The Archive and the Repertoire (2003); Ann Cvetkovich, An Archive of Feelings (2003); Marlene Manoff, 'Theories of the Archive from Across the Disciplines' (2004); Antoinette Burton, ed., Archive Stories (2005: Durba Ghosh, Tony Ballantyne, Adele Perry, Ann Curthoys). Later contributions: Stoler, Along the Archival Grain (2009) and the Bijdragen debate (Gouda, Raben, Schulte Nordholt, 2009); Anjali Arondekar, For the Record (2009); Hartman, 'Venus in Two Acts' (Small Axe 26, 2008); Francis X. Blouin and William G. Rosenberg, Processing the Past (2011); David Zeitlyn, 'Anthropology in and of the Archives' (2012); Marisa J. Fuentes, Dispossessed Lives (2016); Trouillot Remixed (2021). Readers: Frances Gouda, Remco Raben, Henk Schulte Nordholt (2009); Alyssa Goldstein Sepinwall (2013); Marlene L. Daut (2021); Bastien Craipain (2024).
archival_turn.scope_note: A Research-field entry gathering a readership rather than a school: in the History PhD citation graph (release 2026-10-23) the share of Canada + US theses citing two or more of Stoler, Trouillot, Farge, Derrida, Hartman, Steedman, Burton, Fuentes, Blouin and Rosenberg rose from 0 (1990s) to 3.3% (2000–09), 7.1%, 7.6% and 10.4% (2020–25; US 11.8%, Canada 9.0%; Europe 2.1%), with Stoler cited by 10.7% of theses in 2020–25 across 11 of 18 fields and Trouillot by 5.9%; no opposing side is co-cited (cohorts README §5), and Along the Archival Grain entered the global/transnational neighbourhood of PhDs in 2020–25. Six strands: the archive as a site of power (Trouillot, Mbembe, Schwartz and Cook); reading along the grain (Stoler); allure, fever and dust (Farge, Derrida, Steedman); absence, violence and critical fabulation (Hartman, Fuentes); archive stories and the ethnography of archives (Burton, Dirks, Zeitlyn); the archivists' turn in Canada and South Africa (Cook, Schwartz, Harris, Brothman). Research of 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-archive.md): read in full — Gouda (2009), Schulte Nordholt (2009), Ottevaere (2004), Schultz (2015), Craipain (2024), the Chicago obituary and the finding aid for Trouillot; in part — Cook (2001), the Bulamah–Goyatá–Pereira introduction (2020), Davidson (2020); abstracts and contents only — Stoler 2002, Schwartz and Cook 2002, Mbembe 2002, Manoff 2004, Trouillot 2003, Along the Archival Grain, Archive Stories, From the Margins, Haunted by Empire, Duress, For the Record, The Archive and the Repertoire. Unread: the bodies of Silencing the Past (the four-moments passage is given as later writers list it and as Davidson quotes it, unpaginated; wording awaits re-verification on a library copy of ch. 1), Along the Archival Grain, Carnal Knowledge, Archive Fever, Dust and the AHR essay, Le goût de l'archive, 'Venus in Two Acts', Dispossessed Lives, The Imperial Archive, Processing the Past, Zeitlyn 2012, the HHS 1999 issue, Sepinwall 2013, Daut 2021, Carby's foreword. Richards (1993), Blouin and Rosenberg (2011) and the HHS issue are named in the works list but not dated as events (no page reached). Indigenous data sovereignty and the digital archive are out of scope (see web_history for the 2024 uptake of Stoler's phrase).
