strands.title: The archive as a site of power: Trouillot, Mbembe, Schwartz and Cook
strands.focus: Trouillot's Silencing the Past (1995) holds that silences enter historical production at four moments — 'fact creation (the making of sources)', 'fact assembly (the making of archives)', 'fact retrieval (the making of narratives)' and 'retrospective significance (the making of history in the final instance)' (as quoted by Davidson, 2020) — and that 'in history, power begins at the source' and 'archives are the institutions that organise facts and sources' (as quoted by Davidson, 2020, unpaginated; wording awaits re-verification on a library copy of ch. 1). Craipain (2024) reads the book as a 'critical indictment of Western historiography' whose 'historical guild' relegated 'racism, slavery and colonialism' to 'an historical backburner' (Trouillot, p. 98, as quoted by Craipain). From the archival profession, Schwartz and Cook opened Archival Science's 'archives, records, and power' issues (2002) with the claim that archives 'are not passive storehouses of old stuff, but active sites where social power is negotiated' (abstract); Mbembe's 'The Power of the Archive and its Limits' (2002) begins from the archive as 'a building, a symbol of a public institution' (abstract).
strands.works: Silencing the Past (1995); 'The Power of the Archive and its Limits' (2002); 'Archives, Records, and Power' (2002)

strands.title: Reading along the grain: Stoler's ethnography of the colonial archive
strands.focus: Stoler's 2002 essay asked anthropologists in colonial studies, whose 'archival activity tends to remain more an extractive than an ethnographic one', to move 'from archive-as-source to archive-as-subject' (abstract). Along the Archival Grain (2009) treated Dutch colonial records 'not just as repositories of state power, but as unquiet movements in a field of force' (pp. 32–33, as quoted by Schulte Nordholt), looked 'for the pulse of the archive in the quiescence and quickened pace of its own production' (p. 35) and aimed 'to set a new standard for an ethnography of the archives' (p. 45) rather than an ethnography in them. Gouda: she 'underscores the necessity to read along the grain before trying to read against it, as many postcolonial scholars in recent years have advocated' (2009, p. 552). The reviewers' doubts are part of the record: Schulte Nordholt was 'not quite sure how to identify these "pulses"' and found 'an unexpected colonial flavour' in a book that ignored archives in Indonesia and Indonesian scholars (pp. 560, 562); Gouda found 'so little engagement with the work of contemporary Dutch historians' (p. 555).
strands.works: 'Colonial Archives and the Arts of Governance' (2002); Along the Archival Grain (2009); the Bijdragen debate (2009)

strands.title: Allure, fever and dust: Farge, Derrida, Steedman
strands.focus: Three texts made the historian's experience of the archive their subject. Farge's Le goût de l'archive (1989; English 2013, with Natalie Zemon Davis's foreword) is, in Yale's words, a reflection on the sensory and emotional experience of archival work in the judicial records of eighteenth-century Paris; Arnold Hunt called it 'an eloquent testimony to the materiality of the archive and its power to astonish and delight'. Derrida's Archive Fever (lecture 1994; Diacritics 1995; Chicago 1996), already on the derrida, memory and freud entries, is 'an extended meditation on remembrance, religion, time, and technology' that starts from archiving (publisher). Steedman's Dust (2001) and 'Something She Called a Fever: Michelet, Derrida, and Dust' (AHR 106:4, 2001) answered Derrida with the archive as the repository of 'that which will not go away' and named 'archivization' as the practice of attending to it (publisher description). Terry Cook dated the 'Derrida aftershock', in which historians and others were 'subjecting the archival world to a detailed critique such as it has never before experienced', from inside the profession (2001, p. 21). All three bodies unread.
strands.works: Le goût de l'archive (1989); Archive Fever (1994/1996); Dust (2001); 'Something She Called a Fever' (2001)

strands.title: Absence, violence and critical fabulation: Hartman, Fuentes
strands.focus: Hartman's 'Venus in Two Acts' (Small Axe 26, June 2008) examines a girl's presence and silence in the archive of Atlantic slavery; the MacArthur Foundation describes her 'speculative method she terms "critical fabulation," which questions historical archives as the sole source of credible information about the past' (2019). Scenes of Subjection (1997) 'traces continuities between pre- and post-emancipation eras' (MacArthur). Fuentes's Dispossessed Lives (2016), on enslaved and free women in eighteenth-century Bridgetown, 'interrogates the archive and its historical production to expose the ongoing effects' of slavery's violence, 'combining fragmentary sources with interdisciplinary methodologies that include black feminist theory' (publisher). Both are unread here; the strand records their place in the readership (History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23: Hartman 4.3% of Canada + US theses in 2020–25, from 0 in 2000–09; Fuentes a 2020–25 entrant to the US capitalism and Indigenous networks).
strands.works: Scenes of Subjection (1997); 'Venus in Two Acts' (2008); Dispossessed Lives (2016)

strands.title: Archive stories and the ethnography of archives: Burton, Dirks, Zeitlyn
strands.focus: Burton's Archive Stories (Duke, 2005) collected, in the press's words, ethnographies of the archival world by historians that challenge 'the claims to objectivity associated with the traditional archive'; its introduction is titled 'Archive Fever, Archive Stories', and its contributors include Durba Ghosh on miscegenation in Britain and India, Tony Ballantyne on 'Mr. Peal's Archive', Jennifer Milligan on 'What Is an Archive?' in modern France, Adele Perry on 'The Colonial Archive on Trial' in Delgamuukw v. British Columbia, and Ann Curthoys. Dirks's 'Annals of the Archive: Ethnographic Notes on the Sources of History' opened Part 1, 'Ethnography and the Archive', of From the Margins (2002), the volume that also printed Stoler and Trouillot. Zeitlyn's 'Anthropology in and of the Archives' (Annual Review of Anthropology 41, 2012) and Manoff's survey of 'theories of the archive from across the disciplines' (2004), which found 'a confluence of interests among scholars, archivists, and librarians', mark the turn's consolidation. All bodies unread; the strand rests on contents and abstracts.
strands.works: From the Margins (2002); The Archive and the Repertoire (2003); 'Theories of the Archive from Across the Disciplines' (2004); Archive Stories (2005); 'Anthropology in and of the Archives' (2012)

strands.title: The archivists' turn: Canada and South Africa
strands.focus: The profession's own turn ran beside and partly before the historians'. Cook names 'the pioneering postmodern archivists before Cook' as 'also Canadian, Brien Brothman and Richard Brown' (2001, n. 13). His plenary to the Association of Canadian Archivists (Winnipeg, 8 June 2001), printed as 'Fashionable Nonsense or Professional Rebirth', argued that appraisal should let archives 'acquire in its holdings multiple voices, and not by default only the voices of the powerful', while, 'as Verne Harris notes', not romanticising the marginalised (pp. 31–32), and that 'the Canadian parallel way of archival remembering through macro-appraisal may speak strongly to archivists in this new century' (p. 32). Schwartz (National Archives of Canada / Queen's) and Cook (Manitoba) then edited the 'archives, records, and power' issues of Archival Science (2002), citing Derrida and Harris, not Foucault or Stoler (reference list). Harris's South African work and Refiguring the Archive (2002) are the other pole. Perry's chapter on the colonial archive before the courts in Delgamuukw (2005) is the Canadian historians' link, unread.
strands.works: 'What Is Past Is Prologue' (1997); 'Fashionable Nonsense or Professional Rebirth' (2001); 'Archives, Records, and Power' (2002); Refiguring the Archive (2002)

gu_jiegang.date_label: Letters on the layering of ancient historical traditions (1923) · Gushibian volume1 and autobiographical preface (1926) · Edition of Cui Dongbi/Cui Shu’s writings (1936) · The Chinese Nation Is One (1939) · Index of the Shangshu (1962)
gu_jiegang.description: A Chinese historian, philologist and folklorist who examined the accumulated layers of ancient historical traditions rather than treating transmitted narratives as transparent records. Richter describes both his 1923 critique of unitary origins and his recovery of earlier Chinese source criticism. The relation between that scepticism and his 1939 national-unity thesis remains contested: Jenco reads an open political community, whereas Kim and Zheng stress homogenizing limits. Dirlik reports contemporary Marxist objections to restricting criticism to documents; Lu questions aspects of Gu’s source chronology.
gu_jiegang.representative_figures_and_works: Stratification correspondence (1923); editor, Gushibian (from 1926); autobiographical preface (1926; Arthur W.Hummel’s English translation 1931); edition of Cui Dongbi/Cui Shu (1936); The Chinese Nation Is One (1939); Shangshu index (1962).
gu_jiegang.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-24: Richter’s complete 1982 obituary and the opening/references of her separate China Quarterly article; PKU biography; Lu’s Chinese/English abstracts; Jenco’s publisher abstract; Kim’s English abstract; Zheng’s Gu discussion; Dirlik’s selected epilogue passages. Gu’s original works remain unread. Chinese intellectual and philological traditions are not treated as mere imports of European methods. The 1926 series start is supported by Richter’s references; her obituary’s 1927 date is retained here as a source discrepancy, not silently harmonized. Jenco’s and Kim’s divergent interpretations remain attributed.

history_of_emotions.label: History of emotions
history_of_emotions.date_label: Earlier programme 1941 · Reddy’s framework 2001 · Rosenwein’s essay 2002 and book 2006 · methods discussion 2010
history_of_emotions.description: Emotions become objects and resources of historical inquiry: their valuations, expression and relation to action require evidence rather than an assumption of timeless feeling. Reddy’s emotives and emotional regimes connect expression, experience and enforced norms. Rosenwein’s emotional communities emphasize overlapping groups and movement between them. Their disagreement about political scale remains visible. Earlier programmes, including Febvre’s 1941 call, are resources to examine critically; the selected later works neither found nor delimit the whole field.
history_of_emotions.representative_figures_and_works: Earlier programme: Lucien Febvre, “La sensibilité et l’histoire” (1941; reprinted in Combats pour l’histoire, 1953). Selected frameworks: William M. Reddy, The Navigation of Feeling: A Framework for the History of Emotions (2001); Barbara H. Rosenwein, “Worrying about Emotions in History” (2002), Emotional Communities in the Early Middle Ages (2006; paperback 2007). Named interlocutor: Norbert Elias, The Civilizing Process (1939), through Rosenwein’s 2002 criticism. Retrospective discussion: Jan Plamper’s interview with Reddy, Rosenwein and Peter Stearns (2010); only the specified Reddy/Rosenwein answers were read here.
history_of_emotions.scope_note: A bounded field entry distinguishing selected approaches, not a unified school or a census of its practitioners. Period 4 places the selected 2001–2010 interventions for teaching; the 1941 programme is an earlier root, not a founding date. Primary reading: Reddy’s 2001 publisher preface ix–xiii; Rosenwein’s 2002 essay, 821–822, 826–828 and 842–845; selected own answers in Plamper’s 2010 interview, Reddy 237–243 and Rosenwein 255–256. Existing Febvre reading qualifications remain. Rosenwein’s 2006 book is bibliographically checked but unread. The entry keeps political norms, overlapping communities and the interpretation of representations distinct. Later emotional-practice approaches, the full Stearns emotionology programme, sensory history and Sara Ahmed’s related affect inquiry require separate research; they are not silently equated with these frameworks. Review coverage retains the ordinary 2000 baseline; the selected 2001–2010 interventions do not extend it. No comprehensive review of later or non-European traditions is asserted. Dissertation counts guided discovery only and establish no relationship, agreement or field origin.

representative_people.context: Emotives connect expression with the attempt to shape or explore feeling; regimes concern enforced norms. His 2010 answers allow plural regimes rather than requiring one nation-wide style.
representative_people.works: The Navigation of Feeling (2001), preface; answers in Plamper’s interview (2010), 237–243

representative_people.context: Proposes overlapping emotional communities and challenges a single trajectory toward emotional restraint. Her objection to the regime/refuge model remains distinct from Reddy’s plural-regime qualification.
representative_people.works: “Worrying about Emotions in History” (2002); Emotional Communities in the Early Middle Ages (2006; paperback 2007); answers in Plamper’s interview (2010)

representative_people.context: The 1941 programme is an earlier call for historical inquiry into collective feelings. Rosenwein revisits its assumptions as well as its importance; this is not a claim that he founded all emotions history.
representative_people.works: “La sensibilité et l’histoire” (1941); reprinted in Combats pour l’histoire (1953)

representative_people.context: The Civilizing Process is a named interlocutor in Rosenwein’s criticism of progressive emotional restraint; inclusion records a disputed interpretation, not membership in a unified emotions school.
representative_people.works: The Civilizing Process (1939), as discussed critically by Rosenwein (2002), 826–827

representative_people.context: Distinguishes emotional standards from emotional experience while investigating relations between them. Own2010answer262insists cultural prescription does not necessarily describe experience; joint earlier concept credit to Carol Z.Stearns retained.
representative_people.works: “Emotionology” (with Carol Z. Stearns) (1985); Anger (Carol Zisowitz Stearns and Peter N. Stearns) (1986); American Cool (1994).

representative_people.context: Makes changing collective fears and searches for security objects of historical inquiry. Paillard’s substantive introduction and Delumeau’s1991research inset support this; no claim that all fear has one unchanging religious cause.
representative_people.works: Le Christianisme va-t-il mourir ? (1977); La Peur en Occident (1978); Le Péché et la Peur (1983).

representative_people.context: Examines fear as an embodied and socially patterned practice whose expression can transform feeling.
representative_people.works: Dismembering the Male (1996); An Intimate History of Killing (1999); Fear: A Cultural History (2005; 2006 paperback distinct).

strands.title: Earlier programmes and their assumptions
strands.focus: Febvre’s call makes feelings part of historical explanation. Rosenwein’s retrospective also questions his separation of emotional and intellectual life; an earlier resource need not supply the later method unchanged.
strands.works: Febvre (1941); Rosenwein (2002), 821–822

strands.title: Emotives and enforced emotional norms
strands.focus: Reddy treats speaking about feeling as an intervention that may alter experience or expose an unexpected response. Regimes concern sanctions and conformity as well as shared styles; his 2010 account permits several within a wider polity.
strands.works: The Navigation of Feeling (2001), preface ix–xiii; Reddy in Plamper (2010), 240–243

strands.title: Communities, movement and source interpretation
strands.focus: Rosenwein studies emotional valuations and expected expressions across overlapping social groups. Movement between settings matters. Her Gregory of Tours example examines an author’s emotional representation without assuming the narrated conversation actually occurred.
strands.works: “Worrying about Emotions in History” (2002), 842–845; Emotional Communities in the Early Middle Ages (2006), metadata only

strands.title: Against one progressive-restraint narrative
strands.focus: Rosenwein challenges an Elias-associated account that makes medieval emotion unrestrained and modernity controlled. Her alternative follows changing communities and relations between them; the critique does not make historical variation itself disappear.

strands.title: Regimes and communities: a disagreement with qualifications
strands.focus: Rosenwein objects to a dominant regime/refuge binary; Reddy explicitly accepts plural regimes and emphasizes enforceable norms. These positions partly overlap but are not interchangeable, and neither is an editorially settled theory.
strands.works: Answers in Plamper’s interview (2010): Reddy 243; Rosenwein 255–256

drew_gilpin_faust.label: Drew Gilpin Faust
drew_gilpin_faust.date_label: A Sacred Circle (1977) · Mothers of Invention (1996) · This Republic of Suffering (2008)
drew_gilpin_faust.description: Historian of the American South whose writing links slavery,women’s wartime choices and the cultural consequences of mass death. Faust’s interview with Jim Leach explains how slaveholders’ records can reveal enslaved family ties and how Confederate women’s exhaustion changed their relation to war. Her biographical work uses an individual life to investigate social structures while preserving the distinction between understanding and endorsement.
drew_gilpin_faust.representative_figures_and_works: A Sacred Circle (1977); Mothers of Invention (1996); This Republic of Suffering (2008).
drew_gilpin_faust.scope_note: Selected substantive passages and bibliographic records only; complete monographs not read. Citation counts selected the research queue; they do not prove importance or influence. Life status is separately documented in this local person folder; no lifespan or career interval is inferred.

community_engaged_indigenous.label: Community-engaged and Indigenous-led historical research
community_engaged_indigenous.date_label: Roots: Yukon life histories 1974–90 · THOA by 1984 · Stó:lō field school 1998 · Smith 1999 · Wheeler 2005/2010 · TCPS 2 ch. 9 2010 · TRC 2015 · Shekon Neechie 2018 · CHA statement and open letter 2021 · reviewed through 2022
community_engaged_indigenous.description: Historical research done with, by or under the direction of Indigenous communities, defined by how it is done. Winona Wheeler asks historians to treat Indigenous oral history 'as source and method': elders 'are not official documents; they are human beings and teachers', and 'one develops reciprocal relationships with them' (2010). Margaret Kovach locates method in relationship: 'it is not the method, per se' but its congruence 'with an Indigenous worldview' (2010). The Stó:lō field school's teachers wrote that historians 'could no longer in good conscience claim to be writing Aboriginal history when they were not speaking with Aboriginal people'; community staff set the questions and papers return to the Stó:lō archives (2009). Lianne Leddy, researching her own Serpent River First Nation, found university ethics review 'culturally inappropriate' (2010). Mary Jane Logan McCallum treats Indian Affairs archives as sites of possibility and contestation for Indigenous historians (2018). Shekon Neechie (2018) is 'entirely Indigenous conceived, created, and controlled'.
community_engaged_indigenous.representative_figures_and_works: Sidney, Smith, Ned and Cruikshank, Life Lived Like a Story (1990); THOA and Rivera Cusicanqui (1987); Mamani Condori, Taraqu (1991); Rita and Jackie Huggins, Auntie Rita (1994); Angela Cavender Wilson, AIQ 20:1 (1996); the Stó:lō ethnohistory field school (1998–; Carlson, McHalsie, Schaepe, David Smith, Lutz) and Historical Atlas (2001); Smith, Decolonizing Methodologies (1999; 2012; 2021); Wheeler (2005; 2010); Shawn Wilson (2008); Kovach (2009; 2010); Leddy (2010); Macdougall (2010; 2018); Innes (2013; 2018); McCallum (2014; 2018); Carlson, Lutz, Schaepe and McHalsie, eds., Towards a New Ethnohistory (2018); Shekon Neechie (2018–).
community_engaged_indigenous.scope_note: A grouping created in revision 1.201 by splitting `indigenous`: it gathers practice defined by method (community direction, relationships, protocols, return of results), not by date or by the researcher's identity. Defined from practitioners' own statements, read in full: Wheeler 2010; Kovach 2010; Carlson, Lutz and Schaepe 2009; Leddy 2010; Macdougall 2010 (introduction) and 2018; McCallum 2018; Innes 2018; the Shekon Neechie launch (2018) and open letter (2021); McClellan and Gmelch (1992) on the Yukon collaboration; TCPS 2 chapter 9 (2022 text); SSHRC 2015 and current guidelines; the CHA statement (2021). Known through descriptions or named readers only: Kovach 2009, Shawn Wilson 2008, Innes 2013, McCallum 2014 (Williams 2016), Towards a New Ethnohistory 2018, Smith 2012/2021. Unread: Life Lived Like a Story itself, the Stó:lō–Coast Salish Historical Atlas, Auntie Rita, Native Historians Write Back, Indigenizing the Academy; OCAP's founding documents (year not sourced). Indigenous-authored critique stays in `indigenous`; settler scholarship about Indigenous peoples in `ethnohistory` and `native_newcomer`; works may belong to two. Collaboration does not erase different positions; community and university participants are credited separately. History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23: in Canadian History PhDs the community-engaged monographs are cited more than general methods texts (Macdougall 2010: 35 dissertations; McCallum 2014: 26; Life Lived: 25; Innes 2013: 13; Kovach 2009: 12; Shawn Wilson 2008: 11); context only. Reviewed through 2022: nothing read dates a 2023–24 development.

strands.title: Cree oral history as source and method
strands.focus: Wheeler writes as a Cree historian taught by Stan Cuthand, Ahenakew's protégé. She treats oral history 'as source and method': knowledge keepers establish their sources within their narratives, 'sort of like a "traditional footnote"', and the historian's task is 'to apply the teachings' as well as to study them (2010). Her 1998 critique of 'Indian–White relations' history sits on `native_newcomer`.
strands.works: Cree Intellectual Traditions in History (2010); The Othering of Indigenous History (1998)

strands.title: Relational research methodologies
strands.focus: Indigenous methodologists outside history define method as relationship. Shawn Wilson (Opaskwayak Cree): research is 'the ceremony of maintaining accountability to these relationships' (2008, publisher). Kovach: the conversational method is 'relational at its core'; a decolonizing perspective remains necessary but 'centres the settler discourse' and is 'not the epistemological centre' of an Indigenous methodology (2010). Smith's 1999 agenda is their shared reference. Macdougall (2018) notes that the method texts available to teachers are First Nations-specific.
strands.works: Decolonizing Methodologies (1999; 2012; 2021); Research Is Ceremony (2008); Indigenous Methodologies (2009); Conversational Method (2010)

strands.title: Kinship, community and the archive
strands.focus: Historians who read documentary records through their communities' concepts and relationships. Macdougall reconstructed community history from HBC, mission and scrip records and read them through wahkootowin, a Cree worldview of relatedness in her framing and a concept she credits to Métis Elder Maria Campbell, against a historiography 'preoccupied with race at the expense of culture' (2010). Innes points to Cowessess First Nation's own treaty-land research as the count of the 1880s starvation deaths that historians had not made (2018). McCallum describes reading Indian Affairs records about her own community and interpreting them with others (2018).
strands.works: One of the Family (2010); Elder Brother and the Law of the People (2013); 'Historians and Indigenous Genocide in Saskatchewan' (2018); 'Indigenous People, Archives and History' (2018)

strands.title: Research ethics and Indigenous governance of research
strands.focus: TCPS 2's chapter 9 (2010) opens by acknowledging that research 'has been defined and carried out primarily by non-Indigenous researchers'. It requires community engagement, including for 'interpretation of research results that will refer to Indigenous … history', exempts historical research on public records while asking for 'culturally informed advice', and cites OCAP from the First Nations Regional Longitudinal Health Survey (2022 text). SSHRC's 2015 guidelines make 'co-creation of knowledge' essential. The TRC (2015) asked SSHRC, archives and commemoration bodies to act (Calls 65, 70, 77–79). Leddy's 2010 critique shows how review looked from inside a community.
strands.works: TCPS 2, ch. 9 (2010); SSHRC guidelines (2015); TRC Calls to Action (2015); Leddy (2010)

strands.title: Indigenous historians' own institutions
strands.focus: Shekon Neechie (21 June 2018) describes itself as 'entirely Indigenous conceived, created, and controlled'; it counts community-trained and self-taught historians as historians and gives peer feedback from Indigenous historians. Its board (Macdougall, McCallum, Anderson, Corbiere, Hill, Wheeler, Innes) published an open letter supporting the CHA Council's 2021 genocide statement (13 August 2021).
strands.works: Shekon Neechie (2018–); open letter (2021)

strands.title: Collaborative Yukon life narratives
strands.focus: Three elders and an anthropologist collaborate; life interviewing and transmitted traditions remain distinct practices. The families asked for the recording in 1974; the narrators chose to tell their lives through stories, songs and oratory, and Cruikshank selected and ordered the texts (McClellan 1992). See the packaged entry Life Lived Like a Story.
strands.works: Life Lived Like a Story (1990)

strands.title: Narratives, place and institutional interpretation
strands.focus: Cruikshank’s 1993 discussion contrasts community uses of tradition with institutional demands. Her account of Gitksan and Wet’suwet’en testimony questions treating performed histories only as containers of facts.
strands.works: Claiming Legitimacy (1993), selected sections

strands.title: Distinct voices in collaborative history
strands.focus: Rita and Jackie Huggins’s life-history collaboration and their coauthored place article with Jacobs retain different author positions. Heiss’s 1998 review foregrounds oral testimony and historical authority.
strands.works: Auntie Rita (1994); Kooramindanjie (1995); Heiss on Sister Girl (1998)

strands.title: Stó:lō community–university historical practice
strands.focus: Community priorities, cultural teaching, archives and university instruction contribute different resources. Planning in 1997 preceded the first class in 1998; elders, hosts and students also participated. The teachers call it a 'new ethnohistory': 'collaborative with the people we are trying to understand', with community staff and members setting topics 'beneficial to the community', and papers and interviews going to the Stó:lō archives to 'help build capacity' (Carlson, Lutz and Schaepe 2009, pp. 3–5). The 2018 volume describes community-engaged scholarship that 'invites members of the Indigenous community themselves to identify the research questions' (publisher).
strands.works: Field-school planning (1997); first class (1998); later accounts (2009, 2011, 2016); Historical Atlas (2001); Towards a New Ethnohistory (2018)

strands.title: Community and academic relationships at Serpent River
strands.focus: Family knowledge, scholarly dialogue and mentorship shape historical practice; the roles remain distinct. Leddy, a member of the Serpent River First Nation, found the university ethics process 'culturally inappropriate': it defines Aboriginal participants as a 'vulnerable group', distancing an Aboriginal researcher from her own community. 'We have our own methodologies and ethical practices' (2010, pp. 3, 13–15).
strands.works: Interviewing Nookomis and Other Reflections (2010)
strands.citation_note: Leddy cites Wheeler (2005), Smith (1999, quoted at pp. 140 and 191), Wilson (1996 and 1998), Innes (2009) and Cruikshank with the three Yukon elders (1991 printing), among others. Citation is documented engagement, not proof of sole influence or full reading of those cited works.
